AutoStructor_A_Generative_AI-Based_Frame.text: AutoStructor: A Generative AI-Based Framework for Automated Program Repair with Deep Learning-Guided Fault Localization Hasen ¨Ozayt¨urk Department of Computer Engineering Istanbul Technical University Istanbul, T ¨urkiye ozayturk22@itu.edu.tr Feza Buzluca Department of Computer Engineering Istanbul Technical University Istanbul, T ¨urkiye buzluca@itu.edu.tr Abstract—Current automated program repair (APR) ap- proaches still suffer from two critical limitations: inaccurate fault localization and ineffective patch generation. This paper presents a novel hybrid framework, AutoStructor, that pro- poses a Quality-Aware Graph-Based Machine Learning Fault Localization (GBMFL) and a Large Language Model (LLM)- based patch generation technique to effectively address these challenges. Our key innovation lies in integrating 21 com- prehensive code quality metrics and sophisticated multi-modal attention mechanisms, including quality-aware, graph-aware, sparse, and multiscale attention into the GBMFL architecture, coupled with intelligent test failure analysis for superior code understanding and patch generation. AutoStructor bridges the gap between fault localization and patch generation through an end-to-end pipeline that leverages generative AI for intelligent patch synthesis. We evaluate our approach on the Defects4J benchmark, demonstrating signiﬁcant improvements in fault localization accuracy (81.9% Top-1, 93.4% Top-3) with a Mean First Rank of 1.13, and successful patch generation for 48 out of 61 active Lang project bugs. Notably, our structured test analysis approach enables cost-effective deployment using compact LLMs, achieving effective repair . Keywords—automated program repair, graph-based fault lo- calization, multi-modal attention, test failure analysis, software quality metrics I. I NTRODUCTION Software bugs impose signiﬁcant costs on development teams and end users. Traditional debugging approaches rely heavily on manual inspection, making the process time- consuming and error-prone. Automated Program Repair (APR) has emerged as a promising solution; however, cur- rent approaches face fundamental limitations that hinder its widespread adoption. Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) techniques rely primarily on code coverage information while failing to cap- ture underlying code quality characteristics that correlate with fault-proneness. Existing neural fault localization approaches focus on structural dependencies while neglecting the multi- dimensional nature of code quality. Most critically, existing APR approaches treat fault localization and patch generation as separate, loosely coupled phases, resulting in suboptimal results as patch generation fails to leverage the rich contextual information gathered during localization. This paper makes the following key contributions to ad- dress these gaps: • Quality-Aware GBMFL Framework with Neural Ar- chitecture: We present a novel approach that integrates comprehensive code quality metrics into Graph-Based Machine Learning Fault Localization. Our quality- aware framework incorporates 21 quality metrics across theoretically-grounded categories, including complexity, coupling, cohesion and testability. • Multi-Modal Attention Mechanisms for Advanced Code Understanding : We introduce four specialized attention mechanisms designed speciﬁcally for code analysis: (a) Quality-aware attention with relative posi- tioning and adaptive temperature scaling for sequence understanding, (b) Graph-aware attention that explic- itly models program structure through edge types and connectivity patterns, (c) Sparse attention for computa- tional efﬁciency while maintaining performance through importance-based token selection, and (d) Multi-scale attention for hierarchical feature extraction at different granularities. • Intelligent Failed Test Analysis for APR : We intro- duce LLM-based test failure explanation that system- atically bridges fault localization and patch generation by extracting structured insights from test failures, stack traces, and assertion errors to guide repair synthesis. • End-to-End LLM-Guided APR Pipeline : We develop a comprehensi ve framework that seamlessly integrates deep learning fault localization with generative AI patch generation. • Experimental Evaluation and Analysis : We provide an extensive evaluation on the Defects4J benchmark with a detailed analysis of both fault localization performance and repair success. II. R ELA TED WORK A. Fault Localization Techniques Recent advances have demonstrated remarkable perfor- mance improvements through the integration of deep learn- ing. by integrating spectrum-based, mutation-based, complexity- based, and textual-similarity features, localizing over 50 more faults within Top-1 compared to traditional approaches [1]. GRACE introduced graph neural networks to fault localiza- tion, achieving 195 bug localizations within the Top-1 cate- gory, compared to 166 for the best baseline [2]. DEEPRL4FL treated fault localization as image pattern recognition, achiev- ing 173.1% to 491.7% improvement over statement-level baselines [3]. Traditional SBFL techniques, such as Tarantula [4] and Ochiai [5], have established foundational approaches but suffer from limited precision in complex scenarios. The recent work by Raﬁ et al. [6] introduces Dependency- Enhanced Coverage Graph (DepGraph) that integrates inter- procedural call graph information with traditional AST-based representations, achieving 20% improvement in Top-1 accu- racy over GRACE while reducing computational overhead by 70%. This work demonstrates the importance of incorporat- ing method-level call dependencies for more accurate fault localization. However, existing approaches face critical limitations. Traditional SBFL methods suffer from limited precision in complex fault scenarios. Neural approaches typically focus on single-dimensional features while neglecting the multi- dimensional nature of code quality metrics that correlate strongly with fault-proneness. B. Automated Program Repair The ﬁeld has evolved through several generations, with recent LLM-based approaches showing remarkable capabil- ities. Traditional template-based repair approaches, such as PAR [7], rely on predeﬁned ﬁx templates but are limited by template coverage. Neural program repair approaches like SequenceR employ neural machine translation techniques [8], while CURE combines neural translation with programming language models, ﬁxing 62 bugs on Defects4J [9]. Recent LLM-based advances have revolutionized auto- mated program repair. ThinkRepair leverages Chain-of- Thought prompting for self-directed repair, ﬁxing 98 bugs on Defects4J V1.2 with 27%-344.4% improvement over baselines [10]. LLMAO introduces test-free fault localization using bidirectional adapter layers on frozen LLMs, achieving 2.3%-54.4% Top-1 improvement [11]. Despite these advances, most existing approaches treat fault localization and patch generation as separate phases. This separation often leads to suboptimal results, as patch generation strategies fail to leverage the rich contextual information gathered during fault localization. C. Code Quality Metrics and Fault Prediction The relationship between code quality metrics and fault- proneness has been extensively studied. McCabe established cyclomatic complexity with threshold categories: 1-10 (sim- ple), 11-20 (moderate), 21-50 (complex), and above 50 (very complex) [12]. The Chidamber-Kemerer (CK) metrics suite provides comprehensive object-oriented measurement [13], with Basili et al. validating that CK metrics signiﬁcantly correlate with fault-proneness [14]. Recent empirical studies demonstrate that methods with cyclomatic complexity greater than 10 exhibit a 3.2 times higher fault probability, while cognitive complexity above 15 shows a 4.1 times higher fault rate. Learning-based approaches have shown that design quality metrics can be effectively used for fault detection in identifying error-prone code elements [15]. Our work is the ﬁrst to systematically integrate these comprehensive quality dimensions into Graph- Based Machine Learning Fault Localization architectures. III. A UTO STRUCTOR FRAMEWORK A. System Architecture Overview AutoStructor presents a comprehensive end-to-end pipeline that seamlessly integrates Quality-Aware Graph-Based Ma- chine Learning Fault Localization with Large Language Model-based patch generation. The framework architecture comprises three primary modules: Fault Localization, Test Explainer, and Patch Generation. These modules work in a coordinated manner to ensure accurate fault identiﬁcation and efﬁcient patch synthesis. This end-to-end interaction is illustrated in Figure 1. B. End-to-End Repair Process AutoStructor implements a four-phase repair process: Phase 1: Project Setup and Environment Initialization : The framework checks out the target buggy version from repository, creates isolated workspace environments, and es- tablishes proper compilation and testing environments. Phase 2: Quality-Aware Fault Localization : Our Fault Localization Module adapts the DepGraph architecture from [6] as the foundation and enhances it with our novel quality- aware extensions. We integrate 21 quality metrics across complexity, design, code quality, and maintainability dimen- sions into the baseline graph structure. The module employs a hybrid attention mechanism incorporating four specialized at- tention types: quality-aware, graph-aware, sparse, and multi- scale attention for superior code understanding and fault ranking. Phase 3: Test Analysis and Context Generation : The Test Explainer Module analyzes failing test cases to extract meaningful insights about fault characteristics and expected behavior using lightweight LLM analysis to interpret test failure messages, stack traces, and assertion failures. Phase 4: Iterative Patch Generation and Validation: The Patch Generator Module systematically attempts repair on ranked suspicious methods through multiple iterations, apply- ing advanced prompt engineering, and validating generated patches through automated test execution. While our framework adapts the DepGraph architecture [6] as the foundational fault localization component, our key innovations include: Integration of 21 comprehensive quality metrics beyond traditional coverage-based features, hybrid multi-modal attention mechanisms speciﬁcally designed for quality-aware code analysis and intelligent test failure expla- nation that bridges fault localization with patch generation through structured LLM analysis. C. Fault Localization Module 1) Quality Metrics Framework Our quality-aware GBMFL framework incorporates 21 carefully selected quality metrics organized into four theoretically-grounded categories: Complexity Metrics capture the intrinsic difﬁculty of understanding and maintaining code segments. Cyclomatic and cognitive complexity measure code understanding difﬁ- culty, while nesting depth, method length, parameter count, and return complexity assess structural complexity aspects, comprising 6 metrics in total. Design Quality Metrics assess adherence to fundamental software engineering principles. The Single Responsibility Principle (SRP) score quantiﬁes the extent to which a method focuses on a single concern through domain-speciﬁc re- sponsibility analysis. Coupling metrics quantify inter-module dependencies through analysis of import statements, object instantiations, and method call patterns. Additional metrics include cohesion score, abstraction level, and design pattern usage detection, totaling 6 metrics. Code Quality Metrics assess surface-level characteristics that impact readability and maintainability. Naming quality evaluation incorporates multiple heuristics including length appropriateness, camelCase convention adherence, semantic meaningfulness, and appropriate verb usage for behavioral methods. This category also includes comment ratio, code smells detection, duplication analysis, and magic numbers identiﬁcation, encompassing 5 metrics. Maintainability Metrics predict long-term code evolution costs through assessment of testability, reusability, and error handling quality. Testability evaluation combines multiple factors including method visibility, parameter complexity, static dependency minimization, and correlation with single responsibility adherence. This category encompasses read- ability score, testability score, reusability score, and error handling quality assessment, consisting of 4 metrics. Table I provides the complete speciﬁcation of our 21 quality metrics organized by category. More detailed speciﬁcations and thresholds for all 21 quality metrics are available in our implementation repository [16]. 2) Multi-Modal Attention Mechanisms We introduce four specialized attention mechanisms de- signed speciﬁcally for code analysis: Quality-Aware Attention with Relative Positioning ad- dresses the limitation of traditional attention mechanisms through relative positional encodings, enabling the model to understand sequential relationships between code elements with adaptive temperature scaling for improved convergence. Graph-Aware Attention for Structural Understanding ex- plicitly models program structure through edge types and connectivity patterns. This mechanism incorporates edge type embeddings for different relationship types (control ﬂow, data ﬂow, call dependencies) and implements structure encoding through neighborhood aggregation. Sparse Attention for Computational Efﬁciency reduces computational complexity while maintaining performance through importance-based token selection. Our implemen- tation employs a learned importance scoring network that evaluates pairwise relationships between code elements. captures features at different granularities, enabling both local and global pattern recognition through multiple attention heads operating at different scales with scale-speciﬁc pro- jections and learnable fusion weights. We enhance the baseline DepGraph suspicion scores by integrating 21 code quality metrics through a neural gated fusion mechanism, enabling dynamic weighting based on method characteristics and quality patterns. Despite the integration of quality metrics and multi-modal attention mechanisms, our approach maintains computational efﬁciency comparable to the baseline DepGraph architecture through optimized metric computation and sparse attention mechanisms. D. Test Explainer Module: Failed Test Analysis The Test Analysis Module enhances the patch generation process by extracting structured explanations from failing test cases. Using large language model analysis, this component processes test failure outputs, stack traces, and assertion fail- ures to generate concise contextual descriptions that capture what went wrong and why the test failed. Our approach employs structured prompting to guide the large language model in extracting essential test semantics and failure characteristics. The analysis focuses on three key aspects: the functionality being validated by the test, the type of bug suggested by the failure pattern, and the expected correct behavior. Rather than having the patch generation process deal solely with error messages or test source code alone, this approach provides meaningful context to the patch generator by explaining what the test means in a few key sentences. The structured prompting approach effectively extracts test semantics and failure characteristics. These explanations provide additional context to the patch generator and aim to improve repair quality. E. Patch Generator Module The LLM-based patch generation module transforms iden- tiﬁed suspicious code regions into concrete repair actions through sophisticated integration with modern generative AI capabilities. Suspicious method ranking and selection strategy leverages fault localization scores to prioritize patch generation efforts on the most promising candidates. The selection process considers not only suspicion scores but also practical factors such as method complexity, availability of source code, and likelihood of successful patch application. Test-aware context generation leverages the structured test failure explanations from the Test Analysis Module to provide LLMs with focused contextual understanding about intended behavior and fault characteristics. This approach en- ables more targeted patch generation by informing the model about the correct functionality that failing tests validate. Iterative repair process executes patch generation system- atically for each suspicious method, validating candidates through automated test execution before proceeding to the next method. The framework employs multi-candidate gen- eration, producing alternative patch formulations when initial attempts fail to pass test validation. Prompt engineering for effective patch generation imple- ments sophisticated strategies for providing large language models with appropriate context for patch generation, incor- porating both source code analysis and test failure insights. Our prompts carefully balance speciﬁcity with generality, providing sufﬁcient context about fault characteristics while avoiding overly constraining the solution space. IV . E XPERIMENTAL EV ALUA TION A. Experimental Setup Dataset and Benchmark Selection : We conduct our pri- mary evaluation on the Defects4J benchmark [17], focusing on the Lang project which contains 65 bugs with well- documented fault locations and comprehensive test suites. We exclude deprecated bugs (Lang-2, Lang-18, Lang-25, and Lang-48), resulting in 61 active bugs for comprehensive analysis. Baseline Comparisons : We compare our quality-aware GBMFL approach against the baseline proposed in [6], as the GBMFL baseline already surpasses traditional SBFL methods and neural fault localization models. Evaluation Metrics : We employ standard fault local- ization metrics including Top-N accuracy, representing the percentage of bugs where the faulty method appears in the top N ranked results, and Mean First Rank (MFR), representing the average rank of the ﬁrst correctly identiﬁed faulty method. LLM Implementation Details : Our framework employs separate GPT-4o Mini instances for test failure analysis and patch generation components to ensure proper isolation. Each bug repair session initializes fresh LLM contexts excluding conversation history to prevent information leakage between different repair attempts. This design ensures that each patch generation is based solely on the current bug’s context and fault localization results, maintaining experimental integrity across all evaluations. B. Fault Localization Results Our quality-aware GBMFL approach demonstrates signiﬁ- cant improvements in fault localization accuracy compared to baseline approaches. We re-implement and evaluate the base- line DepGraph method [6] in our experimental environment to ensure fair comparison under identical conditions. Table II presents a progressive evaluation on the Defects4J Lang project, demonstrating the cumulative effectiveness of our quality-aware enhancements. Starting from baseline DepGraph [6], we incrementally add multi-modal attention, quality metrics, and optimization to achieve our ﬁnal Au- toStructor conﬁguration. C ONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK This paper presents AutoStructor, a novel framework that successfully addresses fundamental limitations in automated program repair by integrating Quality-Aware Graph-Based Machine Learning Fault Localization with Large Language Model-based patch generation. Our approach introduces hy- brid multi-modal attention mechanisms, integration of 21 design quality metrics into fault localization, and intelligent failed test explanation bridging fault localization with LLM- based patch generation. These innovations achieve 81.9% Top-1 fault localization accuracy, Mean First Rank of 1.13, and successful repair of 48 out of 61 Lang project bugs at $0.03 total cost, representing a 50% improvement over the best existing LLM-based APR tool while maintaining remarkable cost-effectiveness through compact models. While our evaluation demonstrates strong performance on the Defects4J Lang project, several promising research directions emerge for future work. Scaling our approach to the full Defects4J benchmark and real-world datasets like SWE-Bench would support broader validation across programming paradigms and bug complexity levels. Extend- ing our quality-aware fault localization framework to multi- language environments entails developing language-agnostic dependency representations and adapting quality metrics to language-speciﬁc characteristics. Additionally, integrating dynamic metric weighting and fault localization conﬁdence into patch generation, as well as exploring security-focused repair, represent compelling paths forward. CVE2AP Automated Generation of PDDL-Enco.text: CVE2AP: Automated Generation of PDDL-Encoded Attack Paths via Large Language Models Lin Cui, Vincenzo Scotti, Raffaela Mirandola †KASTEL,Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, Karlsruhe, Germany lin.cui@kit.edu,vincenzo.scotti@kit.edu,raffaela.mirandola@kit.edu Abstract—Attack Path (AP) modeling is fundamental to cyber- security analysis, where the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) has been widely adopted to encode APs into formal and machine-verifiable representations for automated reasoning about vulnerability exploitation, attack progression, and their potential impacts. However, existing AP modeling approaches largely rely on expert-driven manual construction, limiting their scalability and ability to keep pace with rapidly evolving cyber threats. Large lan- guage models (LLMs) are promising candidates, as their extensive pre-trained knowledge and reasoning capabilities enable them to interpret and transform threat intelligence into formal representa- tions. In this paper, we propose CVE2AP, an LLM-based approach for automatically generating PDDL-encoded attack paths from natural language CVE (Common Vulnerability Exposure) descrip- tions. CVE2AP leverages structured prompting and incorporates an error-feedback mechanism that iteratively refines the generated paths using planner-reported syntactic and solvability errors. We conduct a systematic empirical evaluation across multiple LLMs and generation configurations, assessing generation quality across syntactic, solvability and semantic dimensions, together with token consumption and generation time. The results demonstrate that CVE2AP effectively generates high-quality PDDL-encoded attack paths, achieving up to 86.9% syntax correctness, 78.6% solvability, and 93.1% semantic correctness under LLM-as-expert evaluation, while GPT-5.5 offers the best quality-cost trade-off and error feedback yields the most consistent quality improvement. Index Terms—Automated Generation, Attack Path, PDDL, Semantic Quality I. INTRODUCTION Formal and machine-verifiable Attack Path (AP) models provide foundation for cybersecurity analysis by enabling auto- mated reasoning about vulnerability exploitation, attack progres- sion, and their potential impacts [1]. To support such reasoning, the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) [2], origi- nally designed for AI planning, has been adapted for represent- ing attack paths [3]–[9]. By explicitly specifying the required preconditions and effects of every action, PDDL naturally mod- els the causal progression of an attack from the initial vulnera- bility exposure to the resulting security impact. However, driven by the continuous disclosure of new vulnerabilities, the emer- gence of sophisticated attack techniques, and the rapid accumu- lation of cyber threat intelligence, the cyber threat landscape is evolving at an unprecedented pace. This situation require that attack paths must be continuously and rapidly updated to reflect newly feasible attack strategies and changing attack conditions. This work was supported by funding from the Helmholtz Association (HGF), topic 46.23 Engineering Secure Systems (KASTEL) and from the HGF pilot program Core Informatics at KIT (KiKIT) As a result, manually constructing and maintaining attack paths can not keep pace with this rapid evolution. It is of urgent need to automate the generation of PDDL-encoded attack paths. Existing PDDL-based attack path modeling approaches [3], [4], [6]–[8] largely rely on domain experts to manually construct PDDL-encoded attack paths. Creating such planner-ready representations requires translating heterogeneous incomplete, and often implicit cyber threat intelligence into formal PDDL models, demanding expertise in both cybersecurity and AI planning. Consequently, developing and maintaining such models is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. In parallel, recent studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of LLMs in automatically generating general-purpose PDDL domains from natural language inputs [10]–[14]. While these methods substantially reduce the manual effort of planning domain construction, their applicability of PDDL-encoded attack path generation remains largely unexplored. Unlike general planning domains, PDDL-encoded attack paths must satisfy not only syntax correctness and planning solvability, but also cybersecurity-specific semantic requirements including threat model compliance, exploitation mechanism fidelity, attack stage completeness. These observations raise a fundamental research challenge:how can PDDL-encoded attack paths be automati- cally generated while satisfying syntactic correctness, planning solvability, and cybersecurity-specific semantic requirements? In this paper, we address this challenge by proposing CVE2AP, an LLM-based approach for automatically generating PDDL-encoded attack paths from CVE descriptions. CVE2AP combines structured prompting with error-feedback mechanism that iteratively refines generated results using planner-reported syntax and solvability errors. We further conduct a systematic empirical study to evaluate the effectiveness as well as token and time costs of CVE2AP across mutiple LLMs and generation configurations. In summary, the main contributions of this paper are: • We propose CVE2AP, an LLM-based approach for automatically generating PDDL-encoded attack paths from natural language CVE descriptions while satisfying both planning surface-level requirements and cybersecurity- specific semantic requirements. • We investigate generation performance across multiple LLMs and generation configurations, evaluating generation quality using the S3Eval framework [15] from syntactic, solvability, and semantic perspectives, together with token consumption and generation time. arXiv:2610.03383v1 [cs.AI] 2 Oct 2026

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the necessary background. Section III presents the proposed CVE2AP approach. Section IV describes the experimental setup and analyzes the results. Section V discusses related work. Section VI concludes the paper and outlines future research directions. II. BACKGROUND This section presents the problem statement (Section II-A) and the formal representation used to model attack paths (Section II-B). A. Problem Statement Formal attack paths provide a machine-processable representation of vulnerability exploitation, attack progression, and resulting security impacts, supporting automated cybersecurity analysis. CVE descriptions contain rich information about vulnerabilities, their exploitation conditions, and security impacts, making them a natural source for deriving attack paths. For example, CVE-2023-6378 describes a serialization vulnerability in the Logback receiver component of Logback 1.4.11 that allows an attacker to mount a denial-of-service attack by sending poisoned data. CVE-2023-6378.A serialization vulnerability in logback receiver component part of logback version 1.4.11 allows an attacker to mount a Denial-Of-Service attack by sending poisoned data. This description provides rich information relevant to explot- ing the vulnerability, such as the vulnerability characteristics, affected component and version, exploitation mechanism, and intended security impact. However, this information is expressed in natural language and leaves the concrete attack ac- tions and their dependencies implicit. Generating an attack path from a CVE description therefore requires making this implicit attack logic explicit as a feasible sequence of attack actions. We represent the resulting attack path in PDDL to obtain a formal, planner-ready representation that supports automated verification and reasoning. Formally, given a natural-language CVE description C, the task is to generate a PDDL-encoded attack path P=f(C) that connects the vulnerability to its resulting security impact through a feasible sequence of attack actions. The generated representation must satisfy both formal planning and cybersecurity-specific requirements including syntactic validity,planning solvability, andcybersecurity semantic fidelity. B. PDDL for Attack Path Modeling The PDDL [2] is a standard formal language for automated planning. A PDDLdomaindefinesactionschemas, each with typed parameters, preconditions that must hold for the action to be applicable, and effects that describing the resulting world state upon the action’s execution. A PDDLproblemgrounds the domain for a concrete scenario by specifying initial states and goals. A domain-independent planner then searches for a plan, i.e., a sequence of grounded actions that transforms the initial state into one satisfying the goal. In the context of cybersecurity, PDDL has been adapted to model attack paths representing the progression of an attack against a vulnerable system [3], [5], [9]. Each action indicates an operation by attacker, target system, user or infrastructure, with preconditions encoding required capabilities or conditions, and effects capturing the resulting states upon execution. The attack path typically follows stages standardized by theCyber Kill Chain[16]: starting with Reconnaissance, where system exposures and vulnerabilities are identified, followed by Weaponization and Delivery, during which malicious scripts, files, or payloads to exploit the known vulnerability are crafted and transmitted to the target. This is followed by Exploitation that achieves the exploitation goal with a final impact. The resulting impact can be categorized by the established threat classification framework such asSTRIDE[17]: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, and Elevation of Privilege. Figure 1 presents a simplified PDDL-encoded attack path. The first action corresponds to the Reconnaissance stage, identifying that the target system is exposed and accepts external requests. The second action models the Weaponization stage, during which the attacker crafts a malicious payload. Upon execution of step-wise actions, the final steps achieves Denial of service by the successful Exploitation. ;Step 0: Reconnaissance, identify exposed system (:action system-exposes-attack-surface :parameters (?System - system ?Software - software) :precondition (and (runs-vulnerable-software ?System ?Software) (<= (version ?Software) 1001020001) ;version <= 1.1.20.1 (accepts-external-requests ?System)) :effect (and (exposes-attack-surface ?System) (target-accepts-requests ?System))) ;Step 1: Weaponization (:action attacker-crafts-malicious-payload :parameters (?System - system ?Payload - payload) :precondition (exposes-attack-surface ?System) :effect (crafted-payload ?Payload)) ; ... III. METHODOLOGY This section presents CVE2AP, an LLM-based approach for automatically generating PDDL-encoded attack paths from CVE natural language descriptions. Figure 2 provides an overview. Given a natural-language CVE description, CVE2AP generates a PDDL-encoded attack path as output. The approach is model-agnostic and can be instantiated with any LLM that supports either a chat-based or completion-based interface. The generation process is governed by two complementary components: (i)prompt construction, which provides the LLM

A. Model Options CVE2AP is model-agnostic and can be instantiated with any LLM that supports a chat-based or completion-based interface. To cover diverse deployment scenarios and enable analysis across different model scales, we considers two aspects of model instantiation: (i)deployment mode, including online commercial models accessed through remote APIs and self-hosted models deployed locally, and (ii)model scale, considering multiple model sizes within the same model family to isolate, as far as possible, the effect of model scale on attack-path generation quality. The specific model instances used in our experiments are detailed in Section IV-A. B. Prompt Construction CVE2AP supports both structured chat-based interaction, using system–user–assistant messages for instruction-tuned models, and plain completion-based interaction for base models. The appropriate interaction format is automatically selected according to the chosen model. To ensure consistent generation behavior across models, the core prompt content, including the system prompt, task instructions, and few-shot examples, is defined through a common base template and rendered into the corresponding interaction format. The prompt comprises the following components. System Prompt.The system prompt defines the LLM’s role as an expert in both attack path analysis and PDDL modeling, specifies the generation task, and provides constraints for producing valid attack paths. Specifically, it consists of the following elements: • Role and Task: Apart from defining the role, the prompt instructs the LLM to generate a syntactically correct, solvable, and semantically valid PDDL-encoded attack path from a given CVE description. When the description is incomplete or ambiguous, it instructs the LLM to make conservative and reasonable assumptions grounded in common security knowledge rather than introducing unsupported capabilities or attack steps. • Adversarial Model: The prompt constrains the attacker’s capabilities to ensure that generated attack path adheres to a realistic model. The attacker’s initial position and privilege level are consistent with the CVE’s attack context. The attacker has no prior knowledge of or access to system internals, cannot break strong cryptography, and the attack ex- ploits exactly one CVE to achieve exactly one STRIDE goal. The attacker initially holds no capabilities beyond what the authenticated sessions, elevated privileges, crafted artifacts, system internal secrets, and internal network sccess. The attack path may include user-interaction steps (e.g., clicking a link) when the CVE requires user interaction for exploitation. • Attack Stage Reference: The prompt provides a reference framework adapted for the Cyber Kill Chain [16], outlining the typical progression of a single-CVE exploitation through five stages: (i) Exposure (mandatory), confirming the target is vulnerable (system technical composition, access paths, absent security controls, and other observable conditions); (ii) Weaponization, crafting or preparing the malicious artifact; (iii) Delivery, transmitting the malicious artifact or trigger to the target; (iv) Exploitation, target-side processing that triggers the vulnerability, often decomposed into multiple actions; (v) Impact (mandatory), achieving a STRIDE secu- rity outcome. This reference guides the LLM in structuring the attack path without enforcing a rigid linear progression, as not all vulnerabilities follow this exact sequence. • Instructions: The prompt provides fine-grained instructions covering six quality dimensions aligned with the evaluation

criteria defined in S3Eval [15]: – Feasibility: Each action must operate within the adversarial model and correspond to a realistic, executable attack operation. – Atomicity: Each action must represent a single, indivisible real-world attack step with justified effects. – Completeness: The attack path must be causally coherent with all critical intermediate steps present, progressing logically through attack stages. – CVE Fidelity: The path must correctly characterize the vulnerability, uses the right exploitation mechanism, and achieve an appropriate STRIDE goal. – Naming: Action and predicate names must follow readable, descriptive, consistent conventions with clearly identifiable semantics and actors, e.g., attacker, target system, user, infrastructure. – PDDL Conformance: Rules addressing common LLM errors in PDDL generation, including parameter scoping and predicate arity, identifier uniqueness, predicate block well-formedness, version comparison format, and parameter generalization. • Output Format: The prompt specifies the expected output structure. A structured PDDL template can optionally be incorporated to provide explicit structural guidance. Details are described inOutput Templatebelow. Few-shot Learning.CVE2AP supports 0-shot, 1-shot, and 2-shot configurations. In the few-shot settings, examples are ran- domly sampled from a pool of expert-authored reference attack paths, while excluding the target CVE to prevent data leakage. Each example consists of a CVE description paired with its

corresponding PDDL-encoded attack path and is presented as a use–assistent message pair. These examples provide the LLM with concrete demonstrations of the expected output structure, action granularity, style, and level of detail, thereby comple- menting the general constraints specified in the system prompt. Output Template.In the 0-shot setting, the prompt can optionally include a structured PDDL output template that provides an attack-path-specific domain skeleton. The template specifies the overall PDDL structure including (:requirements), (:types), (:constants), (:predicates), (:functions), and action schema (:action <action-name> :parameter(...), :precondition(...), :effects(...)) . It further guides the attack path progression from a mandatory vulnerability exposure action (Step 0) through intermediate exploitation steps to a final action achieving a single STRIDE impact (Step N). This template guides the LLM toward syntactically conformant and domain-appropriate PDDL output without providing CVE-specific content. C. Error Feedback A correct attack path should satisfy syntactic correctness, solvability, and semantic correctness [15]. Even with detailed in- structions, due to limitations such as hallucinations, and factual inconsistencies [18], LLMs may still generate PDDL domains that contain errors, including invalid declarations or action configurations that do not admit a valid plan. When generating PDDL-encoded attack paths, representative errors include using variables in an action’s :precondition or :effect that are not declared in the action’s :parameters (parameter scoping violations), or writing negated predicates such as (not (accepts-external-requests ?Sys)) in the (:predicates) construct, whose application is only permitted in action :precondition by PDDL syntax. To mitigate such errors, CVE2AP optionally incorporates an automated error feedback loop focusing on syntactic correctness and solvability, because existing domain-independent PDDL planners, such as Metric-FF planner [19], can quickly and automatically detect these errors and provide concrete error information, such as syntax errors with their locations, which can be directly incorporated into iterative correction. In contrast, although semantic correctness is essential, existing methods [15] evaluating semantics primarily provide semantic quality judgments (i.e., a binary True/False judgment or a score ranging from 0 to 5 reflecting overall semantic quality) rather than feedback that identifies which elements of the generated attack path should be corrected. We therefore leave semantic feedback as an important direction for future work. Specifically, after the initial generation, a corresponding problem instance is automatically constructed from the domain. Both the domain and problem files are then fed into Metric-FF planner to check syntax correctness and plan solvability. Metric-FF detects syntax errors during its parsing phase and verifies whether a valid plan exists, with support for numeric fluents required for modeling version constraints in vulnerability exploitation. In our implementation, this checking process completes within milliseconds per domain, resulting in negligible overhead to the LLM-based generation process. If the check fails, the specific error messages reported by the planner (e.g., undeclared predicates, type mismatches) are extracted and incorporated into a feedback prompt along with a concise set of common PDDL error correction rules. This resulting feedback is appended to the existing conversation context as a new user message, thereby preserving the generated PDDL and the preceding reasoning context. The LLM is then instructed to produce a revised PDDL domain based on the accumulated context. Listing 3 shows the feedback message template. This feedback loop allows up to three retry attempts within the same conversation, allowing the LLM to progressively correct errors while maintaining awareness of its prior outputs and the specific issues identified. If the generated PDDL passes the check before exhausting the retry budget, the process terminates early. Otherwise, the procedure terminates after the third retry and returns the final generated output. The entire process is automated and does not require human intervention: the LLM receives only the planner-reported error signals and the predefined correction rules, enabling systematic correction while preserving the original generation context. Listing 3: Error Feedback Message Template. Metric-ff errors: <planner-reported error message> Fix all errors in the domain. Critical rules: (1) PARAMETER SCOPING: Every ?Var used in preconditions or effects Must appear in that action’s :parameters. (2) PDDL IDENTIFIER SYNTAX: Names must use only letters, digits, and hyphens. No dots allowed. (3) DECLARED CONSTANTS ONLY: Every bare identifier (non-?var) must be declared in :constants. . . . (6) PREDICATES BLOCK: Never write (not . . . ) inside :predicates declaration; (not . . . ) is only valid inside action :precondition. Output corrected PDDL only. IV. EVALUATION This section describes experimental setup (Section IV-A), the results (Sections IV-B). A. Experimental Setup Our objective is to systematically assess the effectiveness and cost of CVE2AP in generating PDDL-encoded attack paths, and to analyze the impact of key configuration decisions. Accordingly, we address the following research questions: RQ1: Effectiveness.How effective is CVE2AP at automatically generating PDDL-encoded attack paths? RQ2: Cost.What is the cost of CVE2AP for generating PDDL-encoded attack paths? RQ3: Configuration Impact.How do different configuration decisions affect the effectiveness and cost of CVE2AP? Dataset.We use 21 CVEs applied by S3Eval [15], covering diverse vulnerability types. Each CVE includes a natural language description and expert-authored reference PDDL- encoded attack path.

Generation LLM models.We select five LLM models spanning both online commercial and locally-hosted options at different scales to examine the trade-off between capability and deployment cost. • Online commercial: GPT-5.5 [20] (latest flagship), and Deepseek (DS) V4-PRO[21]. • Locally-hosted: Qwen3-{4B, 8B, 14B, 32B} [22], which share the same architecture at different scales, enabling analysis of how model capacity affects judgment quality in a cost-effective, self-hosted setting. Configuration Space.Each generation run is defined by three configuration dimensions: • Few-shot learning:0-shot, 1-shot, and 2-shot. Few-shot examples are randomly selected from the reference pool, excluding the target CVE. • Error feedback:After the initial generation (which proceeds without prior indication of feedback mechanism in the prompt), if the output fails syntax or solvability checks, the specific error messages are fed back to the LLM for up to 3 retry attempts within the same conversation context. • Output template:For different shot mode, a structured PDDL output template can be provided to guide the generation for- mat. We evaluate both with and without the output template. In total, the above three dimensions yield 3×2×2 = 12prompt configurations per model ({0-shot, 1-shot, 2-shot} × {with, without error feedback}×{with, without output template}). Evaluation Metrics.We evaluate the generated PDDL- encoded attack path using the S3Eval pipeline [15], which comprehensively assess the quality of PDDL-encoded AP through a 3-layer structure: • S1 (Syntax):Whether the generated PDDL-encoded APs conforms to the PDDL specification, including valid structure, consistent type declaration, correct predicate arities, and well-defined action schemas. • S2 (Solvability):Whether the domain, together with an automatically generated problem file, admits at least one valid plan, verified by the Metric-ff [19]. • S3 (Semantic):Whether the domain faithfully models the intended attack path. Semantic quality is assessed through embedding-based similarity (Qwen3-Embedding-8B [22]) and LLM-as-expert (Deepseek-R1 [21]), each operating in bothintrinsic (candidate vs. CVE natural language description) and extrinsic(candidate vs. expert-authored reference) settings. The LLM-as-expert applies two rubric variants:simplified, which uses concise criterion descriptions to produce a holistic binary judgment (True/False), anddetailed, which provides fine-grained instructions with violation examples and scores each criterion on a 0–5 scale (0–2 = violation, 3–5 = compliance), with the minimum score across all criteria deriving a binary signal. We report thecorrect rate(proportion of the generations that assessed as correct at each layer) as the primary metric, and the averagegeneration timeandtoken consumptionper sample as cost metrics. Testbed.We conduct all experiments using Python 3.10 on two machines: a macOS laptop equipped with an Intel Core i7-8559U CPU and Intel Iris Plus Graphics 655 (16 GB RAM), and a Linux server equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU (24 GB VRAM, CUDA 13.2) and 62 GB RAM. L Online LLM judges are assessed via API with temperature set to 0, and prompted via chat- or completion-based interfaces depending on model availability. Local models are served via llama.cpp [23] with quantized weights (Q8_0 for Qwen3-{4B, 8B, 14B} , Q4_K_M for Qwen3-32B). We use a fixed random seed of 42 for reproducibility. We note that GPT-5.5 is subject to OpenAI’s content safety filter (cyber_policy), which non-deterministically blocks a negligible fraction of the generation of PDDL-encoded attack paths. When this occurs, we retry the generation request until a valid generation is obtained. This issue can also be solved by applying for OpenAI’s Research Access Program, which grants exemptions from certain content filters. B. Results 1) RQ1 (Effectiveness):Figure 3 reports the correct rate for each evaluation dimension across syntax, solvability, and semantic quality (embedding-based similarity and LLM-as-expert) of all six LLM models. Each bar indicates the mean correct rate over the 12 prompt configurations. Overall, CVE2AP is effective in automatically generating high-quality PDDL-encoded attack paths. With the best- performing model, GPT-5.5, CVE2AP achieves a correct rate of 86.9% for syntax, 78.6% for solvability, 53.8% for embedding-based similarity, and 93.1% for LLM-as-expert. Additionally, the performance of locally-hosted models improves consistently with model size across all evaluation dimensions The weaker performance of smaller local models can be attributed to: (i) limited capability for the multi- constraint reasoning to generate PDDL-encoded attack paths demands; (ii) limited exposure during pre-training to PDDL planning language and cybersecurity, particularly CVE domain knowledge; and (iii) context window limitations. Specifically, few-shot examples, error feedback, the output template increase the input context, which may overwhelm smaller models, such as Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, resulting in empty, ineffective, or malformed outputs. Notably, despite these challenges, Qwen3-32B achieves a syntax correct rate of 39.7% , produces solvable attack paths for approximately one-third of its generations, and satisfies semantic requirements in more than 20% of cases under both embedding-based similarity and LLM-as-expert evaluation. These results are encouraging given the inherent complexity of generating PDDL-encoded attack paths from a CVE description, which demands simultaneously satisfying syntax correctness, solvability, and semantic requirements including action feasibility, action atomicity, and attack stage completeness.

PDDL-based Attack Path Modeling AI planning provides a formal framework for modeling multi-step cyber attacks by representing attack actions as planning operators with explicit preconditions and effects. Among existing planning formalisms, the PDDL has been widely adopted for this purpose. Roberts et al. [3] demonstrated the use of PDDL for personalized vulnerability analysis by encoding attack actions as PDDL schemas and incorporating user activities and system-specific configurations to automatically identify paths targeting to a specific system. Falco et al. [6] formulated adversarial strategy generation for critical infrastructures as an AI planning problem. More recently, Bashir et al. [7] integrated PDDL-based attack graphs with fault trees to support resilience analysis of cyber-physical systems, while Inayat et al. [8] modeled cyber attacks in PDDL to generate attack steps, and recommend security controls. As attack scenario evolve increasingly complex, prior work has also investigated the scalability and maintainability of PDDL models. PDDLAssistant [5] supports the incremental development of PDDL-encoded attack graphs by reconciling different versions of PDDL representations and explaining changes between generated plans. Wang et al. [24] improved the efficiency of PDDL-based attack planning in large-scale networks through a device reachability graph partitioning approach. Despite these efforts, most existing approaches assume that PDDL attack models are manually constructed. In practice, this construction process is labor-intensive and requires expertise in both cyber security and AI planning to specify predicates, action schemas, and their corresponding preconditions and effects. This modeling burden becomes particularly significant as vulnerabilities, attack techniques, system and environmental conditions continuously evolve. To reduce this modeling effort, Bezawada et al. [9] proposed to automatically derive PDDL attack paths from CVE descrip- tion using traditional NLP techniques, including Part-Of-Speech (POS) tagging and rule-based extraction. However, the reliance on handcrafted extraction rules limits the approach’s ability to capture the diverse linguistic expressions and incomplete, implicit and heterogeneous information commonly contained in vulnerability descriptions and threat intelligence. Furthermore, the approach was evaluated only on a limited case study without systematic evaluation across multiple important quality metrics, such as syntax correctness, solvability, semantic correctness. Overall, existing research has established PDDL as an effective formalism for representing multi-step cyber attacks, while automatic construction of high-quality, planner-ready PDDL attack paths remains unexplored. In particular, generating attack-specific PDDL representations from unstructured vulnerability descriptions remains challenging because the generated actions must satisfy not only the formal planning constraints and cybersecurity-specific semantic

B. LLM-based PDDL Domain Generation Recent advances in LLMs have enabled automatic generation of PDDL planning domains from natural language descriptions. Guan et al. [10] investigated the use of pre-trained LLMs for PDDL domain construction, demonstrating the potential of LLMs to translate natural-language descriptions into formal

planning representations. Smirnov et al. [11] further improved the generation quality by incorporating automatic consistency checking and reachability analysis into an iterative refinement loop. Oswald et al. [12] and Huang et al. [13] systematically evaluated the ability of LLMs to generate PDDL domains from natural-language descriptions, highlighting both their potential and remaining challenges in producing semantically correct and executable planning domains. More recently, Huang et al. [14] proposed a fully automated pipeline that leverages multiple LLMs to convert natural-language, step-wise action descriptions into candidate PDDL specifications. These candidates are ranked by embedding-based semantic similarity and further filtered through planner-based solvability checking to identify suitable PDDL domains. Despite these advances, existing LLM-based approaches primarily target general-purpose planning domains and provide limited consideration of cybersecurity-specific attack-path modeling. Unlike general planning domains, attack path modeling introduces additional domain-specific semantic re- quirements beyond syntax correctness and planning solvability. Generated attack actions must, for example, accurately reflect the vulnerability’s exploitation mechanism, and preserve the causal dependencies required for a complete attack progression. These requirements introduce a fundamental distinction between a PDDL domain that is formally valid and solvable and one that faithfully represents a real-world cyber attack. Our work investigates the application of LLMs to automatically generate PDDL-encoded attack paths from CVE descriptions. To assess the resulting attack paths beyond formal PDDL correctness, we employ S3Eval [15] to evaluate three complementary dimensions: syntactic correctness, solvability, and semantic correctness. This allows us to investigate whether LLM-generated PDDL representations are not only planner-executable but also faithful to the underlying vulnerability-exploiting-specific semantics VI. CONCLUSION The rapid evolution of the cyber threat landscape has rendered the manual construction and maintenance of PDDL- encoded attack paths impractical, making automated attack path generation imperative. This paper introducedCVE2AP, an LLM-based approach for automatic generation of PDDL- encoded attack paths from natural language CVE descriptions. By combining specifically designed structured prompting with an iterative, domain-independent planner-guided error-feedback mechanism, CVE2AP improves the syntactic correctness and planning solvability of generated attack paths while preserving their semantic quality. Our systematic evaluation applying S3Eval [15] framework across diverse LLMs and generation configurations demonstrates that CVE2AP is capable of generating high-quality PDDL-encoded attack paths with reasonable generation time and token consumption. The results further reveal substantial differences in the quality-cost profiles of the evaluated LLMs, with GPT-5.5 providing the best generation performance and the most favorable quality-cost trade-off. Furthermore, configuration analysis shows that error feedback is the most consistently effective strategy for improving generation quality, whereas the benefits of few-shot examples and structured output templates diverse. These findings highlight the importance of jointly considering model capability, generation cost, and configuration strategy when deploying LLM-based methodology to generate PDDL- encoded attack paths. Despite these encouraging results, the current implementation of CVE2AP focuses on attack paths involving the exploitation of a single vulnerability. As future work, we plan to extend the approach to support the generation of multi-vulnerability attack paths and chained exploitations. VII. End-to-end PDDL Planning with Hardcoded.text: End-to-end PDDL Planning with Hardcoded and Dynamic Agents Emanuele La Malfa1,3∗ Ping Zhu1∗ Samuele Marro2,3 Sara Bernardini1 Michael Wooldridge1 1Department of Computer Science, University of Oxford 2Department of Engineering, University of Oxford 3IDAI [Code & Results] Abstract We present an end-to-end framework for planning supported by verifiers. An orchestrator receives a human specification written in natural language and con- verts it into a PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language) model, where the domain and problem are iteratively refined by sub-modules (agents) to address common planning requirements, such as time constraints and optimality, as well as ambiguities and contradictions that may exist in the human specification. We support two categories of agents: hardcoded, which are informed by logs and error traces and have a pre-defined goal (e.g., fix issues with PDDL syntax, check temporal constraints), and dynamic, which have no predefined goal but adapt to the specific domain and revise the latent planning abstraction. The validated do- main and problem are then passed to an external planning engine to generate a plan. The orchestrator and agents are powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and require no human intervention at any stage of the process. Finally, a module translates the final plan back into natural language to improve human readability while maintaining the correctness of each step. We demonstrate the flexibility and effectiveness of our framework on GPT-{4o, 5-mini, 5.4}, and Gemini-{2.5, 3}-flash across more than ten domains and tasks, including the Google NaturalPlan benchmark, Planbench, and classic planning problems like Sokoban, Blocksworld and the Tower of Hanoi, where LLMs are known to struggle even with small instances. Our framework can be integrated with any PDDL planning engine and validator (we successfully tested Fast Downward, LPG, POPF, V AL, and uV AL) and represents a significant step toward end-to-end planning aided by LLMs. 1 Introduction Planning is a cornerstone of intelligent behaviour: from robotics and logistics to digital assistants and collaborative environments, agents must translate high-level goals into structured sequences of actions. Automated planning, one of the most longstanding subfields of AI, offers guarantees of correctness and optimality [ 7, 9]. However, it requires expert-crafted domain models, typically in PDDL (Planning Domain Definition Language) [24], and is ill-suited to handle ambiguous, incomplete, or underspecified requirements expressed in natural language. In contrast, Large Language Models (LLMs) excel at interpreting complex instructions but struggle to produce long-horizon or multi-agent plans directly, often hallucinating steps or producing infeasible sequences [37, 41]. Recent work has sought to bridge these paradigms by using LLMs as front-ends to symbolic solvers, translating natural language descriptions into structured representations [1, 12]. The framework includes the first JSON and PDDL plan generator, and the agentic sub-component, which refines an existing plan (right). reduce the modelling burden, they typically rely on fixed, pre-defined workflows. Multi-agent systems allow for planning with shared resources, asynchronous execution, and dynamic coordination [21, 26]. Addressing these challenges requires systems that are simultaneously linguistically capable, formally grounded, and robust to diverse scenarios. In this paper, we present the first end-to-end agentic framework for planning that unifies natural language understanding, dynamic agent orchestration, symbolic reasoning, and plan interpretation (Figure 1). Unlike prior approaches with static role assignment [6], our orchestrator LLM dynamically creates multi-agent workflows on the fly, asynchronously invoking agents to construct PDDL domains and problems, which are first merged, then iteratively refined by a sequence of specialised agents depending on the task at hand. The refined PDDL problem is then solved by a planner to guarantee correctness with respect to the specification and, potentially, cost-optimality. The resulting plan is automatically translated back into natural language, which ensures accessibility and interpretability while preserving formal correctness. Our contribution is threefold: • We introduce a fully automated, end-to-end multi-agent planning pipeline that closes the gap between natural language intent communication and optimal plans, enabling the system to move from free-form specifications to validated plans with no human intervention. We show how hardcoded agents can mitigate some longstanding obstacles in planning, including ambiguity resolution in a human specification [10, 34]. On the other hand, dynamic agents enhance the flexibility of planning workflow generation. • We run experiments on more than ten benchmarks that cover long-horizon planning tasks and constraint satisfaction problems (CSP). On the former, our approach outperforms vanilla LLMs and has nearly perfect success rate. On the latter, the gap with vanilla models remains large for non-frontier models such as GPT-5-mini and Gemini-2.5 but reduces on models like GPT-5.4. Also, our method solves hard instances of the Tower of Hanoi and Blocksworld, where LLMs are known to struggle [25, 28]. • Our work identifies CSP as the setting where PDDL+LLMs (but, in general, neuro-symbolic techniques) still struggle. It is also a call for action for the research community to carefully develop evaluation techniques to mitigate the brittleness of LLMs as-a-judge when the ground truth label and the final plan are expressed in natural language. Overall, our framework represents a step toward unifying LLMs and symbolic planning into general- purpose autonomous systems. By dynamically orchestrating multiple agents, grounding reasoning in solvers, and ensuring human-auditable outputs through natural language back-translation, we push the frontier of end-to-end multi-agent planning toward real-world applicability. This positions our approach as both a practical and conceptual advancement in the integration of language models and multi-agent symbolic reasoning. 2

2 Background and Related Work We provide an overview of research at the intersection of LLMs, automated planning, and agentic systems, highlighting key trends in the literature. LLMs for planning.Early attempts to use LLMs for planning focused on directly generating action sequences from natural-language task descriptions. However, studies show that LLMs alone are brittle, with even modern models exhibiting subpar performance [12]. In fact, a line of works [16, 38] reinforces that while LLMs by themselves are poor planners, they perform notably better when augmented with symbolic components. Valmeekam [ 36] also underlines that without extra tooling, LLMs alone are unreliable at reasoning about their planning decisions (a pitfall that our system circumvents by introducing external feedback). More robust frameworks integrate LLMs with symbolic solvers. InLLM+Ppipeline [ 20], LLMs attempt to directly translate language into PDDL specifications and subsequently call planners. Other approaches integrate LLMs with search algorithms:SayCan[ 1] uses LLMs with value functions to ground high-level instructions. Similarly, SayCanPay[ 13] introduces coupling an LLM with A* search to guarantee cost-feasible plans. Another promising line treats planning as a form of program synthesis. Silver [32] shows the potential of GPT-4 as a generalised planner by synthesising Python programs that generate valid plans for PDDL domains, using iterative prompting and automated debugging loops to improve reliability. Mahdavi [22] leverages LLMs to generate valid PDDL domains and problems that are then fed to a solver, but requires access to the model’s logprob, which is not available in any recent API-based LLM. Overall, the literature shows a shift from using LLMs on their own to hybrid systems that combine the generative flexibility of LLMs with the correctness guarantees of symbolic planners. Multi-agent and agentic systems.Modern research on multi-agent planning emphasizes learning- based coordination. Lowe [ 21] proposed a multi-agent actor-critic algorithm that addresses non- stationarity in concurrent learning via centralised critics. Differentiable communication channels [8, 33] further enable emergent coordination strategies. Benchmarks such as MeltingPot [ 19] and MPE [21] evaluate cooperative and competitive multi-agent behaviours. Additionally, recent work integrates LLMs as agents in collaborative environments. For example, Wu [39] introducedCoBlock, a collaborative Blocksworld domain where two LLM-driven agents coordinate on construction tasks. The results show that incorporating chain-of-thought reasoning into agent prompts significantly improved coordination success rates and ensured more balanced workloads. However, prompts still included the world state at each decision iteration, reinforcing the challenges current LLMs face when holding complex states in persistent memory and underscoring the benefit of outsourcing this task to a symbolic engine. Automated planning and PDDL.Automated planning has long served as the formal backbone for generating autonomous behaviour. The STRIPS formalism [7] laid the foundation for domain- independent planning, later standardised in PDDL [24]. Planners such as GraphPlan [ 3], FF [15], and Fast Downward [ 14] achieve efficient heuristic search across domains. However, designing correct PDDL models remains a bottleneck in the widespread adoption of verifiable planning. Recent work leverages LLMs to automate or assist with this process. [41] show that LLMs are often better at generating formal specifications (in PDDL) than directly producing valid plans. Additionally, benchmarks such as Planbench [37] highlight that, while LLMs struggle to outperform solvers, they are promising for lowering the modelling barrier. Oswald [ 27] explores using GPT-4 to generate entire PDDL domains, though the proposed system still requires iterative refinement. Tools, benchmarks, and datasets.A wave of benchmarks and open-source resources has supported modern evaluation of multi-agent planning in the context of LLMs. Zheng [40] introducedNATURAL PLAN, a benchmark for realistic language-based planning tasks (e.g., trip planning, scheduling). Planbench [37] offers standardised domains and metrics for LLM planning, while Planetarium [41] provides a large dataset (145k pairs) for text-to-PDDL evaluation with equivalence checking tools. For multi-agent collaboration, CoBlock [ 39] explicitly tests human-LLM and LLM-LLM collaboration in Blocksworld scenarios. Embodied benchmarks such as ALFRED [ 30] and its symbolic variant ALFWorld [31] bridge natural language instructions with embodied planning. Other environments, including BabyAI [5], remain popular for testing instruction following and sequential decision-making. 3

3 Agentic End-to-End Planning In this section, we introduce planning as an optimisation problem, and the architecture to solve, in an end-to-end fashion, a wide range of planning tasks. We assume there is a specification and a ground truth plan, both written in natural language, which is the domain where our framework operates. Our notation does not conflict but extends that of Mahdavi [22] as it assumes one can either verify the final PDDL plan (if any) or the natural language representation of it. 3.1 Planning as an Optimisation Problem A planning task consists of a specification s, i.e., the description of the problem, and its ground truth solution y; we assume that both s and y live in Σ∗, which denotes the Kleene closure of all the possible strings in an alphabet of symbols, including natural language and PDDL specifications. Our agentic framework F receives as input a task s and produces a candidate solution for the task, which consists of a PDDL domain and problem (d, p), namely F:s− →(d, p). We denote with V a solver that turns the PDDL domain and problem into a candidate plan, i.e., ˆy=V(d, p). While F iteratively selects the best candidate from a finite pool of agents A={a 1, ..., an} to produce the new candidate PDDL domain and problem,Vproduces the PDDL plan and can be any PDDL solver. While for some tasks the correctness of a candidate solution can be judged by comparing two PDDL plans (e.g., the Tower of Hanoi), in a generic scenario the ground truth plan is expressed in natural language: in both cases, we rely on an oracle that scores a candidate solution ˆy(or ˆynl) as right (1) or wrong (0) againsty, i.e.,Ω : (ˆy, y)− → {0,1}.2 For a pair of problem specifications and a ground truth solution sampled from a distributionT , namely (s, y)∼T, our framework optimises the following: max F E(s,y)∼T [Ω(ˆynl, y)] s.t.ˆy nl = (V◦F(s)) ◦b b∈N >0, (1) where (V◦F(s)) ◦b denotes how our framework F alternates with the solver V to produce the candidate PDDL plan, while consuming abudget b >0. In other words, we look for the agentic system F that optimises the choice of agents at each substep (more details in the next section). The optimisation problem outlined above pertains to the case where the ground truth plan is expressed in PDDL. W.l.o.g., the extension to natural language involves a translation moduleN l(an LLM agent) that turns the candidate planˆyinto natural language, i.e.,ˆynl =N l◦(V◦F(s)) ◦b. 3.2 Planning as a Sequential Agentic Problem Our design of Eq. 1 and function F are inspired by recent advances in agentic LLMs [4, 35], which combine the ability of LLMs to identify which parts of a plan should be refined with the formality of PDDL solvers and validators. Our process begins by instantiating an orchestrator agent that generates a structured representation of the environment, the agents, their goals, and their constraints from the natural language task description. We adopt JSON as the intermediate representation because it flexibly captures heteroge- neous data and is widely represented in open- and closed-source LLM pre-training corpora [29]. The orchestrator then produces an initial PDDL domain and problem, which are passed to a solver (e.g., Fast Downward or POPF2) to compute an initial candidate plan. The domain and problem are then iteratively refined. Using the logs produced by an external PDDL validation tool (V AL/uV AL), the orchestrator selects the most suitable agent from a pool of available agents. Some agents are hardcoded, i.e., they provide fixed procedures to repair PDDL syntax errors, adapt the domain and problem to the target solver, generate the final natural language plan, or terminate the computation early. In addition, we introduce an agent with no predefined prompt, which adapts to the current execution state. The “Refiner” block can call agents whose prompt is pre-defined and solves specific issues with the current planning task (e.g., PDDL syntax errors), or generates a prompt for a dynamic agent that adapts to the current context. With a finite pool of hardcoded agents A={a 1, . . . , an}, the pointwise objective in Eq. 1 can be rewritten as a⋆ ∈arg max a∈A E(s,y)∼T  Ω � ˆynl(s;a), y  ,(2) where ˆynl(s;a) denotes the candidate solution obtained when agent a is selected. This corresponds to a standard multi-armed bandit problem, in which each agent is an arm with unknown expected reward. When the orchestrator can choose between hardcoded and dynamic agents, the problem becomes a⋆ ∈arg max a∈A max θ∈Θa E(s,y)∼T  Ω � ˆynl(s;a, θ), y  ,(3) where Θa ⊆Σ ∗ denotes the configuration space of agent a, such as prompts or generated programs. This objective selects the agent a∈ Awith the highest achievable task performance, where per- formance is measured by the number of correctly solved instances (success rate). For each agent, an inner optimisation is carried out over its configuration space Θa, yielding the best performance attainable by that agent under an optimal configuration. Hence, the outer optimisation selects the agent, while the inner optimisation searches over its configurations. This changes the nature of the problem: instead of selecting among a fixed set of arms, one must solve a potentially high-dimensional and combinatorial optimisation problem for each agent. Consequently, the main difficulty shifts from statistical estimation to structured search, and the resulting formulation no longer reduces to a standard bandit problem. Beyond informing our results, these observations call for improved methods for reasoning and planning under constraints, and provide empirical support for recent position papers advocating more rigorous evaluation [17]. Planning benchmarks are ambiguous, if not wrong.In the Google Natural Plan benchmark, we identified several issues with the ground truth labels. Both our method and vanilla models perform well on calendar scheduling but poorly on trip planning, prompting manual inspection. In calendar scheduling, some instances admit multiple valid solutions despite a single labeled answer. In trip planning, the ground truth ambiguously counts travel days as time spent in both locations, which can be unrealistic (e.g., long trips). GPT-5-mini and GPT-5 instead count travel as time spent only in the origin location, leading to lower measured accuracy. In contrast, Planbench provides well-defined tasks and solutions, though it focuses on classic planning domains (e.g., logistics, depots). We thus raise the attention of the research community to benchmarks that, if not inspected manually, can mislead our interpretation of LLMs’ planning capabilities. We advocate for benchmarks rigorously validated by humans before release. This opens up to the discussion on LLMs as-a-judge to evaluate the correctness of a plan when the ground truth is not available. The issues of LLMs as-a-judge.Last but not least, we want to emphasize how difficult (and potentially, ill-posed) it is to use an LLM-as-a-judge to evaluate the correctness of a plan. As discussed in other works [11], unless an LLM has performance that is proven to be superior to that of the model they judge, there is a risk that the judge itself cannot solve the task, and thus understand whether a solution is correct or wrong. Finding better ways to evaluate a plan (e.g., asking a model to output a formatted solution that is tested against the ground truth), is an open problem in planning as well as benchmarking [23] the research community is still addressing. To quantify the uncertainty of the LLM as-a-judge, we run three evaluations on the same set of results of Planbench and the Google Natural Plan benchmark, using, as a planner, GPT-5.4 (see Table 1), and, as a judge, GPT-5-mini. We then measure the variation between evaluations (the difference between max and min success rate). As we report in Table 3, the max variation in the success rate for the vanilla is 12% (meeting planning) with an average variation of 6.8% across the seven tasks; for our technique, the max variation is 10% (depots), with an average 3.7% variation across the seven tasks. 5 Conclusion and Future Work We introduce a fully automated, end-to-end multi-agent planning framework that combines natural language understanding, dynamic orchestration, symbolic reasoning, and plan interpretation. Our approach enables LLM-based agents to generate workflows, iteratively refine PDDL, and leverage solvers to handle complex planning tasks, with outputs translated back into natural language for interpretability. Across ten benchmarks (e.g., Google Natural Plan, Planbench, Blocksworld, Hanoi, Sokoban), our method improves success rates on long-horizon planning tasks, while offering smaller gains on CSPs. It also provides a flexible paradigm for handling ambiguity, hallucinations, and coordination via both hard-coded and dynamic agents. Future work includes scaling orchestration, incorporating multimodal inputs, and applying the framework to real-world and embodied settings, as well as developing theoretical guarantees for dynamically generated workflows. 9

6 Appendix 6.1 The Agents in the Agentic Framework We implemented several agents, each specialised in a specific task. The core implementation of our framework stands on the following agents. • FastDownwardsAdapter: it adapts the current PDDL domain and problem to be compliant with the syntax of a specific solver (e.g., FastDownwards). • DeepThinkPDDL: it identifies inconsistencies between the constraints, the goal, and the final plan. • DeepThinkConstraints: it focuses on the constraints expressed in the natural language prompt and the JSON representation, to see if they match the PDDL domain and problem. • SyntaxPDDL: it ensures that the PDDL domain and problem are syntactically correct and can be executed by the solver. It specifically focuses on the output of the validator (e.g., uV AL). • TemporalConsistency: it assesses whether the events/actions in the PDDL problem are temporally consistent with the input prompt and the JSON representation. • AgentNaturalLanguage: it turns the final plan into natural actions and the response for the user. • NoOpAgent: it recognises the task has been solved in advance (i.e., without using the whole budget), and terminates the computation. An overall overview of their usage in the Google Natural Plan Benchmark and Planbench is reported in Figure 5. Other agents that are effective in boosting the success rate of the model in particular scenarios, but are less employed in our experimental evaluation, are: • AgentAsynchronicity: it optimises the plan so that asynchronous actions are executed at the same time step, if possible. If the solver does not support asynchronous actions, it defines a dummy time variable that allows for async actions (though that is not directly employed by the solver). • AgentEnforceMultiAgency: it checks whether the PDDL domain and plan correctly imple- ment the specification as a multi-agent system (this is useful when the specification requires multiple actors to perform async actions). • AgentHallucinations: it detects and fixes hallucinations (arising from the LLM, usually) in the authored PDDL domain and problem.
