An essential aspect is the development and integration of AI systems, which is an intricate and critical process for the successful application of AI in various in- dustries. Like many of the AI technologies, such as machine learning (Zaharia et al., 2018) and computer vision (Olszewska, 2019), AI planning involves a specialised process from con- ceptualisation to deployment into real-world applications. This process starts with the iden- tification of requirements and finishes with the execution of fully functional planning sys- tems. The development pathway is full of complexity and specific activities such as choosing the right planning types and constructing domain models (Silva, Silva, & Vaquero, 2020). Throughout this pathway, there is a continuous need for collecting and analysing planning 19

2 Contributions data to refine and improve the system’s functionality. Journeying through this pathway is akin to navigating on an unmarked road, where frequent consultations with locals are nec- essary to obtain guidance on the correct and best route to the destination. In other words, developing AI planning systems is a complex and uncharted process, highlighting the need for a comprehensive understanding of their development life cycle. Problem Developing an AI planning system shares similar phases with traditional software development (Munassar & Govardhan, 2010), such as requirement analysis, system design and implementation, and testing. However, it presents unique challenges unaccounted for in standard software development life cycles. These include the formulation of adequate planning models for applications, the selection of suitable planning types, functionalities, languages, and tools, and system monitoring. Moreover, AI planning requires continuous system refinement to meet evolving planning goals and guarantee satisfactory system perfor- mance given the many influencing factors, such as data volume and type, quality of domain models, algorithm configuration, explicit user feedback, and plan quality with its implica- tions. Furthermore, the development and maintenance of planning systems would likely require collaboration among individuals with di fferent backgrounds, including domain ex- perts, planning experts, software engineers, and data scientists. This interdisciplinary nature can make the communication and transfer of knowledge and artefacts more challenging than in traditional settings. These complexities indicate that AI planning system development and management are more intricate than those for traditional software, revealing a pressing need for a specialised software development framework that provides a common and comprehen- sive understanding of how planning system software is engineered. Contributions To tackle these challenges, a dedicated software development life cycle is de- veloped for engineering AI planning systems (Georgievski, 2023a, 2023c). Named PlanXFlow, the life cycle adopts a structured approach akin to a waterfall model but with iterative flow through ten phases, illustrated in Figure 2.1. Each phase is defined by its purpose, along with approaches and tools available to execute it. The work introduces additional contributions: • A common framework and terminology, enabling not only cooperation between in- volved parties, such as individuals, groups, and mixed AI-human teams but also fa- cilitating the deployment of AI planning in practical applications. • For the first time, rendering some essential elements of AI planning necessary for build- ing planning technology. These include the definition of the planning model, selection of planning types and tools, system monitoring, and data provenance. • Support for the incorporation of system-wide quality attributes so that developed plan- ning systems are not only functional but also adhere to high-quality standards. 20

The life cycle consists of ten phases in a waterfall but iterative structure (Georgievski, 2023c). 2.1.2 Composing, Integrating, and Deploying AI Planning Systems Context Consider a system that would be classified as intelligent, such as a pre-teen child. This child possesses many cognitive and reasoning abilities, emotional intelligence, and so- cial skills, which are all integrated in such a way that enables the child to engage with the world. Let’s say any single ability from this child can be extracted, such as laughing at a joke or making plans to hang out with a friend after school. If one were to implement this ability in a software system, the resulting software might be highly capable in a narrow seg- ment. Even if more abilities are added, such software might still excel in limited contexts but would lack the holistic intelligence of the child. Thus, intelligence is not merely the sum of individual abilities but rather the integrative e ffect of these elements within a system. In other words, intelligence is an emergent property of a well-architected system, one that inte- grates and orchestrates a coherent set of abilities. There is a recognised need for integrating AI components (Brachman, Gunning, & Burke, 2020; Minsky, Singh, & Sloman, 2004; Thóris- son, 2007). Thórisson (2007) advocates for a holistic approach to the successful integration of AI systems, whereas Brachman, Gunning, and Burke (2020) go even further by emphasis- ing the necessity of a fundamental approach for the integration of AI capabilities to achieve general intelligence. This need for integration encompasses AI planning components as well, not only because of those ultimate objectives but also because many applications in the real 21

2 Contributions world require robust and advanced AI planning systems consisting of various capabilities (see Section 1.2). Problem Current planning tools are not designed with composition and integration in mind, creating a fragmented landscape of planning software with disparate data structures and de- sign approaches, which considerably limits the interaction between the tools (see Barriers 5 and 6). Enabling their interactions requires studying the inner workings of the planning tools, which is a challenging, time-consuming, and error-prone task. This endeavour de- mands expertise not only in planning but also in software engineering. These challenges highlight the need for e ffective approaches for composing, integrating, and deploying AI planning systems. Contributions Such an approach is proposed in (Georgievski & Breitenbücher, 2021), start- ing with the following hypothesis: Composition, integration, and deployment of planning functionalities will be not only pos- sible but also e ffective and e fficient by modularising planning functionalities, incorporating architectural patterns, and enabling configuration and orchestration of planning systems. The work presents a critical analysis of AI planning tools, with a set of observations on their functionalities along with properties and issues related to software, architecture design, con- figuration, and management. Based on these observations, a set of essential prerequisites for the successful composition, integration, and deployment of AI planning technology is pro- posed. Specifically, a discussion is presented on the separation of concerns, loose coupling, portability, automated deployment, and automated management of planning systems. The proposed approach consists of four universal steps for designing and deploying com- posed AI planning systems, moving from a conceptual model to an executable solution that enables and enhances the communication and functionality among disparate planning tools: • Design a Logical Composition Model (LCM), which is a graph with planning compo- nents as nodes and typed composition relationships between the components as edges. • Convert the LCM into a Logical Integration Model (LIM) using messaging technology to enable communication among di fferent planning components (instead of their di- rect invocation, which would be impossible without dedicated glue code). Specifically, LIM injects additional nodes for integration and communication components, such as queues, message routers, and message translators (Hohpe & Woolf, 2004). • Transform the LIM into an Executable Deployment Model (EDM) by inserting hosting components based on the technical requirements of planning and integration compo- nents (e.g., programming languages, required libraries, etc.) and channel adapters to integrate the planning tools with the messaging system (Hohpe & Woolf, 2004). 22

Efforts should strive towards building systems where planning function- alities are not isolated units but components of an interconnected architecture that can sup- port intelligent planning operations in diverse application domains. It should be recognised that the intelligence of a planning system emerges from the coordinated interplay among these planning functionalities. Despite these advancements, the challenge of the architecting of planning systems remains open. The argument is that the architecting of interconnected planning functionalities rests upon the premise that these functionalities exist as distinguishable units. However, such treatment of planning functionalities and their architecting and integration into coherent, deployable, and maintainable AI planning systems remain largely unexplored. Considering this gap and the fact that a system’s intelligence is influenced by its architecture and how well it can integrate diverse planning functionalities, a need arises to investigate the architecting of AI planning systems. 2.1 Design-Driven Planning Note that these contributions are directly relevant to Phases 4, 6, and 8 of the PlanXFlow life cycle (see Figure 2.1). 2.1.4 Toolbox for Building and Integrating AI Planning Systems Context The architectural design of systems that incorporate various planning components is essential for the practical application of AI planning. This development process requires engaging several groups of users, including planning experts, system and software engineers, domain experts, data scientists, and system administrators. The users perform a range of tasks, from general ones, such as installation, configuration, and testing of planning compo- nents, to more specialised technical work, such as formulating planning models and system monitoring. To successfully architect AI planning systems, these user groups need support- ive resources that bridge the gap between the variety of tasks and expertise. Problem The landscape of AI planning tools is characterised by a stack of challenges that complicate the architecting of AI planning systems (Georgievski, 2022b). At the stack’s bot- tom is the complication of distinguishing planning functionalities offered by the tools as sep- arate components. For example, extracting a parsing functionality from one tool to integrate it elsewhere is extremely challenging. Above the distinction challenge is the lack of interop- erability among the tools; even with a shared syntax, there is no foundation for the tools to communicate with each other (see Barrier 5). At the top of the stack is the heterogeneity of these tools, which vary greatly in their expressiveness, programming languages, dependen- cies, and other factors. The shortage of resources that address this stack of challenges is an important obstacle to building and deploying AI planning systems. Contributions Adopting the service-oriented framework proposed in (Georgievski, 2022b), the PlanX Toolbox is presented as an open-source collection of planning functionalities to tackle the challenges outlined above ( Georgievski, 2023b). This paper’s contributions are manifold: • Identification and extraction of several core planning functionalities from existing tools and their encapsulation as distinct services. • Design and implementation of additional planning services to support more user groups. • Realisation of these planning services as microservices for ease of integration and scal- ability (Di Francesco, Malavolta, & Lago, 2017). • The PlanX Toolbox as a collection of nine microservices that can work together and exchange messages via a unifying messaging service, see Figure 2.3.2 2The PlanX Toolbox currently has ten services, where the front-end composite service is decomposed into two distinct services, one for domain modelling and plan visualisation and another for system management. 25

Among these, Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) planning emerges as a preferred planning type due to its support for e ffective representation of complex and rich domain knowledge and its potential e fficiency in plan generation ( Georgievski & Aiello, 2015). These features have made HTN planning a go-to method in various domains, from gaming (Humphreys, 2019) and cloud deployment (Georgievski, Nizamic, et al., 2017) to sustainable buildings (Georgievski, Nguyen, et al., 2017) and autonomous vehicles (Alnazer et al., 2022). As the demand to de- sign solutions that tackle complex, real-world problems increases, the indispensability of HTN planning becomes even more evident. The successful integration of HTN planning systems into such solutions critically depends not only on their capabilities to address real- world challenges but also on the soundness of their system design to meet the requirements of robustness and reliability. Problem The field of HTN planning has a history of influential software tools, from pio- neering planners, such as NOAH (Sacerdoti, 1975) and NONLIN (Tate, 1977), to advanced systems, such as SIPE-2 (Wilkins, 1988) and O-Plan2 (Currie & Tate, 1991). These systems have made significant contributions to the algorithmic, knowledge, and systems engineer- ing aspects of AI planning. However, they have not transitioned into modern system archi- tectures likely due to their dated designs and inaccessibility. Another landmark planner is 26

2.1 Design-Driven Planning (J)SHOP2 (Ilghami, 2006; Nau et al., 2003), which can handle complex problems but has a monolith architecture, posing challenges for the functional modularity and integration be- yond basic library use. Recent HTN planners, such as PDDL4J (Pellier & Fiorino, 2018), HyperTensioN (Magnaguagno, Meneguzzi, & de Silva, 2021), PANDA (Höller et al., 2021), Lilotane (Schreiber, 2021), and pyHiPOP (Lesire & Albore, 2021), showcase their e fficiency in tackling benchmark planning problems of limited expressiveness in controlled settings. Beyond quick plan generation, the designs of these planners have not considered the design choices needed to function as integral parts of complex systems. This creates a substantial gap in architecting HTN planning systems as they must not only solve isolated planning problems but also fit into the dynamic and interconnected real-world environments they aim to serve. Contributions A response to these challenges is the continuous development of SH, an open-source HTN planning system ( Georgievski et al., 2024). While built on the ground- work laid in the author’s doctoral thesis ( Georgievski, 2015), SH is architected with a dual nature in mind: capture the expressiveness of real-world domains and facilitate integration through intentional system design. The key contributions are: • SH o ffers several planning functionalities that adhere to the separation of concern prin- ciple: parsing planning problems described in the Hierarchical Planning Definition Language (Georgievski, 2013), converting HPDL problems into programming-level ob- jects, grounding them during the plan generation phase, and plan generation supported by a depth-first search strategy. • SH supports expressing and reasoning in real-world domains with capabilities for first- order logic and functions. • SH o ffers its functionalities as modular services, enabling standalone use and integra- tion in other systems. • SH has a modular architecture that allows individual components to be replaced or extended and new functionality to be easily added. Through SH, the aim is to redefine the integration of HTN planning within system archi- tectures, providing a robust tool that aligns with the complexities of real-world problem- solving. SH is a potential asset in both academic and industrial applications, empowering users to tailor it to their specific requirements. 27

2 Contributions 2.2 Real-World Planning 2.2.1 Understanding Real-World AI Planning Domains Context The foundational stage in developing AI planning systems involves a deep under- standing and scoping of the domains where these systems will be employed. This stage en- compasses understanding, identification, gathering, and formulating the multifaceted knowl- edge about the targetted real-world domain. The acquired insights are not just preliminary outcomes; they are crucial in guiding the subsequent phases of the software development life cycle for AI planning systems. This is the point where the complexities and characteristics of domains must be captured and translated into suitable elements that will shape subse- quent planning elements, including requirements, planning models, domain models, system design and capabilities, and data provenance. Problem Understanding and scoping out domain knowledge for AI planning is challeng- ing. Domains are inherently diverse, encompassing numerous aspects ranging from physical properties to functional behaviours to qualitative attributes. The current approach to dis- tilling domain knowledge into domain models tends to be individualised and artisanal – if they exist at all, the sources and formats of relevant domain requirements and specifications are unspecified and unstandardised. This leads to domain knowledge and domain models that are influenced by the personal expertise and domain interpretation of individual knowl- edge engineers. This ad-hoc approach raises concerns about the consistency and quality of the resulting domain models. Furthermore, there is no consensus on what aspects constitute comprehensive domain knowledge and the conditions for characterising the realism of do- main models. This lack of clarity and suitable resources present obstacles for engineers to adequately scope knowledge of real-world domains and transform that knowledge into do- main models. The contributions presented herein aim to bridge this gap by answering the following research question: “What are the realistic aspects that should be considered in the process of developing AI planning systems for real-world domains, and how those aspects can be meaningfully organised?” Contributions The primary contribution in (Alnazer & Georgievski, 2023) is the introduc- tion of a conceptual framework that defines the realistic aspects of planning domains. As il- lustrated in Figures 2.4 and 2.5, the framework organises the aspects into seven key categories of multi-level granularity: objectives, tasks, quantities, qualities, constraints, determinism, and agents. Further contributions include: • A top-down exploration, analysis, and collection of characteristics of planning domains as reported in the literature. • A conceptualisation of realism in planning domains. 28

2.2 Real-World Planning • A common and inclusive terminology for various concepts encountered in real-world planning domains. The conceptual framework provides the foundation for engineers to navigate the initial challenges posed by complex problems. It also provides a means for a qualitative assessment of domain models and planning tools by their support and conformity to real-world domain aspects. Finally, the conceptual framework can inform and drive future research on the de- velopment of AI planning techniques and tools and the practical application of AI planning technology across diverse domains. 2.2.2 Risk is Real: Transforming HTN Planning to Embrace Risk Context The conceptual framework shows that real-world environments have an open- world nature, with inherent non-determinism and uncertainty, along with the limited avail- ability of resources, such as energy, time, money, and effort. In the current AI planning land- scape, uncertainty is typically considered through the incomplete initial state and actions with multiple, possibly probabilistic, e ffects. On top of this, a significant oversimplifica- tion is the assumption of uniform costs of actions that incur costs on the limited resources. This assumption contrasts with the reality where costs vary, lack precise predefinition, and sometimes remain completely unpredictable. In fact, the range of uncertainty in action costs spans from totally known probability distributions over costs to totally unknown and even unknowable costs and probabilities, see (Lo & Mueller, 2010). This variability indicates that the choice of actions during planning must be based on its probable cost, leading to the com- putation of plans with a probabilistic nature and variable resource consumption. Therefore, planning in these contexts must involve making decisions that weigh potential risks against costs. Thus, this necessitates not only planning under uncertainty but also planning that embraces risk. Problem Despite the significance of uncertainty and risk in decision-making fields, they remain insufficiently distinguished and integrated as two concepts into AI planning. Non- deterministic planning studies have solely focused on uncertainty, often blurring the lines with risk. In the area of HTN planning, which is particularly desirable for real-world appli- cations, existing approaches dealing with uncertainty generate the most probable or optimal plans based on the assumption of uniform action costs, effectively taking only a stance of risk neutrality. These limitations reveal a gap in AI planning, and specifically, HTN planning, where the ability to account for risk and the multifaceted nature of action costs are absent, making them insufficient for risk management in real-world domains. Contributions To address these gaps, a novel paradigm calledrisk-aware HTN planningis in- troduced in (Alnazer,Georgievski, & Aiello, 2022b). This paradigm enhances HTN planning with the ability to consider different risk attitudes and compute plans with a sensitivity that 29

These domains also provide the planning community with a common ground for assessing the plan generation time and plan quality. So, benchmark domains play a crucial role in driving the enhancement of the plan generation capabilities of AI planners. Beyond evaluation, bench- mark domains can serve as educational resources, helping to understand planning syntax, domain modelling, and workings of planning algorithms. They can also serve as the basis for the development of more complex, real-world domains and, by implication, inspire the development of new planning approaches. In the context of HTN planning, benchmark HTN domain models have been collected for the IPC 2020. Potential contributors were encouraged to submit domain models that go beyond the capabilities of classical planners and exploit the high expressive power of HTN planning (Behnke, Höller, & Bercher, 2021). In the end, there were two sets of collected HTN domains, benchmark HTN domains considered for the IPC and other HTN domains that did not qualify due to the limiting expressiveness constraints of IPC. Some of the domain models in the benchmark set were individually designed while other were translated from benchmark domains for classical planning. 32

2.2 Real-World Planning Problem HTN planning distinguishes itself by structuring the domain knowledge into hier- archical networks of tasks, thereby requiring benchmark domain models that can effectively demonstrate its advantages, such as the representation of rich domain knowledge, handling complex domain models, and efficient plan generation. However, there is a tendency to over- simplify benchmark domain models, which limits their usability beyond IPCs and compar- isons of plan generation time. For example, a notable shortcoming is the lack of multiple methods to achieve tasks, which is a central feature of domain expressiveness and strength of plan generation. While this simplification may fit the IPC needs, it restricts the usabil- ity of benchmark domain models in scenarios with real-world complexities, where choices between alternatives do exist and influence plan quality. Furthermore, the reliance on HTN domain models translated from classical planning benchmarks introduces further limitations and obsolescence. The translated HTN domain models somehow encode hierarchical struc- tures and alternatives, knowledge that is otherwise absent in classical planning benchmarks. At the same time, many of the classical planning benchmarks are dated and do not reflect modern advancements and trends. Contributions The work presented in (Alnazer, Georgievski, & Aiello, 2022a) seeks to ad- dress the gap between the theoretical potential of HTN planning and the practical demand of its benchmark domain models by aligning the domains more closely with real-world com- plexities, extending beyond the constraints of IPCs. Specifically, the work’s contributions are: • A preliminary set of aspects that can make HTN domain models more realistic. These can be considered when refining existing domain models or designing new ones. • A set of structural metrics to characterise the structural diversity of HTN domain mod- els and a set of domain-richness metrics to characterise the depth of encoded domain models in terms of involved objects and their relationships. • An analysis of current benchmark HTN domain models using the structural metrics shows that most benchmark domain models lack strict alternatives 3 with few domains without alternatives at all. • Extensions of two benchmark domain models, Satellite and Rover, considering four aspects: realism, structural diversity, alternative methods, and recent technological de- velopments. Think about the case of sustain- able buildings. The design and implementation of smart energy systems for these buildings strongly influence the efficiency of energy use. These systems should leverage the full poten- tial of digital infrastructure within buildings by incorporating real-time monitoring, recogni- tion, prediction, automation, and optimisation capabilities. The systems need to be designed not only for e fficiency but also to adapt to evolving technologies. The ultimate success of these systems depends on their ability to manage energy in a way that aligns with the needs and well-being of the users – be they facility managers overseeing building operations or occupants whose daily activities are impacted by energy management decisions. Problem Transitioning towards smart energy systems introduces several challenges that re- quire rethinking the design and operation of existing energy systems. Take commercial build- ings as an example. Their energy management systems have been designed with a narrow focus on a specific way of operation, leading to systems with coarse-grained and rigid archi- tectures. Such limitations hinder the integration of emerging technologies and techniques. Additionally, these systems often lack mechanisms for recognising and taking advantage of opportunities for energy savings while considering user needs, especially in real-time. These observations reveal new requirements that are fundamental and defining of a new type of energy system, calling for specific mechanisms and techniques for their satisfaction. 34

2 Contributions Contributions Occupant activity recognition is addressed by framing it as an HTN planning problem (Georgievski, 2022a, 2025b). The contributions can be summarised as follows: • A formulation of key activities, concepts, and features integral to occupant activity recognition, establishing a baseline for understanding the domain. • Formalisations of occupant activity recognition problem and its correspondence to an HTN planning problem. • An extension to temporal HTN planning, where the output consists of recognised ac- tivities with start and end times. • A strategy for engineering domain models based on direct connections between occu- pant activities and the interaction of occupants with objects at specific locations. • An approach to incorporate sensor readings as temporal facts in the initial state, akin to (Fernandez-Olivares & Perez, 2020). • Design and integration considerations of a service for occupant activity recognition as HTN planning. • A use case in o ffice buildings to demonstrate the feasibility of the approach. • Two temporal HTN domain models for occupant activity recognition in Office Buildings and Homes. • Evaluation of the accuracy of the approach on a real-world dataset using the Homes domain and the SIADEX planner (Castillo et al., 2006). The results show oscillating accuracy between 50% and 90%, depending on the activity, due to reliance on single sensors and irrelevant data. • Comparative analysis wiith existing studies, demonstrating advances over data-driven approaches and comparable performance with hybrid ones, see Table 2.4. 2.3.4 Occupant Activity Learning Context In sustainable buildings, the ability to recognise and react to occupant activities in real time has been an important step forward. In this context, the previous approach to occupant activity recognition is capable of identifying occupant activities from historical data or as early as possible upon receipt of relevant IoT data. While this approach enables energy systems to react to the detected activities, these systems still lack the proactive capability to anticipate future occupant activities. Anticipating activities before they occur presents new opportunities for energy saving and improving occupant well-being. 40

Therefore, the question arises of how to enable energy systems to not only react to recognised occupant activities but also to anticipate the activities based on building IoT data. Contributions In (Georgievski, Gupta, & Aiello, 2019), the reaction to and anticipation of occupant activities is cast as an activity learning capability. Specifically, activity learning is the problem of recognising occupant activities and predicting whether they will occur in the future and how long they may last. The proposed approach can learn di fferent occupant activities and can be applicable across various room types. The work’s contributions are as follows: • A formalisation of activity learning as a decomposition of two sequential subproblems: activity recognition and activity prediction. • A definition of these two problems upon a formalised concept of the building environ- ment (Georgievski, Nguyen, et al., 2017). • A correspondence of these two subproblems to classification and regression problems, respectively, within machine learning. • Design and implementation of a system prototype that embodies the formal model and its deployment in an office building at the University of Stuttgart in Germany. • System performance evaluation using standard accuracy metrics. The results show high accuracy in occupant activity recognition, largely attributed to the incorporation of in- direct labelling during the preprocessing step. The results highlight the superiority of classical machine learning algorithms, such as Random Forest, AdaBoost, and k-NN, 41

The reason for such a distinction might be due to the challenges neural networks face with small datasets and data non-linearity. 2.3.5 Temporal Planning for Sustainable Buildings Context The building coordination problem encompasses the requirement of selecting, or- dering, and executing actions of devices and other building components in such a way that balances energy e fficiency with occupant needs, given the current conditions of the build- ing. This problem closely aligns with problems addressed by AI planning, suggesting that AI planning technology could be instrumental in addressing various facets of the building coordination problem. Problem Addressing the building coordination problem introduces several unique and com- plex challenges. First, operating building devices must be compliant with their properties and constraints to ensure minimising building costs. Furthermore, building environments are inherently temporal, much like many real-world domains (Alnazer &Georgievski, 2023). For example, a device operation might be defined using start time, earliest start time, latest finish time, and duration, or there might be operational deadlines, such as heating up a room before its occupant arrives. Additionally, the integration of buildings with smart grid tech- 42

2.4 Author’s Contributions nologies introduces dynamic energy pricing and the availability of battery storage. This inte- gration offers new opportunities for improving the efficiency of building coordination. Thus, an important question arises how can AI planning be utilised in making buildings more sus- tainable and cost-effective considering the temporal nature of building environments and the potential of integrating dynamic energy pricing and storage? Contributions To address these challenges of building coordination, a planning system is presented in ( Georgievski, Shahid, & Aiello, 2023). The design of the planning system is systematically approached by following the first seven phases of the software development lifecycle for engineering planning systems (see Figure 2.1). The specific contributions are: • Capture of domain-oriented and functional requirements, highlighting the importance of application domain knowledge and planning system functionality. • Selection of temporal planning as the most suitable planning type based on the identi- fied requirements. • Construction of a domain model according to the domain-oriented requirements. The domain model is encoded in PDDL version 2.1 (Fox & Long, 2003) and enhanced with timed initial fluents (Piacentini et al., 2015). • Design and implementation of the planning systems based on the gathered require- ments. The system can generate building coordination plans considering various de- vices, environmental conditions, energy prices from the day-ahead energy market, and a battery. • Evaluation of the e ffectiveness of the planning system using scenario analysis, focus- ing on the energy profile of a medium-sized commercial building and using day-ahead prices for February 6, 2023. The results show that the system can achieve an average energy cost reduction of 43% compared to a baseline. Additionally, the system com- pensates with a low cost in the evenings for charging the batteries in the mornings, see Figure 2.9. 2.4 Author’s Contributions The author’s contributions to the collaborative works are attributed as follows. 3 Conclusion and Outlook The habilitation thesis took an unexplored step in framing the problem of adoption in AI planning and outlined seven major barriers to the broader application of AI planning. Rather than challenging existing norms in the AI planning field, the objective was to uncover the missing elements that could facilitate the transformation of AI planning into a powerful tool for innovation. By putting systems engineering into perspective, the habilitation thesis proposes a holistic approach to engineering operational AI planning systems for real-world domains. Under this unity, the work was guided by four overarching research questions fo- cusing on engineering challenges, methodologies, tools, and the application of AI planning in the domain of sustainable buildings. The Design-Driven Planning theme suggests that planning systems are primarily guided or influenced by design principles and considerations from their conceptualisation to their implementation. A significant portion of the presented contributions add to one’s under- standing of systems engineering within AI planning. The thesis presented a software de- velopment life cycle tailored for AI planning systems, encompassing ten typical phases for the design, development, and deployment of these systems. This life cycle is not only a gen- eralised process but also o ffers flexibility for customisation to specific project requirements and circumstances, such as modifying phases, changing their order, or integrating additional life cycles within specific phases, e.g., (Silva, Silva, & Vaquero, 2020). The adoption of the PlanXFlow life cycle, which is also available online in the PlanX Universe,1 can have a signif- icant influence on the development of AI planning in both academic and industrial settings. The execution of some individual phases and the overall life cycle can be challenging, though. One challenge is the di fficulty of formulating suitable planning models, an impor- tant blueprint for the subsequent system design and development. This could be mitigated by exploring recommendation and decision-support solutions (Farshidi et al., 2018), which can facilitate the selection of planning models based on varying requirements and prefer- ences. Another challenge is the accessibility of planning software, especially planners. The information about this software is scattered across websites, textbooks, and scientific publi- cations. A unified platform for sharing planning software could significantly alleviate this challenge and facilitate the adoption of planning. Determining the most suitable planning technique for specific situations requires a deep understanding of planning, a knowledge that is not readily available to users. While portfolio- 1The PlanX Universe is a collection of resources for building, composing, and integrating advanced AI planning systems, accessible at https://github.com/PlanX-Universe. 45

3 Conclusion and Outlook based approaches o ffer some solutions in the selection of the right planner for a task of a specific planning type, more efforts are needed in this context. Exploring holistic testing strategies for planning software and developing a data prove- nance model for AI planning are important research directions. Data provenance is espe- cially crucial not only for understanding the life cycle of plans, see e.g., (Polyak & Tate, 1998; Vaquero, Silva, & Beck, 2011), but also for ensuring the quality of other planning artefacts, such as domain models problem instances. This can help improve the planning process, es- tablish responsibility (e.g., who is responsible for which data), support explainability, and improve system performance. The exploration into Phases 4 and 8 (see Figure 2.1) has uncovered the complexity and potential within planning system design and development in areas such as the separation of concerns and achieving loose coupling in planning functionalities. The presented analysis and proposals pave the way for deeper investigations, such as finding the balance between the abstraction and standardisation of planning services, briefly discussed in (Fratini, Policella, & Donati, 2013) and the author’s doctoral thesis (Georgievski, 2015), and identifying recurring design problems in planning software and proposing solutions for them, known as design patterns (Gamma et al., 1993). The challenge of modularising planning functionalities, as attempted with the PlanX Tool- box, highlights the di fficulty of achieving granularity with planning functionalities. Most of the toolbox’s functionalities are realised using PDDL4’J implementation (Pellier & Fior- ino, 2018), which required the toolbox to adopt PDDL4J’s data structure as a common data model. This raises questions about the suitability and adaptability of this data model across different planning tools and the potential of incorporating additional data models and plan- ning services for a wider inclusion of planning tools and broader application of the toolbox. Useful insights into the usability and applicability of AI planning could be gathered by com- paring the PlanX Toolbox with the Unified Planning Python library (Kapellos, Micheli, & Valentini, 2023; Sadanandam et al., 2023). Designing and integrating a planning system for a particular performance factor might have a significant impact on the function and the form of planning services and systems. Furthermore, engaging with industrial practitioners of AI planning can o ffer valuable in- sights into the challenges of implementing, integrating, and using AI planning in real-world settings. These areas remain open for further exploration. The Real-World Planningtheme encompasses planning with the capacity for modelling and reasoning the complexities and constraints of real-life scenarios. Substantial contributions are made to the integration of realism in planning, primarily advancing knowledge engineer- ing and algorithmic perspectives. The thesis proposed a conceptual framework for real-world domains to help engineers understand and navigate complex challenges, assess domain mod- els and planning tools qualitatively, and guide future planning research. For example, the development of metrics to evaluate a domain model’s realism and validate the conceptual 46

framework across domains remains an open question. In the context of benchmark domains, the thesis identified realistic aspects often over- looked in benchmark HTN domains. It went on to extend two domain models and presented initial sets of structural and domain-richness metrics to assess their level of realism. This opens up opportunities for further research, particularly in exploring the suitability of exist- ing HTN planners to handle the extended domains and understanding the impact of these domains on the performance of planners. The thesis has explored the enhancement of HTN planning with the realistic concept of risk, work that is novel in both HTN planning and the broader AI planning fields. Future research could explore how an agent’s risk attitude might adapt during planning influenced by resource consumption or planning history. A critical challenge lies in how the planning agent manages limited resources to maximise expected utility, especially because the current approach operates under the presumption of unlimited resources. Generally, the capacity of real-world planning can benefit significantly from the integra- tion of planning with other techniques, such as Large Language Models (LLMs). These mod- els have exhibited strong capabilities in generating code and other specifications from natural language input. In the field of AI planning, initial research has explored the use of LLMs to generate PDDL domain models and generate plans, e.g., (Guan et al., 2023; Kambhampati, 2024). However, this remains largely uncharted territory (Pallagani et al., 2024), including exploring the use of LLMs to generate realistic domain models, characterise realism in bench- marks, and support plan generation. The Planning for Sustainability theme refers to the application of AI planning to address challenges related to sustainable development. A significant portion of this thesis was ded- icated to facilitating the adoption of AI planning for sustainable buildings by presenting models, methods, and tools for addressing the building coordination problem. These contri- butions represent a convergence of the three engineering perspectives. The focus was on designing systems and strategies for addressing the multifaceted chal- lenges of building coordination. Specific qualities of energy systems and a blueprint for systems have been designed, emphasising the integration of Activity Recognition and Build- ing Coordination Services, requiring domain models and specific planning goals. This led to the development of an approach for automatically learning action models from building IoT data. While effective, the approach faces some limitations, such as the requirement for a partial domain model. Future work can explore easing such constraints, potentially through advanced reasoning capabilities or LLM integration. The formation of building coordination objectives around occupant activities has been ex- plored, where HTN planning has been utilised for activity recognition based on IoT data. It has been shown that the performance of the approach is comparable with data-based and hybrid approaches. Exploring the potential of the approach, especially compared to ontology-based methods or in terms of real-time performance, offers research opportunities. 47

3 Conclusion and Outlook Future work could also look into integrating problem instance generation mechanisms for other planning languages, enhancing the versatility of the approach. Another focus was predicting occupant activities to allow sustainable buildings to antici- pate and adapt to occupants’ needs. A model that learns single-occupant activities has been presented, suggesting the potential to scale this approach to recognise and predict multiple occupants. Integrating such a model into the building coordination could yield significant benefits in energy efficiency, occupant comfort, and space utilisation. The application of the software development life cycle has been demonstrated in engineer- ing a planning system for managing commercial buildings. This system, which incorporates temporal planning, aims to reduce energy costs using environmental conditions, day-ahead energy pricing, and a storage battery. The developed domain model is general but incor- porates specific building elements, such as lighting, and fixes action durations. This sim- plification may not align well with reality, indicating the need for domain model expansion and further experimentation to evaluate the domain model’s quality and its impact on the performance of the planning system. Planning for Sustainability is undoubtedly a critical area of focus, but an equally impor- tance notion is the mirroring Sustainable Planning. While planning operations are resource- intensive, the optimisation of AI planning technology primarily focuses on reducing plan generation time, overlooking energy consumption. With growing environmental concerns and the growing imperative for green software (Verdecchia et al., 2021) and green AI (Schwartz et al., 2020; Verdecchia, Sallou, & Cruz, 2023), understanding and optimising the energy efficiency of AI planning technology is highly importance. One can start by investigating whether a fast planner necessarily means a green planner. 48

The cover image shows a fragment of a traditional Macedonian iconostasis from the Church of the Nativity of the Virgin Mary in Bitola, Macedonia. Carved in deep wood relief by Jane Krstevski, it represents a visual language shaped by tradition, discipline, and intention. Both require a deliberate shaping of material, be it wood or symbolic representations, to reveal order within complexity. © 2025 Ilche Georgievski

Grounded Evaluation and Repair for NL-to.text: Grounded Evaluation and Repair for NL-to-PDDL Problem Generation Joana Rosa1,3, Pedro Santos1, Valdemar Oliveira4, Rom˜ao Silva4, L. Miguel Silveira1, 2, 3, Bruno Martins2, 3 1INESC INOV , Lisbon, Portugal 2INESC ID, Lisbon, Portugal 3Instituto Superior T´ecnico, Universidade de Lisboa, Lisbon, Portugal 4Motamineral Minerais Industriais S.A. {joana.rosa, pedro.santos}@inov.pt {bruno.g.martins, lms}@tecnico.ulisboa.pt {valdemar.oliveira, romao.silva}@mota-sc.com Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown promise for translating Natural Language (NL) planning descriptions into PDDL problem instances. However, standard evaluation cri- teria such as syntactic validity or planner success can sub- stantially overestimate faithfulness to the described task: a generated problem may be parseable and solvable while mis- representing the intended initial state, goal, object structure, or optimization target. This paper studies an end-to-end NL- to-PDDL pipeline that combines LLM generation, checks in terms of PDDL parsing, planning and validation, a domain- conformance checker, an LLM critic, and iterative repair. Fine-grained repair feedback is constructed from the do- main description, the generated problem, the natural language problem description, and operational diagnostics. Reference- based comparisons against curated benchmark PDDL prob- lem descriptions are used for post-hoc benchmark analysis, and these offline checks include renaming-invariant structural matching and semantic equivalence, where domain support is available. Across Planetarium, AutoPlanBench, and curated PDDL 2.1 problems, results show that operational success and benchmark-reference reconstruction can diverge substan- tially. Results also show that structured repair can be useful, and that PDDL 2.1 remains challenging for reference recon- struction, even when operational success improves. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to translate Natural Language (NL) task descriptions into formal planning representations that can be solved by sym- bolic planners (Liu et al. 2023; Gestrin, Kuhlmann, and Seipp 2024). Within this setting, NL-to-PDDL generation has emerged as a central problem. The Plan Domain Def- inition Language (PDDL) is the standard formal language for symbolic planning, being supported by many classical and temporal planners. Still, writing PDDL specifications requires substantial expertise. Translating natural language task descriptions into PDDL offers a natural interface be- tween non-expert users and symbolic planning systems, but it is also demanding: small errors in object declarations, ini- Copyright © 2026, Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (www.aaai.org). All rights reserved. tial predicates, goals, optimization metrics, or numeric flu- ents, may significantly alter the resulting planning problem. A major difficulty in this area concerns evaluation. A generated instance may be parseable and even solvable, while encoding the wrong initial state, omitting required predicates, specifying a subtly incorrect goal, or optimizing the wrong quantity. Stronger result validation protocols are therefore needed beyond parseability and planner success alone (Zuo et al. 2024), although strong semantic evalua- tion is challenging and likely only available for a restricted subset of planning domains. Considering the aforementioned challenges, this paper reports a detailed analysis guided by three main ques- tions: how can NL-to-PDDL generation be evaluated in a deployment-realistic setting that considers few-shot exam- ples and iterative repairs; how large is the gap between oper- ational acceptance and stricter reference-based benchmark reconstruction metrics; and how well do operational eval- uation and repair procedures transfer to PDDL 2.1 bench- marks with temporal and numeric constructs. Through ex- periments, we show that few-shot prompting and iterative repair improve operational performance in several settings, although reconstructing the curated benchmark references remains difficult, especially in the case of PDDL 2.1. Feedback-guided repair is an established strategy in LLM-assisted planning model generation, where prior work has used formal, symbolic, validator, and environment feed- back to refine generated models. This paper studies the same general repair philosophy in the narrower setting of NL-to- PDDL generation of problem descriptions, assuming that the domain model is already given. Concretely, we com- bine parser, domain-conformance, planner, validation with V AL, and NL critic feedback in a unified problem genera- tion loop. We also distinguish operational acceptance from benchmark-reference reconstruction, and empirically exam- ine how these signals diverge across Planetarium, AutoPlan- Bench, and curated PDDL 2.1 settings. 2 Background Research connecting LLMs and automated planning has de- veloped along two broad directions. One line of work stud- ies whether language models can act as planners directly arXiv:2609.09898v1 [cs.AI] 9 Sep 2026

(Verma et al. 2025), often generating or selecting plans from NL task descriptions (Valmeekam et al. 2023; Silver et al. 2024). Another direction instead uses language mod- els as planning formalizers, translating user descriptions into structured representations that can be processed by sym- bolic planning systems (Oswald et al. 2026). This second direction has become increasingly important because it sep- arates two difficult problems: interpreting natural language and solving the resulting planning problem once a correct formal model is available. Planning formalization has indeed been increasingly treated as a language generation task. Some studies focus on restricted forms of formalization, such as translating NL goals into structured planning goals (Xie et al. 2023), while others consider richer settings in which complete plan- ning representations must be recovered from text (Huang and Zhang 2024). Recent datasets have pushed the problem beyond closed benchmark descriptions and toward open- domain procedural text, showing that performance degrades substantially once the input becomes less templated and more semantically demanding (Zhang et al. 2024). A related line of work has also begun to address domain generation, moving beyond problem-instance specification toward full planning model acquisition from natural language (Gestrin, Kuhlmann, and Seipp 2024; Oswald et al. 2024). Several closely related systems use feedback to refine generated planning models. Guan et al. use PDDL val- idators and human corrective feedback to improve gen- erated world/domain models. In turn, Mahdavi et al. use environment-interaction feedback for automated PDDL translation and planning, while Oswald et al. study sym- bolic feedback-driven search over planning domain model spaces, including validator output (Guan et al. 2023; Mah- davi et al. 2024; Oswald et al. 2024, 2026). Recent surveys position this line of work as part of a broader shift from using LLMs directly as planners toward using them as planning formalizers that construct or refine symbolic planning mod- els for downstream planners (Tantakoun, Muise, and Zhu 2025). Together, these studies show that formal, symbolic, and interaction-based feedback are increasingly central to LLM-assisted planning formalization. Related work has further shown that language models can be combined with formal verification or satisfiability-based reasoning tools to handle planning problems more reliably than by direct plan generation alone (Hao et al. 2024). 3 Method We define a pipeline that takes as input a NL problem de- scription and a PDDL domain file and produces a candi- dateproblem.pddl. The overall workflow combines ini- tial generation, operational evaluation, feedback construc- tion, and iterative repair. As shown in Figure 1, the same generation step is reused throughout the loop: a candidate instance is generated, checked for operational acceptabil- ity, and either accepted or revised through structured feed- back. The same architecture is used for both classical PDDL and PDDL 2.1, with the latter additionally requiring metric- sensitive checking and planner selection that distinguishes temporal-only from numeric-fluent problems. Figure 1: Overview of the proposed NL-to-PDDL genera- tion, evaluation, and repair pipeline. 3.1 Initial Generation Given a NL problem description and a PDDL domain file, a language model is prompted to generate a complete problem.pddlinstance, including objects, initial state, goals, and, when applicable, optimization metrics and nu- meric initializations. The output must be consistent with the predicate vocabulary and action schema defined in the PDDL problem domain specification. In selected settings, the prompt is augmented with a small number of same-domain few-shot examples. Each example pairs a NL planning description with its corresponding refer- enceproblem.pddl, thereby demonstrating how descrip- tions in that domain map to object declarations, initial facts, and goal conditions. These examples are distinct from the target instance and serve only as demonstrations of the in- tended translation pattern. The model must infer the correct inventory of objects, de- termine which relations belong in the initial state, identify the intended goal, recover the intended optimization target when one is present, and preserve consistency with the for- mal domain definition. 3.2 Online Operational Evaluation and Offline Benchmark Analysis The pipeline distinguishes betweenonline operational eval- uation, which determines whether the repair loop should stop, andoffline benchmark analysis, which is computed for benchmarking and when a referenceproblem.pddl is available. This distinction is central to the experimental methodology adopted in this work. Online Operational Evaluation.Each generated prob- lem is first subjected to a sequence of checks. 1.Parsing:The generatedproblem.pddldescription must be parseable. 2.Domain Conformance:A static checker verifies that all referenced objects are declared, predicate names belong to the domain vocabulary, predicate arities are respected, and typing constraints are not violated. The checker is intentionally local and conservative, in the sense that it detects violations of the given domain rather than proving full semantic faithfulness to the NL description. 3.Planning and Validation:If parsing and static checks succeed, a planner is executed and any returned plan is validated with V AL1. For classical domains, we use the 1https://github.com/KCL-Planning/V AL

Fast Downward planner2. For PDDL 2.1, time-simple do- mains are handled with TFD 3, and numeric-fluent do- mains are processed with ENHSP4. 4.LLM Critic:An additional LLM critic compares the NL description with the generatedproblem.pddl, taking into account the domain file and the automated diagnos- tics. When it rejects an input instance, it returns a struc- tured judgment identifying each detected problem, its lo- cation, and its type. A candidate is accepted only if it is parseable, domain- conformant, solvable, V AL-valid, and accepted by the LLM critic. We refer to this conjunction of conditions asoper- ational success. This criterion is deliberately stricter than parser/planner success alone, yet it does not depend on ac- cess to a curated reference problem file. The LLM critic is instructed to be conservative. In partic- ular, it must anchor its claims in explicit evidence from the NL description, the domain, or the generated PDDL. It must also distinguish object-existence issues from state-level is- sues, and prefer reporting ambiguity rather than inventing unsupported mismatches. Together, parse success, domain conformance, planner success, V AL validity, and critic ac- ceptance, provide the operational backbone of the pipeline. Stopping Criteria.The repair loop stops under any of the following conditions. •Operational Success:All the aforementioned online checks succeed. •Unchanged Generation:The currentproblem.pddl is identical to the previous attempt, indicating that the model is not making progress under the current feedback. •No Actionable Feedback:The evaluator cannot provide concrete repair guidance, even though operational suc- cess has not been reached. •Maximum Attempts Exhausted:The configured value for the maximum number of attempts is reached. Theunchanged generationandno actionable feedback conditions are important in practice because they prevent the loop from wasting attempts once it has become stagnant or diagnostically uninformative. Semantic Evaluation:When the domain has semantic support, the generated problem can be evaluated against the reference instance through a semantic-equivalence proce- dure. In this work, this is possible for domains supported by the Planetarium (Zuo et al. 2024) benchmark, which rep- resents PDDL problems as graphs over objects and propo- sitions, and checks equivalence after completing partially specified goals. This support is domain-specific, as seman- tic evaluation is available only for domains for which the required oracle and graph-construction functions have been implemented. Note that semantic equivalence is used only as anoffline benchmark-analysis signal. This signal is highly informative for reference-based analysis, but it is not used 2https://www.fast-downward.org/latest/ 3https://tfd.informatik.uni-freiburg.de/ 4https://sites.google.com/view/enhsp/ inside the repair loop because a reference problem instance would not be available. Structural Evaluation.In all runs, a renaming-invariant structural comparison can be computed between the gen- erated problem and the reference instance. The comparison checks four components explicitly: • the typed object declarations in:objects, • the atomic facts in:init, • the atomic facts in:goal, • the optimization objective in:metric. For PDDL 2.1, the same comparison also evaluates nu- meric fluents structurally, by checking the corresponding as- signments and numeric initial values in canonical form. The metric clause is evaluated strictly: both the optimization di- rection (e.g.,minimizevs.maximize) and the optimized expression itself must match after canonicalization. Rather than requiring literal identity of object names, the comparison abstracts away from naming and searches for a consistent bijection between generated and reference objects. To reduce unnecessary computation, the structural comparison first checks whether an identity mapping already yields a match when the object names coincide. Only if that fast path fails does it search over alternative bijections. Af- ter aligning objects under the selected mapping, it compares the resulting object declarations, initial facts, goal facts, and metric clause. The comparison is order-insensitive and based on a canonical PDDL problem representation (e.g., line comments are ignored before fact extraction so that an- notations do not introduce spurious mismatches). When semantic support is available, both semantic equiv- alence and structural matching can be computed offline. However, neither is used as the online acceptance crite- rion, due to the dependence on access to a curated refer- ence problem file. Instead, both serve as post-hoc measures of benchmark-reference reconstruction, allowing us to quan- tify the gap between operational success and recovery of the curated reference encoding. An example for the structured matching procedure is provided in Appendix E. 3.3 Iterative Repair Whenever the generated problem fails the online accep- tance criterion, feedback is constructed and returned to the model for repair. The feedback includes both coarse-grained and fine-grained signals. Coarse-grained feedback reports whether the instance parsed successfully, whether it passed the domain checker, whether a plan was found, whether val- idation succeeded, and whether the critic accepted it. Fine- grained feedback is constructed from the checker diagnos- tics, planner/validator outcomes, and critic output, identify- ing issues such as undeclared objects, predicate-arity mis- matches, domain-incompatible facts, critic-identified initial- ization or goal mismatches, or suspected discrepancies be- tween the NL description and the generated problem. As illustrated in Figure 1, the repair loop does not rely on a separate repair module. Instead, the generation step is in- voked again with the same task inputs, augmented with the previously generatedproblem.pddland the structured

feedback derived from evaluation. The loop continues until operational success is reached, the generation stops chang- ing, no actionable feedback is available, or the maximum attempt budget is exhausted. 3.4 Offline Benchmark Analysis Across Different Planning Tasks The same generate-and-repair pipeline was applied across both the Planetarium and the AutoPlanBench bench- marks. When reference problems are available, we compute benchmark-based analysis signals offline. In domains with Planetarium semantic support, this includes both seman- tic equivalence and renaming-invariant structural matching. In unsupported domains, the available offline signal is the structural criterion alone. This yields a unified operational pipeline with broader domain coverage and stronger post- hoc analysis whenever benchmark references exist. We additionally considered PDDL 2.1 planning, using six manually curated benchmark domains de- rived from IPC 2002 domains:depot-numeric, depot-time-simple,driverlog-numeric, driverlog-time-simple,rovers-numeric, and rovers-time-simple. In this setting, the generation and repair logic are the same, while planner support is split across Temporal Fast Downward (TFD) for time- simple domains, and the Expressive Numeric Heuristic Search Planner (ENHSP) for numeric-fluent domains. This allows testing the pipeline on temporal and numeric PDDL 2.1 settings, using efficient planners according to different problem requirements. Overall, we assessed a unified operational evaluation-and-repair framework for NL-to-PDDL tasks, that can be applied across benchmarks and planning formalisms, while retaining semantic and structural comparison as offline benchmark analysis signals whenever they are available. 4 Experimental Setup We now discuss the considered experimental setup. 4.1 Benchmarks and Data As mentioned in the previous section, two main bench- mark sources were used for classical planning experiments. The first was Planetarium (Zuo et al. 2024), which pro- vides native support for semantic equivalence checking in selected domains. The second was AutoPlanBench (Stein et al. 2025), which provides NL resources across a broader range of planning domains. AutoPlanBench was integrated through a dataset adapter that normalizes each instance into a common representa- tion, consisting of a NL input, a domain file, and a reference problem.pddlfile. In this setting, the NL input was not read from per-instance description files. Instead, it was gen- erated automatically from each referenceproblem.pddl using AutoPlanBench’s domain-level natural language re- sources, which provide object-name mappings and predicate verbalizations through templates. This yields a standardized NL description of the objects, initial state, and goal, while preserving the benchmark’s domain-specific verbalization. The experimental analysis covers three main subsets. •Classical, Semantically Supported:Planetarium and AutoPlanBench domains for which Planetarium-style se- mantic support is available, namelyblocksworld, gripperandfloor-tile/floortile. Each run attempts 60 problem instances. •Classical, Structurally Evaluated:AutoPlanBench do- mains without Planetarium semantic support, namely depot,logisticsandsatellite. A total of 60 problem instances are considered. •PDDL 2.1, Structurally Evaluated:Six sets of manually curated domain variants derived from IPC 2002, namelydepot-numeric, depot-time-simple,driverlog-numeric, driverlog-time-simple,rovers-numeric, androvers-time-simple. Each of the six sets contains ten benchmark instances together with a same-domain few-shot example. To characterize the benchmark instances more concretely, we also computed simple size statistics from the curated ref- erence problems. Classical semantically supported examples contain on average 8.2 objects (range 4–19), 13.0 initial facts (6–57), and 4.8 goal atoms (1–11). Unsupported classical AutoPlanBench examples are somewhat larger in the initial state, with 13.4 objects (6–18), 20.0 initial facts (5–28), and 2.5 goal atoms (1–5). The curated PDDL 2.1 examples con- tain 9.1 objects (7–13), 23.4 initial facts or numeric initial- izations (10–44), and 1.6 goal atoms (1–3), with a metric clause present in all instances. 4.2 Prompting Conditions Experiments were conducted withgpt-4.1-minias the base generation model and the critic. Each example was pro- cessed with up to three attempts, consisting of one initial generation followed by up to two repair iterations. All LLM calls used a default decoding temperature of0.0, including generation, repair, and critic calls. Two prompting conditions were considered: •Baseline:Direct generation from the PDDL domain file and natural language description. •Baseline + Few-Shot:The baseline prompt augmented with one same-domain few-shot example. Few-shot selection is dataset-specific: Planetarium uses local same-domain examples with a compatibility fallback when needed, while AutoPlanBench uses the benchmark’s domain-specific few-shot resources aligned with the adapted problem.pddl. PDDL 2.1 uses one same-domain exam- ple from each of the six benchmark sets. The initial prompt asks the model to generate only a valid problem.pddlfile from the natural language description, target domain name, and exact domain PDDL, including ob- jects, initial state, goals, and metrics when applicable. The repair prompt reuses the same inputs, adds the previous draft and structured evaluator feedback, and asks for the small- est set of edits needed to restore domain compliance and faithfulness to the NL description. The critic prompt is sep- arated from both generation and repair: it receives the NL

description, domain, generated problem, and automated di- agnostics, and returns a structured acceptance judgment to- gether with localized issues when the instance should be re- vised. Additional runs withgpt-5.5andopus-4.7are reported in Appendix C and show the same qualitative pat- tern: operational acceptance is often high, while reference- based reconstruction remains more variable, especially in PDDL 2.1. 4.3 Evaluation Protocol All planning-based checks were performed with the Fast Downward solver and with V AL in classical domains. In the case of PDDL 2.1 problems, time-simple domains were evaluated with TFD and V AL, while numeric-fluent domains were evaluated with ENHSP and V AL. For all experiments, the online pipeline used the same operational acceptance criterion: a candidate problem.pddlwas accepted only if it parsed, passed the domain-conformance checker, yielded a plan, produced a V AL-valid plan, and was accepted by the LLM critic. If any of these conditions failed, structured feedback was constructed and returned to the model together with the previous candidate, yielding an iterative repair loop that executes for up to three total attempts. When benchmark references were available, renaming- invariant structural matching was computed offline after the run, with semantic equivalence available as an additional signal in domains supported by the corresponding Planetar- ium oracle. These offline metrics quantify how often an op- erationally accepted instance also reconstructs the curated benchmark reference problem. In other words, they mea- sure the gap between deployment-realistic acceptance and benchmark-reference reconstruction. 4.4 Evaluation Metrics The evaluation protocol separates operational acceptance from benchmark-reference fidelity. Offline structural and se- mantic comparisons should not be interpreted as assessing whether a generated PDDL problem is the only correct rep- resentation of the intended planning instance. Rather, they measure how closely the generated problem reconstructs the curated benchmark reference encoding, up to the equiva- lences supported by each benchmark. For this reason, the analysis combines operational acceptance metrics, offline benchmark analysis metrics, and repair-oriented measures. The main online metric isoperational success rate(Op.), which corresponds to the fraction of examples that satisfy the full acceptance criterion: OpSucc = 1N NX i=1 1[parsei∧checki∧solvei∧V ALi∧critici]. We also report the individual component rates in appendix: parse success, domain conformance (Domain Conf.), solve success, V AL plan validity (V AL-valid), and critic accep- tance (Critic Acc.). Metrics are reported for the initial gen- eration (Step-0) and/or for the final output after any re- pair. Gains denote final minus Step-0 accuracy for the cor- responding metric. Each experimental run evaluates results over 60 examples, unless stated otherwise due to timeouts. The termNdenotes completed examples, so60−Ncor- responds to example-level timeouts. We also report average end-to-end runtime per completed example. Because the loop may terminate without success, we ad- ditionally report the main non-success stopping outcomes: unchanged generation (Stop: Unchanged) and maximum- attempt exhaustion (Stop: Max Att.). The no-actionable- feedback condition did not occur in the reported runs and is omitted from the tables. These statistics are important for interpreting whether repair failures arise from stagnation or from limits in the attempt budget. Using the benchmark references, we additionally com- pute offline reference-based metrics. Renaming-invariant structural accuracy (Struct.) is the common offline signal across all benchmarks, defined as exact agreement with the curated reference problem up to a consistent object renam- ing over:objects,:init,:goal, and:metric. This criterion is intentionally strict, in that a failed structural match does not necessarily imply that the generated problem is invalid or useless as a planning instance. Instead, it indi- cates that the generated problem does not recover the partic- ular reference encoding used by the benchmark. We there- fore interpret structural accuracy as benchmark-reference re- construction accuracy, and not as an absolute test assess- ing the preservation of task semantics. In semantically sup- ported domains, semantic equivalence (Sem.) is also com- puted through the corresponding domain-specific oracle. We explicitly report the divergence between online and offline criteria throughOp. Non-Struct., i.e. the fraction of exam- ples accepted operationally but not structurally matched, and Struct. Non-Op., i.e. the fraction of structurally matched but not operationally accepted instances. To quantify iterative improvement in the offline analysis, repair gainis defined as the difference between the final reference-match rate and the reference-match rate at the ini- tial generation step: RepairGain = RefMatchfinal −RefMatch step0. For all reported settings, we compare operational suc- cess with structural benchmark matching in order to identify cases in which an instance is accepted by the online pipeline but fails the offline reference-match criterion, or matches the reference structurally but fails an operational check. 5 Experimental Results We first analyze classical domains with semantic support, then unsupported classical domains, and finally PDDL 2.1

The diver- gence rows make the gap explicit: operationally accepted but structurally unmatched outputs account for 0.500 of the baseline run and 0.667 of the few-shot run, while no struc- turally matched output fails operational acceptance. This in- dicates that operational feedback helps produce accepted PDDL 2.1 instances but does not by itself recover metric- sensitive benchmark structure.
