s10515-025-00549-x.pdf.text: Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10515-025-00549-x Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have made significant advancements in code-relat- ed tasks. In the field of automated debugging, fault localization (FL) and automated program repair (APR) are two prevalent topics attracting significant research effort. Recently, in the field of FL and APR, many novel LLM-based approaches have emerged. However, most existing LLM-based studies primarily focus on the GPT models from OpenAI or open-source LLMs. With the rapid development of LLMs, various internet giants have introduced new closed-source models. In addition, due to policy restrictions, some regions can only access the commercial LLMs provided by specified companies. Despite the LLMs of OpenAI, the effectiveness of the other closed-source LLMs in FL and APR remains unknown. To better understand the ef - fectiveness of contemporary closed-source models, we conduct a large-scale empiri- cal study on their performance with respect to FL and APR. Specifically, our study involves 4 recent commercial closed-source LLMs (i.e., GPT-4o-Mini, Ernie-3.5, Qwen-turbo, and Doubao-pro) and 1 open-source LLM (i.e., DeepSeek-V3-chat). Note that only the GPT models have region restrictions among all LLMs we stud - ied. We designed a total of 12 distinct prompt templates, 6 each for FL and APR, incorporating various formats and information sources. We conducted experiments to evaluate the effectiveness of FL and APR on 1036 real Java bugs from two da - tasets, Defects4J 2.0 and ConDefects. The key findings of the experiments indicate that (1) different LLMs tend to succeed on different sets of bugs in both FL and APR, with relatively little overlap among successful cases, implying the models possess distinct strengths in handling specific kinds of bugs, (2) the effectiveness of prompt templates varies across different models, and (3) the effectiveness of FL and APR capabilities of the studied models is significantly correlated with the bug type. We summarized all 14 findings obtained into 3 implications, which could help researchers further improve the performance of LLMs on FL and APR. Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 Keywords Large language models · Software debugging · Fault localization · Automated program repair · Empirical study 1 Introduction Bugs are pervasive in modern software systems, posing significant risks to various aspects of daily life. Debugging these issues is a notoriously time-consuming and challenging task, often consuming more than half of a developer’s programming time (Gazzola et al. 2018). Therefore, substantial research efforts have focused on developing automated debugging techniques to mitigate this burden for programmers. Two prominent research areas within the field of automated debugging are Fault Localization (FL) and Automated Program Repair (APR) (Chen et al. 2025; Wong et al. 2016; Martinez et al. 2017; Zhang et al. 2023). FL techniques are designed to automatically identify and localize buggy code elements, such as lines or meth - ods (Lou et al. 2020; Meng et al. 2022; Lou et al. 2021; Xie et al. 2022), while APR techniques aim to automatically generate patches to repair these bugs without human intervention (Zhang et al. 2023; Zhu et al. 2023; Ye et al. 2022a, b; Lutellier et al. 2020). Both FL and APR have increasingly leveraged deep-learning models, which have been instrumental in capturing and understanding the context of buggy code (Zhang et al. 2023; Meng et al. 2022; Lou et al. 2021; Xie et al. 2022). Despite their advancements, the performance of these approaches remains limited. For exam- ple, although their training data could include billions of historical bugs or patches, their data scale is still far from large enough (Chen et al. 2025). Additionally, their models still have certain shortcomings in understanding code structure and seman - tics, such as being unable to handle long-range dependencies when representing code. In recent years, the remarkable success of Large Language Models (LLMs) has spurred interest in applying these models to FL (Kang et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024) and APR (Fan et al. 2023; Xia and Zhang 2024; Fan et al. 2023; Xia et al. 2023). Existing LLM-based FL and APR studies almost leverage the LLMs provided by OpenAI (such as the family of ChatGPT and CodeX) or open-source LLMs (such as CodeT5 Wang et al. 2021 and CodeLlama Roziere et al. 2023). For example, the most recent peer-reviewed paper by Xia and Zhang, which was published in 2024, still employs ChatGPT-3.5 (Xia and Zhang 2024) to perform conversational program repair. With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), companies and research institutions are continuously introducing new closed-source models. Nota - bly, to date, only commercial closed-source models from the OpenAI family (such as Codex and GPT models) have been extensively studied in the context of FL and APR. In contrast, the new closed-source LLMs from other technical companies have received limited attention in the academic community. Furthermore, due to policy restrictions, many internet companies impose regional limitations on the use of their models, resulting in significant variations in model accessibility and performance across different regions. Although we could opt to use the best-performing models, such as those from the GPT series, for SE tasks, it remains critical to evaluate other closed-source models, especially since models from different regions may offer differ- 1 3 26 Page 2 of 42

Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 ent capabilities due to access restrictions. Exploring the effectiveness of these models and comparing them with contemporary open-source LLMs is crucial for providing a comprehensive guide to LLM users and for shaping future research directions. These considerations have motivated us to conduct this study, aiming to fill existing gaps in the literature and offer a more thorough understanding for LLM users. In this paper, we intend to evaluate the effectiveness of recent closed-source general-purpose LLMs in FL and APR. We conducted a large-scale empirical study on 1036 real-world Java bugs from 2 bug datasets, where 760 bugs from Defects4J 2.0 (Just et al. 2014) and 276 bugs from ConDefects (Wu et al. 2024). Our study covers 5 LLMs, including 4 commercial closed-source LLMs (i.e., GPT-4o-Mini, Ernie-3.5, Qwen-turbo, and Doubao-pro) and 1 open-source LLM (i.e., Deepseek- V3-Chat). We employ the latest open-source LLM to provide a baseline for compar- ing the performance differences between open-source and closed-source LLMs in FL and APR tasks, offering insights for users to choose the most suitable models. Among these models, GPT-4o-Mini is from OpenAI and is restricted in some regions, while the others have no region restrictions. We design a total of 12 distinct prompt tem - plates, 6 each for FL and APR, by incorporating various formats and information sources. Specifically, we involve various elements, including source code, stack traces, and failure assertions in different prompts, utilizing 2 different formats, each specifying either the target code lines or the surrounding code context. To achieve a direct understanding of the capabilities of LLMs, following existing LLM-based studies (Xia and Zhang 2022; Fan et al. 2023; Xia et al. 2023), we perform zero-shot setting by interacting APIs of these LLMs, i.e., performing FL and APR directly gen- erate feedback from LLMs under the non-conversational style, without fine-tuning or training on corpus of bugs. We conducted the experiments on both FL and APR. The results indicate that all these LLMs could successfully localize 558 (53.9%) and fix 181 (17.5%) out of all bugs. We further analyzed the results and gained 14 key findings. These findings can be summarized as follows. 1. Although Deepseek-V3 and GPT-4o-Mini achieved the highest overall perfor - mance, the other models exhibit low overlap in successfully located/repaired bugs, indicating varied capabilities across different models. For FL, Deepseek- V3 and GPT-4o-Mini successfully locate 365 and 345 out of 1036 bugs, respec- tively, while the remaining LLMs locate 126 (i.e., 84 Defects4J bugs and 42 ConDefects bugs) bugs that are uncovered by them. For APR, Deepseek-V3 and GPT-4o-Mini correctly fix 149 and 115 bugs, respectively, while the remaining LLMs supply 19 more bugs (i.e., 11 Defects4J bugs and 8 ConDefects bugs). 2. For complex code-related tasks such as FL and APR, prompt design plays a cru- cial role. For ChatGPT 3.5, the trend is clear that the prompts with more infor - mation exhibit better performance in FL. However, for another model, adding more information may decrease the FL performance. Our analysis of different prompts for FL and APR reveals that each task has a distinct prompt that per - forms significantly better than others (i.e., FL P5 and APR P2). This suggests that when designing prompts, providing concise yet essential contextual information while specifying a clear and simple output format can effectively enhance the 1 3 Page 3 of 42 26

Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 performance of LLMs. For instance, all the prompts specified to directly return code snippets significantly outperform the prompts specified to encapsulate the results with a JSON format, while for FL, the prompts with stack traces but with- out test assertions outperform others. 3. We further analyze the correlation between bug types and the bugs successfully localized or fixed by LLMs, confirming a significant relationship between them. Most bugs located or fixed by LLMs are simple bugs within a single line or even a single expression. While the bugs of complex bug types challenge the effective- ness of current LLMs. Based on the findings, we summarized 3 implications that can help developers better utilize closed-source LLMs for FL and APR, while also providing researchers with valuable insights for proposing new methods in the future. In summary, our paper makes the following contributions: ● We perform a large-scale empirical study on FL and APR, considering the recent closed-source LLMs that are rarely explored. We studied 5 LLMs on 1036 real- world Java bugs from 2 datasets. ● We evaluate different prompt templates for FL and APR, respectively. For each task, we design 6 templates considering the context and output format, and evalu- ate their effectiveness on each model. ● We first analyze the correlations between the bug types and the FL and APR ef - fectiveness of LLMs. ● We observed 14 key findings from the experiment results and summarized 3 im- plications for guiding future research and practice use for LLM-based FL and APR. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we elaborate on the design of our study. In Section 3, we show the evaluation results and the findings analyzed from the results. In Seciton 4, we discuss the implications of our study and the threats to validity. In Section 5, we present the related work on LLM for code tasks, FL, and APR approaches. In Section 6, we conclude this paper. 2 Study design In this section, we illustrate the design of our study. 2.1 Overview Figure 1 illustrates the overview of our study. For each bug from the selected bench- mark, we create prompts by customizing a predefined template with context informa- tion extracted from the code and test failure messages. We designed distinct prompt templates specifically for FL and APR. These tailored prompts are then sent to the 1 3 26 Page 4 of 42

Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 target LLMs via invoking their APIs, and their responses are collected and processed. If the prompt length exceeds the token limit of the LLMs, we truncate it accordingly to fit within the constraints. For the FL results generated by the LLMs, we auto - matically evaluate whether the identified lines or statements fall within the actual bug locations. For APR results, we automatically apply the generated patches and execute them against the whole test suite. If a patch successfully passes all test cases, we further conduct a manual analysis to determine whether it is semantically equivalent to the developer’s patch. Note that these evaluation settings align with established practices in both research fields. 2.2 Research question We investigate the performance of selected LLMs in FL and APR by answering the following research questions (RQs). ● RQ1: How do different closed-source LLMs perform in FL? ● RQ2: How do different prompts affect the effectiveness of closed-source LLMs in FL? ● RQ3: How do different bug types affect the effectiveness of closed-source LLMs in FL? ● RQ4: How do different closed-source LLMs perform in APR? ● RQ5: How do different prompts affect the effectiveness of closed-source LLMs in APR? ● RQ6: How do different bug types affect the effectiveness of closed-source LLMs in APR? The first three RQs explore their effectiveness for FL, while the last three RQs explore for APR. As explained before, due to regional restrictions driven by policy, we specifically target closed-source commercial LLMs released in China. All the models we studied claim that they support coding-related tasks and provide API access. For each model, we select the most recent version to evaluate its current capacities in FL and APR. The details of the selected models are shown as Table 1. 2.4 Datasets We intend to evaluate the debugging capabilities of LLMs on real bugs. We employ the widely studied benchmark Defects4J v2.0 (Just et al. 2014), a dataset containing 760 real-world Java bugs from 17 high-impact open-source projects. The bugs of Defects4J are collected from the development procedure of these projects. Each bug from Defects4J contains a buggy version extracted from the development history, a fixed version which is the developers’ patch for the very bug, and at least one failed test to trigger the bug. The bugs from Defects4J 2.0 are considered source-code- related, reproducible, and isolated (Sobreira et al. 2018). Defects4J is considered to be the baseline benchmark in the field of FL (Li et al. 2019; Lou et al. 2021; Benton et al. 2020; Zou et al. 2019; Zeng et al. 2022; Meng et al. 2022; Yang et al. 2024) and APR (Xin and Reiss 2017; Xiong et al. 2017; Xin and Reiss 2017; Wen et al. 2018; Jiang et al. 2018; Ye et al. 2022a; Xiao et al. 2024; Xiong and Wang 2022; Ye et al. 2022b; Zhu et al. 2023; Wang et al. 2024; Xin et al. 2024; Xia and Zhang 2024). To mitigate the risk of overfitting by the LLMs on widely used benchmark datas - ets, we utilized an alternative dataset, ConDefects (Wu et al. 2024), which is derived from programming competition problems hosted on AtCoder1 along with their corre- sponding solutions. Table 2 illustrates the projects and their bugs. 2.5 FL experiments setups In our study, we directly use a zero-shot fashion single-round conversation to perform FL. Directly querying an LLM for answers remains a widely used baseline approach in research and also in development practice. Note that although the multi-round conversation typically improves the performance, we adopt the one-round setting to evaluate the LLMs in a simpler, more straightforward context. This allows us to elim- inate the potential confounding effects of complex interactions on the results. The study of one-round interactions provides a benchmark for future multi-round studies, helping to more clearly identify and quantify the benefits of multi-round interactions. Furthermore, single-round conversations still have practical significance, especially in resource-constrained or time-sensitive environments. For each bug from Defects4J and ConDefects, we extract the surrounding context and incorporate it into predefined prompt templates, then feed the prompts to LLM and check whether the localization results. If the bug is located within a method, we use the method containing the bug as the context. If the bug is outside of a method (e.g., in a field), we include the class’s field section as the context. For bugs located within a single method but spanning multiple hunks (i.e., multi-hunk bugs), we consider localization successful if at least one of the hunks is correctly identified. For bugs distributed across multiple methods, all relevant methods must be correctly identified for the localization to be considered successful. This setup follows the conventions used in existing FL studies (Zou et al. 2019; Pearson et al. 2017). Moreover, since current LLMs have limitations on the Dataset Project # of Bugs Defects4J Chart 23 Defects4J Cli 37 Defects4J Closure 171 Defects4J Codec 15 Defects4J Collections 2 Defects4J Compress 42 Defects4J Csv 14 Defects4J Gson 17 Defects4J JacksonCore 24 Defects4J JacksonDatabind 100 Defects4J JacksonXml 5 Defects4J Jsoup 84 Defects4J JxPath 20 Defects4J Lang 60 Defects4J Math 92 Defects4J Mockito 35 Defects4J Time 19 ConDefects - 276 Total - 1036 Table 2 The real-world bugs used in our study 1 3 Page 7 of 42 26

This setup also aligns with the practical con - straints of LLMs. 2.5.1 Evaluation metrics For each bug, we classify the localization results into the following three categories: ● Correct: The model accurately identifies the statement containing the bug. ● Incorrect: The model identifies a statement, but it is not the real buggy statement. ● Failed: The model is unable to complete the localization due to errors in under - standing or other issues. Note that the number of all bugs equals the sum of the bugs that are labeled by Cor- rect, Incorrect, and Failed. As aforementioned, in this study, we use a zero-shot fashion FL approach, where the LLM directly returns the statement it believes is most likely to contain the bug in a single-round conversation. Our setup is thus equivalent to calculating Top-1 in traditional fault localization (FL). We count the number of Correct bugs as our Top-1 score, which follows the existing study of LLM-based FL (Yang et al. 2024). Addi- tionally, we aim to minimize the number of Incorrect and Failed results. Among these, Incorrect results are particularly harmful because they could confuse develop- ers and would cost more time for debugging. In other words, when the number of Correct localization results is the same, fewer Incorrect localization results indicate better performance. 2.5.2 Prompts for FL Since our fault localization (FL) process is conducted in a zero-shot, single-round conversation fashion, we directly instruct the LLMs to identify and return the buggy statement. Effective prompt engineering requires consideration of various informa - tion sources, as highlighted in prior studies (Guo et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024). Specifically, we incorporate three key types of information: source method code (i.e., src), stack trace (i.e., stack), and bug-triggering assertion code (i.e., assert). ● Source method code of the target method provides the static context of the pro - gram, enabling the model to analyze the structure and semantics of the code. ● Stack traces offer dynamic runtime information extracted from test executions, which can help pinpoint the location of the bug by revealing the execution flow at the time of failure. ● Bug-triggering assertion code represents the specific conditions under which the bug manifests, providing additional context for the model to identify the faulty behavior. 1 3 26 Page 8 of 42

To explore this aspect, we instruct the LLMs to generate outputs in two distinct formats: ● Returning the line number of the buggy statement. ● Returning the statement itself. These elements are systematically combined into different prompt templates, as out- lined below. By varying the combination of information sources and output formats, we aim to evaluate their influence on the model’s performance in fault localization tasks. This approach allows us to better understand how different prompt designs can leverage the strengths of LLMs in understanding code structure, semantics, and runtime behavior. ● FL Prompt 1: “Source code: ” + src + “There is a bug in the above code, please help me locate it. Following the experience of the existing study (Yang et al. 2024), we use the lay - out placing the instructions at the tail of prompts, which helps LLMs better under - stand and remember the requirement of the task. By comparing the results of these prompts, we can evaluate how the dynamic information and test code affect the FL performance. Note that the ConDefects dataset has no stack trace or assertion, so we only evaluate the FL capabilities of these LLMs by prompts 1 and 4 against this dataset. 2.6 APR experiments setups Following the existing study that leverages the LLMs for APR, we adopt the zero- shot fashion (Xia and Zhang 2022; Xia et al. 2023; Fan et al. 2023). This querying mode is still important in research and practice. More specifically, given a buggy code fragment, we instruct the LLMs to return the correct version of the whole frag- ment directly. We follow existing LLM-based APR approaches, which perform repair given by perfect fault localization (Xia et al. 2023; Xia and Zhang 2022, 2024), i.e., the buggy lines or statements are specified. Same as the setting of the FL experi - ments, we also adopt the single-round conversation by the similar reason. Evaluating the effectiveness of a single-round conversation can be used as an important baseline. Therefore, we believe the model providing a correct patch in a single response is of practical value. To this end, we only consider the first result returned by LLM, which is similar to the Top-1 metric used in FL. 2.6.1 Evaluation metrics Similar to the setup of FL, we also classify the results returned by LLM into several categories by their distance to the correct patch. ● Correct: The patch given by LLM is semantically equal to the one of the devel - opers. ● Incorrect: The patch given by LLMs is incorrect. An Incorrect patch may lead to compiler errors, failed tests, or overfitting. Note that an overfitting patch passes all tests, but it does not behave as the developers intend (Qi et al. 2015; Xiong et al. 2017). ● Failed: The model can not generate a patch, due to truncation on response or misunderstanding the given task. We automatically extract the patches from the response of LLMs and apply them to the corresponding buggy program, then compile and run the patched program. If the patch enables all tests to pass, we manually check whether it is semantically correct, which follows the common practice of APR (Zhang et al. 2023). Since tests do not provide a complete specification of a program’s correctness, we have to manually compare the semantics of the generated patches to those of the developers’ patches. We only consider the case of Correct as a successful repair. 1 3 26 Page 10 of 42

Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 2.6.2 Prompts for APR For the task of Automated Program Repair (APR), we follow the APR strategies via LLMs established in existing studies (Fan et al. 2023; Xia et al. 2023). We assume that the buggy code fragment has been correctly located, and the buggy code along with its surrounding context is provided to the model. This approach aligns with common practices in LLM-based APR (Fan et al. 2023; Xia et al. 2023), as it ensures that the model has sufficient contextual information to generate accurate fixes. More specifically, we instruct the LLMs to perform repairs in three distinct ways: ● “Fix line X of the given code" : This targets a specific line number, allowing the model to focus on localized changes. ● “Fix the statement S of the given code": This directs the model to repair a specific statement, which may span multiple lines. ● “Fix the last line of the given code": This tests the model’ s ability to handle edge cases where the bug is located at the end of the code fragment. For the output formats of APR, we explore two options: ● Returning the whole fixed method: This provides a complete view of the repaired code, ensuring that the model considers the overall structure and semantics. ● Returning the patched lines specified by line numbers: This focuses on the mini- mal changes required to fix the bug, which is useful for understanding the model’s precision. The prompt templates are as follows. ● APR Prompt 1: src + “There is a bug in line X of the code, please help me fix it. Please return the complete fixed method. Do not skip or omit any part of the code. Do not include “‘ java or “‘ markers in the response." ● APR Prompt 2: src + “There is a bug in S, please help me fix it. Please return the complete fixed method. Do not skip or omit any part of the code. Do not in - clude “‘ java or “‘ markers in the response." ● APR Prompt 3: src + “There is a bug in the last statement, please help me fix it. Please return the complete fixed method. Do not skip or omit any part of the code. Do not include “‘ java or “‘ markers in the response." ● APR Prompt 4: src + “There is a bug in line X of the code, please help me fix it. Please return the results in a strict JSON format as described below. Please follow these instructions carefully: ..." ● APR Prompt 5: src + “There is a bug in S, please help me fix it. Please return the results in a strict JSON format as described below. Please follow these in - structions carefully: ..." ● APR Prompt 6: src + “There is a bug in the last statement, please help me fix it. Please return the results in a strict JSON format as described below. Please follow these instructions carefully: ..." 1 3 Page 11 of 42 26

The study of Fan et al. (2023) indicates that LLMs of the OpenAI family perform differently when specified by the line number or by the buggy code line, which inspires us to design the prompt tem - plates 1, 2, 4, and 5. The study of Xia et al. (2023) indicates that different LLMs are sensitive to various types of context, so we designed prompt templates 3 and 6 with only the previous context before the bug. 2.7 Bug types We have observed that in existing work on using LLMs for bug fixing and local - ization, even the best-performing methods still fall short of practical applicability. For instance, in the latest study by Xia and Zhang ( 2024), after applying various prompt-engineering techniques, ChatGPT was able to fix only about 28.9% of bugs in Defects4J v1.2, leaving a significant number of bugs unresolved. As observed in Find - ings 1–3 and 8–10, each LLM tends to succeed on a different subset of bugs, indicat- ing that their effectiveness varies significantly across fault types and task conditions in both FL and APR. While Deepseek-V3 and GPT-4o-Mini exhibit the best overall performance, the remaining models still demonstrate unique strengths by success - fully addressing bugs that the top performers fail to handle. For example, although Deepseek-V3 and GPT-4o-Mini together localized 365 bugs in FL, 126 bugs were successfully localized only by the other two models. In APR, all models suffer from a high proportion of Failed patches under the complex output format, but the fail - ure modes differ notably across models. These results highlight the importance of analyzing the characteristics of bugs that each model handles well or poorly. A bet - ter understanding of the conditions under which specific LLMs succeed can inform targeted model selection strategies, which could improve the reliability of automated debugging in practical settings. 1 3 Page 31 of 42 26

Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 4.1.2 Characterizing prompt design for different LLMs. The second key implication we learned is for designing prompts for a specified mis- sion and a specified LLM. Based on Findings 4 and 8, we discovered that adding more information to the prompt does not always lead to better performance for some models. Therefore, it is essential to design concise prompts tailored to the specific characteristics of each model, rather than merely feeding on more information. We can also observe that prompts requiring the LLM to return the line number of a faulty statement consis - tently result in worse performance than those asking it to return the code snippet itself. This phenomenon may be related to the capability of LLMs in counting line numbers and how they are trained. We should consider this factor in designing prompts. Findings 5-6 and 12-13 further reveal that the effectiveness of different prompts varies significantly across LLMs. This suggests that in FL and APR, developing dis- tinct and task-specified prompt strategies for each model is crucial. Additionally, since different prompts resulted in unique successes in both FL and APR, an approach that integrates the results from various prompts could enhance the overall performance. Moreover, our study reveals that zero-shot, single-round conversation prompting for FL and APR still leaves room for improvement. While this approach provides a baseline for evaluating direct model performance, it is unclear whether multi-round conversations, RAG, or other advanced techniques could substantially enhance the repair and localization accuracy. 4.1.3 Novel FL and APR approach for complex bug types. The third implication we learned is that the LLMs tend to handle some bug types more sophisticatedly. By Findings 7 and 14, we observed that the capability of LLMs to localize and repair different types of bugs varies significantly. LLMs perform better in localizing and fixing more localized bugs, such as Expression Fix and Single Line, but struggle with more complex bugs like Code Moving, which involves relocating large blocks of code. This insight has implications for the future design of LLM-based localiza - tion and repair methods. To address the challenges LLMs face with complex bug types like Code Mov- ing, several improvements can be made. (1) It may be beneficial to specialize LLMs for handling specific types of bugs, allowing for more precise models tailored to categories such as Expression Fixes. (2) Hybrid approaches combining LLMs with traditional program analysis tools could be a solution for more complex tasks like Code Moving, where structural analysis could complement LLMs’ semantic under - standing. (3) Targeted training could improve LLMs’ ability to manage complex bug fixes by exposing them to multi-step refactoring tasks. (4) LLMs could be enhanced to retain larger contexts, allowing them to process multi-line or multi-file dependen- cies. These strategies have the potential to improve the handling of complex bugs in LLM-based FL and APR. 1 3 26 Page 32 of 42

Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 4.2 Threats to validity In this section, we discuss the potential threats to the validity of our study. 4.2.1 Internal threats One internal threat to validity arises from the code implementation of our study. To mitigate this risk, we conducted the analysis with great care and open all our imple - mentation and results for policy check. Additionally, for all the APR patches that pass all tests, we manually validate their correctness (i.e., whether they are overfitting patches). To mitigate this risk, for all these patches, one author labeled the results, and another sampled the labeled for validation. Another internal threat arises from the data leakage issues, where the buggy and fixed versions of the dataset Defects4J (Just et al. 2014) have been introduced into the training data of the LLMs we studied, leading to unreliable FL and APR results. To mitigate this risk, we employ another dataset ConDefects (Wu et al. 2024) that avoids this problem. 4.2.2 External threats We evaluate three recent closed-source LLMs on two datasets, by three prompt tem- plates for one debugging task, which is of enough scale for observing findings from the experiments. However, our results may still not generalize well to other LLMs and other types of programming languages. 4.2.3 Construct threats The main construct threat arises from the evaluation metrics we used, e.g., the num - ber of Top-1 located bugs in FL and the number of Top-1 fixed bugs in APR. Never- theless, both metrics are widely adopted in FL and APR communities, and play as the main metric in evaluation. 5 Related work In this section, we introduce the related work of this study, including LLM for code- related tasks, FL, and APR appraoches. 5.1 LLM for code tasks LLMs have demonstrated significant potential across a wide range of coding tasks (Wang et al. 2024; Fan et al. 2023). The introduction of the Transformer model (Vaswani et al. 2017) has greatly expanded the scale at which deep learning models can be trained, paving the way for the development of LLMs. These models operate based on natural language instructions, known as prompts. Users can interact 1 3 Page 33 of 42 26

The versatility of LLMs across various coding tasks has been widely explored in recent research. LLMs have shown promise in facilitating code generation (Khojah et al. 2024; Mu et al. 2024), where they can autonomously generate code snippets based on high-level descriptions. Additionally, LLMs are increasingly being used for test generation (Yang et al. 2024; Ryan et al. 2024; Schäfer et al. 2023; Yuan et al. 2024), helping to automate the creation of test cases that ensure code reliability and correctness. Furthermore, LLMs have been applied in code analysis tasks (Mu et al. 2024; Endres et al. 2024; Wang et al. 2024) and comment generation (Shin et al. 2023; Mu et al. 2023), where they assist in understanding, refactoring, and optimiz - ing existing code. Among the various applications of LLMs, LLM-enhanced debug- ging has emerged as a particularly promising area of research, encompassing Fault Localization (FL) and Automated Program Repair (APR), which potentially allevi - ates developers from the heavy burden of software maintenance. Most of the studied LLMs are either from the facility of OpenAI (e.g., Chat - GPT and CodeX), or open source models (e.g., CodeT5 Wang et al. 2021, CodeL- lama Roziere et al. 2023, and DeepSeekCoder Guo et al. (2024) 2024). However, various internet giants are continually releasing new models, particularly commercial closed-source models. The capabilities of these models in handling coding tasks have not been thoroughly studied. Therefore, our study aims to fill this gap by evaluat - ing some of these newly released closed-source models. Specifically, due to policy restrictions, some regions are unable to access OpenAI’s LLMs. Therefore, we have deliberately selected models that are accessible in these restricted regions. 5.2 Fault localization FL is a critical task in software debugging, aimed at identifying the exact locations of faults within a program (Wong et al. 2016; Chen et al. 2025). Over the years, various techniques have been developed to improve the accuracy and efficiency of FL, rang- ing from traditional approaches like Spectrum-Based Fault Localization (SBFL) and Mutation-Based Fault Localization (MBFL) to more advanced machine learning and deep learning methodologies. 5.2.1 Traditional FL approaches Early work in FL predominantly focused on statistical methods, particularly SBFL and MBFL. SBFL approaches rely on program spectra—information about which parts of the code are executed during passing and failing test cases—to assign suspiciousness scores to code elements, such as Ochiai (Abreu et al. 2006), Taran- tula (Jones and Harrold 2005), and DStar (Wong et al. 2013). MBFL employs the result of mutation analysis to compute the suspicious score of code elements, such as MUSE (Moon et al. 2014), Metallaxis (Papadakis and Le Traon 2015), and BLMu (Wang et al. 2025). 1 3 26 Page 34 of 42

Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 5.2.2 Machine learning-based FL approaches Machine learning techniques have been increasingly applied to enhance the accu - racy of FL. Early approaches focused on statistical machine learning methods, such as learning-to-rank techniques (Xuan and Monperrus 2014; Zou et al. 2019). These methods aimed to improve the precision of FL by leveraging historical bug data and combining suspicious scores from various SBFL approaches. Additionally, models like PageRank (Zhang et al. 2017, 2019) and SmartFL (Zeng et al. 20220 employed probabilistic modeling to further refine FL results. In recent years, deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for FL, with research- ers developing models that utilize neural networks to analyze program behavior and locate bugs. Approaches such as DeepFL (Li et al. 2019), which incorporates Multi- layer Perceptron and Recurrent Neural Networks, and Grace (Lou et al. 2021), which represents program entities via graphs, have shown significant promise. Other meth- ods have explored the use of CNNs for predicting coverage matrices (Li et al. 2021), and graph neural networks for two-phase FL (Li et al. 2022a). Recent advancements include the development of FixLocator (Li et al. 2022b), which targets co-change fixing defects, and GNet4FL (Qian et al. 2023), which combines static and dynamic features to train graph convolutional models. These deep learning-based approaches demonstrate the potential of advanced neural network architectures to improve the precision and effectiveness of FL. Most recently, researchers have employed LLMs for FL (Kang et al. 2024; Yang et al. 2024; Qin et al. 2024). However, these studies only covered the models from the GPT family. For example, AgentFL (Qin et al. 2024) uses multi-agent equipped with ChatGPT for resolving project-level localization. 5.3 Automated program repair APR holds the promise of fixing buggy programs without human intervention, and it has garnered significant attention in the last decade (Gazzola et al. 2018; Monperrus 2018; Zhang et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2025). Generally, APR techniques primarily refer to the Generate and Validate (G&V) repair methods, where patches are generated and then validated by running tests. If a patch passes all tests, it is considered correct. Gen- Prog (Le Goues et al. 2011) was a pioneering work in G&V APR, and since then, repair techniques have garnered significant attention from the software engineering community. Based on the evolution of APR techniques over the past decade, we roughly categorize them into traditional APR, deep learning-based APR, and large model-based APR. 5.3.1 Traditional APR In the development of APR, approaches before deep learning-based techniques are categorized as traditional APR. The earliest approach is search-based APR, repre - sented by GenProg (Le Goues et al. 2011), which typically relies on genetic algo - rithms (Le Goues et al. 2011; Yuan and Banzhaf 2018; Wang et al. 2022, 2024) or random search (Qi et al. 2014) to generate repair patches. Then, researchers proposed template-based repair techniques, where predefined bug-fixing templates are applied 1 3 Page 35 of 42 26

Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 to generate patches, such as PAR (Kim et al. 2013), Anti-Pattern (Tan et al. 2016), and TBar (Liu et al. 2019). Enumeration-based repair systematically generates and evaluates potential patches by exhaustively exploring a predefined search space, such as Kali (Qi et al. 2015) and IBugFinder (Xin et al. 2024). Later, some research - ers leveraged statistical methods to generate patches, including Genesis (Long et al. 2017), ACS (Xiong et al. 2017), SimFix (Jiang et al. 2018), CapGen (Wen et al. 2018), ssFix (Xin and Reiss 2017), and Hanabi (Xiong and Wang 2022). Another important class of traditional APR methods is semantics-based APR, where program semantics are translated into constraints and solved using solvers to generate patches, such as SemFix (Nguyen et al. 2013), Nopol (Xuan et al. 2016; Martinez et al. 2017), JAID (Chen et al. 2017), Angelix (Mechtaev et al. 2016), DirectFix (Mechtaev et al. 2015), and ExtractFix (Gao et al. 2021). 5.3.2 Deep learning-based APR With the increasing availability of large open-source code repositories, deep learn - ing-based APR techniques, which apply self-trained deep learning models to address APR, have gained significant attention. For more detailed information, please refer to the survey of Zhang et al. (2023). DLFix is the early deep-learning-based APR (Li et al. 2020), which employs a tree-structured RNN to learn from bug fixes and their surrounding AST con - texts. CoCoNuT (Lutellier et al. 2020) transforms the APR problem to the neural machine translation (NMT) problem, and proposes a novel context-aware NMT model. RewardRepair (Ye et al. 2022a) involves test execution information inside its model. SelfAPR (Ye et al. 2022b) changes the learning paradigm from supervised training to self-supervised. Recoder (Zhu et al. 2021) implements a novel encoder- decoder architecture to ensure syntactically correct patch generation. KNOD (Jiang et al. 2023) proposes a novel three-stage tree decoder and a domain-rule distillation for patch synthesis. Tare (Zhu et al. 2023) introduces a type-aware neural model designed for program repair, learning typing rules to enhance the effectiveness of the patch generation process. 5.3.3 LLM-based APR Most recently, with the emerging LLM techniques, numerous APR approaches lever- aging LLMs have been proposed. Xia et al. (2023) and Fan et al. (2023) first leveraged LLMs to generate patches. Zhang et al. proposed GAMMA, which leverages an LLM to predict the correct code for masked code as a fill-in-the-blank task (Zhang et al. 2023). Huang et al. con - ducted a large-scale empirical study on the effectiveness of fine-tuning open-source LLMs for APR (Huang et al. 2023). Xia et al. proposed FitRepair (Xia et al. 2023), an LLM-based APR approach enhanced with fine-tuning strategies. Xia et al. used a multi-turn dialogue mechanism to enable GPT to generate better patches (Xia and Zhang 2024). Referring to the ongoing survey of Zhang et al. Automated Software Engineering (2026) 33:26 6 Conclusion In this paper, we present an empirical study evaluating the FL and APR capabilities of recent LLMs, particularly the closed-source models that are uncovered by existing studies, across various prompt templates. We conducted the experiments covering 5 LLMs, 12 prompt templates, and 2 real-world datasets. In particular, Ernie-3.5, Doubao, and Qwen are not covered by existing studies in the research area of auto - mated debugging. Our experiments yielded 14 key findings, which we distilled into 3 practical implications for optimizing the use of LLMs. Additionally, our results offer insights that could guide future research in the fields of FL and APR. In conclusion, different models have their unique capabilities for handling some types of bugs, and should be invoked by well-designed prompts. Scalable LLM-based PDDL Domain Generatio.text: SPAR: Scalable LLM-based PDDL Domain Generation for Aerial Robotics Songhao Huang ∗1, Yuwei Wu∗1, Guangyao Shi 2, Gaurav S. Sukhatme 2, Vijay Kumar 1 Abstract— We investigate the problem of automatic do- main generation for the Planning Domain Definition Lan- guage (PDDL) using Large Language Models (LLMs), with a particular focus on unmanned aerial vehicle (UA V) tasks. Although PDDL is a widely adopted standard in robotic planning, manually designing domains for diverse applications such as surveillance, delivery, and inspection is labor-intensive and error-prone, which hinders adoption and real-world de- ployment. To address these challenges, we proposeSPAR, a framework that leverages the generative capabilities of LLMs to automatically produce valid, diverse, and semantically accurate PDDL domains from natural language input. To this end, we first introduce a systematically formulated and validated UA V planning dataset, consisting of ground-truth PDDL domains and associated problems, each paired with detailed domain and action descriptions. Building on this dataset, we design a prompting framework that generates high-quality PDDL domains from language input. The generated domains are eval- uated through syntax validation, executability, feasibility, and interpretability. Overall, this work demonstrates that LLMs can substantially accelerate the creation of complex planning do- mains, providing a reproducible dataset and evaluation pipeline that enables application experts without prior experience to leverage it for practical tasks and advance future research in aerial robotics and automated planning. I. INTRODUCTION The Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) [1] is a fundamental formalism in automated planning, widely used in diverse areas such as robot task planning, logistics, and human-robot interactions [2]–[4]. Despite its expressive power, creating correct PDDL domain and problem files is often time-consuming and requires significant expertise, even for experienced users, which limits its broader adoption in planning systems for real-world applications, particularly in dynamic and safety-critical domains like Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UA V) operations. These domains involve complex three-dimensional environments, GPS-denied conditions, ex- ternal disturbances, and limited observations, making speci- fication technically non-trivial. Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising opportunities to automate the generation of PDDL from natural language descriptions. Prior work has demon- strated notable success in generating PDDL problem files [5, 6], which specify concrete initial states and goals. Unlike problem files, domain files define reusable action schemas that model the structure, dynamics, and constraints of a planning environment, requiring abstraction, consistency, and logical reasoning. Consequently, automating domain generation and transfer has attracted increasing research attention [7]–[11]. Nevertheless, these reasoning capabilities remain difficult for LLMs to reliably demonstrate. Moreover, the success of LLM-based domain generation is highly sensitive to the amount and quality of information provided. Existing studies often assume access to detailed task descriptions, expert knowledge, or ground-truth domain models [12, 13]. While such conditions yield promising re- sults, they do not reflect realistic scenarios where non-experts provide ambiguous or incomplete descriptions of unfamiliar tasks, or they don’t have access to real-world environments. In these cases, LLM-generated domain files frequently ex- hibit syntactic and semantic errors, logical inconsistencies, and incomplete action definitions. This discrepancy raises a critical question:How can we empower LLMs to au- tomatically construct reliable PDDL domain definitions for novel tasks, even when faced with unfamiliar actions and limited prior knowledge? To address these challenges, we study UA V planning as a representative and demanding domain involving com- plex tasks with diverse constraints. To enable a systematic evaluation of LLMs in generating diverse and previously unseen planning domains, our first step involves the follow- ing procedures: (1) define a domain complexity metric that quantifies difficulty across planning domains; (2) create a new PDDL domain evaluation dataset, which covers hand- crafted and LLM-generated domains from diverse sources to ensure novelty relative to LLM training data. This dataset includes a wide range of UA V scenarios (e.g., navigation, inspection, delivery) and diverse actions (e.g., detection, loading, recharging); and (3) defines a set of evaluation metrics for assessing both syntactic and semantic correctness. Building on this foundation, we introduce SPAR(Fig. 1), a generation framework designed to address two common issues in LLM-generated domains: syntax errors and se- mantic errors. To mitigate syntax errors, the framework adopts an action-by-action generation process with a func- tional syntax checker in a feedback loop for iterative cor- arXiv:2509.13691v1 [cs.RO] 17 Sep 2025

rection. To mitigate semantic errors, it incorporates chain- of-thought (CoT) reasoning to guide step-by-step action generation. Furthermore, inspired by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [14], the framework retrieves the most relevant examples from a curated dataset to support in- context reasoning. Our main contributions are as follows: •We present afirstmulti-domain PDDL dataset for UA V applications, consisting of 30 domain-problem pairs with aligned natural language descriptions. The dataset includes both logical and numeric domains designed to be unseen for current LLMs. •We propose a domain generation framework that com- bines CoT prompting, relevant-example retrieval, and an action-by-action feedback generation schema to im- prove generation ability. •We benchmark multiple LLMs and prompting strategies on our dataset across multiple evaluation metrics and validate the framework in UA V simulation experiments, demonstrating the practical feasibility for downstream planning and execution. II. RELATEDWORK A. Using LLMs in Task Planning LLMs have recently been explored in various capacities to assist with task planning in symbolic domains. a) LLMs as task planners:One line of research at- tempts to use LLMs as task planners to generate valid, executable plans directly from natural language instructions. However, naively prompting LLMs often leads to issues with correctness and completeness, especially for complex or long-horizon tasks [15]–[18]. To mitigate these issues, recent works propose augmenting LLMs with high-level reasoning, optimization methods, or domain-specific priors to improve reliability [19, 20]. In the context of PDDL-based planning, few-shot prompting has been explored [19], showing that careful prompt engineering and example selection can sub- stantially improve the quality and validity of generated plans. b) LLMs for problem or goal generation:Since LLMs struggle to serve directly as planners with correctness guar- antees, an alternative approach is to use them for generating PDDL problem specifications from natural language, given a known domain model. These generated problems can then be solved using traditional structured and symbolic planning approaches. For example, LLM+P [5] is designed to generate PDDL problem instances in robotic settings by conditioning on both the domain file and natural language input. Similarly, Xie et al. [21] showed that LLMs are capable of converting high-level natural language goals into structured, machine- interpretable representations. These efforts illustrate how LLMs can serve as problem generators, bridging flexible language interfaces with robust symbolic planning systems. However, all of the above methods assume the availability of a predefined symbolic world model, specifically a PDDL domain. Therefore,PDDL domain generationbecomes a more foundational challenge, since the accuracy and utility of problem generation and plan synthesis are determined by the quality of the underlying domain model. B. Planning Domain Generation Generating planning domains with LLMs requires strong reasoning capabilities. Prior work has explored several strate- gies to improve the quality of LLM-generated PDDL. Guan et al. [22] employed in-context learning with curated exam- ples to improve syntactic correctness, while Zhang et al. [13] introduced Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) prompt- ing to enhance reasoning and support open-domain genera- tion. Mahdavi et al. [12] further proposed an environment- feedback loop to refine domains based on semantic similarity. A key challenge in domain generation lies in the quan- tity and quality of input information. Providing additional knowledge, such as predicates [11, 13] or structural descrip- tions [12] often improves accuracy, but such inputs are not always available in real-world scenarios [22]. To address this, we leverage RAG to retrieve the most relevant examples for in-context learning under limited input conditions to improve semantic fidelity. Feedback mechanisms are also crucial for domain quality. Guan et al. [22] proposed a syntax validator with human-in-the-loop refinement, while Smirnov et al. [23] and Mahdavi et al. [12] automated feedback through con- sistency checks or environment evaluation. However, these methods often assume access to the ground-truth (GT) envi- ronment. Moreover, many validators (e.g., Tarski [24]) lack support for numeric conditions. Since our dataset includes numeric operators, we extend the validator from Guan et al. [22] and incorporate LLM-friendly feedback to improve syntax correctness during action-by-action generation. C. UAV Task Planning Benchmark Existing UA V task planning benchmarks primarily focus on a single task type or the UA V platform itself, such as inspection with heterogeneous UA Vs [25], object detection [26], and goal navigation [27]. With VLA/VLN, more UA V benchmarks have been proposed in both simulation and real-world settings [28, 29]. To broaden UA V applications, our dataset encompasses not only standard tasks such as navigation, detection, coordination, and exploration, but also non-standard scenarios, including aerial transportation with aerial manipulators, flying cars, and others. In addition, few works have introduced PDDL-based benchmarks for UA V task planning. To bridge this gap, we formulate all task planning problems in PDDL, extending the standard STRIPS formalism [30] to incorporate numerical cases, thereby mak- ing our dataset more representative of real-world conditions. III. PROBLEMFORMULATION A. Preliminaries The PDDL is a standardized language used in artificial intelligence and robotics to formally describe planning problems. It separates a problem into two parts: thedomain, which defines the general rules of the world (such as types of objects, predicates, and actions), and theproblem, which specifies a particular scenario with initial conditions and goals. For example, in a UA V surveillance task, the domain might define actions such asfly,take-photo, and return-to-base, along with predicates like(at ?uav

Then, a specific problem could describe a UA V starting at the base, visiting two waypoints, and taking photos at each. Using PDDL, a planner can automatically generate a sequence of actions to fulfill the task, such as(fly base waypoint1)→(take-photo waypoint1)→ (fly waypoint1 waypoint2)→(take-photo waypoint2)→(fly waypoint2 base). Such a structured representation makes it easier to design, share, and solve planning tasks across different domains. B. Problem Statement We formally introduce the notation used throughout this paper. A planning problemTis defined in PDDL as a tuple T={D, P}, whereDdenotes the PDDL domain, which specifies the general planning environment, andPdenotes the PDDL problem, which grounds a specific planning in- stance within that environment. We assume that the problem Pwill be available after the domainDis generated. The domainDconsists of a set offluentsFand a set ofactionsA. Fluents represent the state variables of the environment, typically including both predicates and numeric functions. Each actiona∈Ais defined by a set of parameters, along with its preconditions Pre(a), which must hold before the action is executed, and its effects Eff(a), which describe how the environment changes after execution. We denote the natural language description of the domain asN d, and the natural language description of thei th action ai ∈AbyN ai. We say thatN ai isincompleteif it does not explicitly describe all the conditions in Pre(a i)and Eff(a i) using natural language one-by-one. Additionally, we denote the declared parameter types and requirements of the domain as Extern. Before generation, LLM does not have access to the GT domain; that is, it has no prior knowledge of the environment’s state or actions. Given a tuple(N d, NA,Extern), where some action de- scriptionsN ai ∈N A may be incomplete, we aim to use LLMs to automatically generate a PDDL domain ˆD= ( ˆF ,ˆA). With a corresponding problem instance ˆP(manually specified or LLM-generated), a classical plannerCsolves the task ˆT={ ˆD, ˆP}, producing a planPlan⊆ ˆAthat transitions the system from the initial state to the goal state. IV. APPROACH In this section, we will first describe the benchmark dataset we created and then explain the proposed domain generation and evaluation pipeline as illustrated in Fig. 2. A. Dataset Generation 1) PDDL dataset:We introduce a multi-domain PDDL dataset for UA V applications that consists of 30 domains, each representing a distinct UA V-related planning scenario. To reduce the risk of evaluating LLMs on data seen dur- ing training, we curate the domains from diverse sources, including academic literature on UA V planning, practical application studies, and modified versions of domains from the International Planning Competition (IPC) [31]. Unlike prior datasets that often rely on procedural, step-by-step instructional text [13], our domains are designed to cap- ture the underlying structure of UA V environments, ensur- ing semantic coherence beyond surface-level instructions. In addition, several domains incorporate numeric fluents, extending beyond the classical STRIPS to model realistic UA V planning problems. Each domain is paired with 9 problem instances: 3 simple, 3 medium, and 3 hard. Simple problems can be solved with 1–2 actions, medium problems involve nearly the full action set, and hard problems require the complete set of actions while introducing additional complexity, such as multi-robot coordination. 2) PDDL Domain Complexity Metric:To systematically quantify the complexity of a PDDL domain, we introduce a composite metric that captures both structural and semantic characteristics of the domain. Specifically, the metric incor- porates the following nine components:1) Number of actions, object types, predicates, and functions; 2) Average number of preconditions and effects per action; 3) Interdependency score: the average number of actions referencing a given predicate or function; 4) Action coupling: the number of

conditions in an action’s effects that appear as preconditions in other actions. The final complexity score is computed as a weighted sum of each component. Across our dataset,domain complexity scoresrange from 2.79 to 15.23, capturing a broad spectrum of diffi- culty—from simple navigation tasks to multi-agent coor- dination and numeric reasoning challenges. This diversity enables robust evaluation of LLMs across varying lev- els of domain complexity. For reference, the well-known BLOCKSWORLD [32] domain (complexity: 5.23) ranks 17th out of 30, from most to least complex. Based on this, we divide the dataset into 14 simple (≤5.23) and 16 complex (>5.23) domains-a split used throughout our evaluation. B. Generate PDDL domain with LLMs We adopt an action-by-action strategy to generate each action within a domain. For actionˆa i, given the input tuple (Nd, Nai,Extern), we employ a coarse-to-fine approach to retrieve the most relevant example from our dataset for in- context learning. We then construct a prompt using a chain- of-thought method and feed it into LLM. The resulting PDDL action is validated by a syntax checker, which pro- vides feedback if syntax errors are detected. This process is repeated by re-prompting LLMs with feedback until either a syntactically correct output is generated or a maximum iteration number is reached. Example 1: Action Description Abstraction Original Action Description This action enables a uav to move from its current position to a new position if two positions are connected. This costs one unit of energy. For example, the uav moves from position_1 to position_2 if there is a connection between them. This costs one unit of energy. After Abstraction This action enables a uav to move from [position1] to [position2] if [position1] and [position2] are [state1]. This action will increase [value1] by [value2]. 1) Retrieval for Most Relevant In-context Example:In- context learning is critical for enabling LLMs to perform structured generation tasks such as PDDL domain modeling, especially in zero-shot or low-resource settings. Similarly to RAG, we utilize our dataset as an external source of domain-specific knowledge. We extract all actions from the dataset and convert each into an abstract representation using LLM to focus on semantic structures rather than lexical similarity, mitigating lexical noise. Specifically, LLM replaces concrete nouns, adjectives, and numeric values with abstract placeholders such as[object],[state], and[value], while preserving subject and verb tokens to emphasize action semantics. LLM maintains a list of commonly used verbs. If a verb in the description is semantically similar to one in the list, it is replaced. Otherwise, it is added to the list and retained in the abstraction. We hypothesize that actions with similar semantic structures often correspond to similar PDDL formulations. The example below shows an action’s original and abstracted forms, retaining key elements like ‘uav’, ‘move’, and ‘increase’, while replacing other specifics with placeholders. We encode all abstracted action represen- tations into embeddings using theall-mpnet-base-v2 model [33], and store them in a searchable embedding index. The retrieval process consists of two stages. In the coarse stage, we abstract the target action descriptionN ai and embed it as a query (Eg. 1); cosine similarities are com- puted across the stored index, and the top-Kmost relevant examples are retrieved. In the fine stage, these top-Kcan- didates are fed into LLMs to re-order and select the most semantically relevant example for in-context learning. 2) Prompt with Chain of Thought:To improve the reasoning capability of LLMs in PDDL domain generation, we employ a CoT prompting that directs the model to explicitly decompose the problem. The CoT process is embedded within context examples across three progressive reasoning steps. First, we askWhat are the objects?, prompting LLM to infer which objects are involved in the action based on the given context. This helps the model determine the correct action parameters. Second, we askFor each object, what are the preconditions? State them using predicates or functions.This encourages the model to reason about the conditions for action execution from the perspective of each object. Precondition can be either newly created or retrieved from an existing fluent list, and is paired with a natural language explanation to reinforce understanding. Third, we askFor each object, what are the effects? State them using predicates or functions.which mirrors the second question but focuses on the state changes resulting from the action. This reinforces object-centered reasoning and ensures the model considers the outcome comprehensively. Finally, we promptWrite the action in the following formatto elicit a well-structured PDDL action. 3) Iterative Generation of Actions:Because the set of fluents is unknown in advance, we maintain a dynamic list of fluents throughout the generation process. After generating each action, LLMs identify newly generated fluents, which are then added to the list and reused in subsequent actions. This strategy mitigates LLM context length limitations and enables incremental domain construction, reducing redundant or inconsistent fluents. Providing feedback to LLMs is key for iterative refine- ment. While prior works rely on human [22] or environment- level feedback [12], these methods face scalability and ac- cessibility challenges. Existing PDDL syntax checkers/parser also lack support for domains involving numeric. Here, we extend a simple STRIPS-style syntax validator in [22] to support numeric checking and producing error feedback that can be directly used in the prompt, enabling a self- improvement loop. EVALUATION This section presents a series of evaluations conducted on our dataset to assess our prompt design. We aim to validate the following hypotheses: •H1:The proposed prompt designs will mitigate syntax errors, leading to a syntactically correct domain. •H2:The proposed prompt designs will increase the semantic correctness of the generated domains. Semantic correctness is assessed using three criteria:1) Executability, defined as the problem-solving success rate; 2) Feasibility, which measures whether plans generated in a domain can be executed on the GT domain; and3) Interpretability, which measures whether the GT plan can be executed within the generated domain. We evaluate two LLMs: GPT-4.1-mini-2025-04-14 (GPT) and DeepSeek-Chat , using four existing prompting varia- tions as benchmark methods. The compared methods and their abbreviations are:1) Format[22]: Prompted with two regular examples for format referencing.2) Format+CoT (FCoT): Prompted with two regular examples for format referencing, both including chain-of-thought reasoning.3) Format+Semantic (FS): Prompted with one regular example for format referencing and one semantically relevant example for content referencing.4) Retrieval+CoT (Ours): Our framework retrieves one regular example for format refer- encing and one semantically relevant example for content referencing, both including chain-of-thought reasoning. Evaluation of Semantic Correctness 1) Executability:From the previous steps, the generated domains are ensured to be syntax-error free. We then evaluate the problem-solving rate of all four methods across our dataset. We first use LLMs to generate 9 problem files (3 simple, 3 medium, and 3 hard problems) for each generated domain. Each problem shares the same initial states and goals with its corresponding GT problem in our dataset. We then feed both the generated domain and its generated problem files into a classical planner, the ENHSP-20 solver [34], and report the results in the first row of Fig. 3. Overall, the GPT model outperforms DeepSeek-Chat in solving rate. The FCoTmethod improves performance by approximately 16% when using GPT. In contrast, theFSshows limited variation across the two models. The solving rate generally decreases as the problem level increases and the domain complexity increases. Among the four methods,Oursachieves the highest solving rate of 95.19%, surpassing theFormat method by about 14%. The next best performers areFS andFCoT, suggesting that both chain-of-thought prompting and example retrieval contribute positively to solving perfor- mance, while their combination yields greater improvement. However, successfully solving a problem merely indicates that a valid sequence of actions can be found from the initial state to the goal, i.e., the LLM-generated logic can be executable by a planner. This does not imply that the solution is semantically meaningful or feasible for execution by a robot in the ground-truth domain. Therefore, further evaluation of semantic correctness is essential. 2) Feasibility and Interpretability:To further assess the semantical correctness of the generated domains and verify whether the solved plans are feasible, we adopt a bidirec- tional domain validation strategy, inspired by [11, 12]. We treat the GT Domain as the optimal formulation of the environment, and the GT Plan was solved from the GT Domain and GT Problem as a valid and feasible action sequence from the initial state to the final goal. In the forward validation, we assess the feasibility of the generated domain by executing the plan (Gen Plan) produced in the generated domain on the GT Domain using V AL [35]. If the Gen Plan can be executed on the GT Domain, it implies that the generated domain produces a feasible plan. The higher the number of feasible Gen Plans, the more reliable the generated

domain is in terms of feasibility. In inverse validation, we assess domain interpretability by executing the GT Plan within the generated domains (see Fig. 2). Successful execution of the GT Plan indicates that the generated domain can reproduce the same action behaviors as the GT Domain, thereby demonstrating its interpretability. A higher number of executable GT Plans reflects greater interpretability of the generated domain. Feasibility and inter- pretability results are presented in the second and third rows of Fig. 3. Overall, interpretability scores are consistently higher than feasibility scores across all generated domains. The highest feasibility and interpretability are achieved by theOursmethod using GPT. Notably, theFCoTmethod yields slightly lower feasibility and interpretability scores compared to theFormat, indicating that CoT alone does not improve domain feasibility or interpretability. However, incorporating relevant examples (FSandOurs) significantly boosts performance in both metrics. VI. CONCLUSION In this work, we introduced a framework for automatic PDDL domain generation via LLMs, with UA V planning as a representative scenario. By developing a validated dataset of UA V domains and problems and designing a prompt framework tailored for domain generation, we demonstrated that LLMs can effectively produce domains that are both syntactically valid and semantically accurate. Our evalu- ations show that the generated domains not only satisfy structural requirements but also have strong feasibility and interpretability relative to ground-truth counterparts, enabling faster development, testing, and evaluation cycles. Software Development Life Cycle for Engi.text: Software Development Life Cycle for Engineering AI Planning Systems Ilche Georgievski a Service Computing Department, IAAS, University of Stuttgart, Universitaetsstrasse 38, Stuttgart, Germany Keywords: AI Planning, Software Development Life Cycle, Software Engineering, AI Engineering. Abstract: AI planning is concerned with the automated generation of plans in terms of actions that need to be executed to achieve a given user goal. Considering the central role of this ability in AI and the prominence of AI planning in research and industry, the development of AI planning software and its integration into production architectures are becoming important. However, building and managing AI planning systems is a complex process with its own peculiarities, and requires expertise. On the one hand, significant engineering challenges exist that relate to the design of planning domain models and system architectures, deployment, integration, and system performance. On the other hand, no life cycle or methodology currently exists that encompasses all phases relevant to the development process to ensure AI planning systems have high quality and industrial strength. In this paper, we propose a software development life cycle for engineering AI planning systems. It consists of ten phases, each described in terms of purpose and available tools and approaches for its execution. We also discuss several open research and development challenges pertaining to the life cycle and its phases. 1 INTRODUCTION In 1966, Shakey was the first general-purpose mobile robot with the ability to plan its own actions (Nils- son, 1984). Shakey also marked the inception of Ar- tificial Intelligence (AI) planning, a research and de- velopment discipline that deals with the computation of plans of actions for achieving a user goal (Ghal- lab et al., 2004). In other words, AI planning is con- cerned with solving planning problems that consist of an initial state of the world, a planning domain model in terms of actions that can change the world, and a goal state of the world that represents the user goal. A plan, which is a course of actions, is solution to a planning problem if it leads from the initial state to the goal. The field of AI planning is now abound in approaches, algorithms and tools for addressing is- sues of various aspects of the planning process (see Figure 1). In the last few years, there is a growing demand for AI planning technology in real applica- tions, such as space exploration (Chien and Morris, 2014), robotics (Karpas and Magazzeni, 2020), and autonomous driving (Alnazer et al., 2022). These developments highlight the need for devel- oping AI planning systems and integrating them into existing software architectures. Within AI planning discipline, the engineering and developing AI plan- a https://orcid.org/0000-0001-6745-0063 ning systems is often portrayed as two things: the development of algorithms and engineering of plan- ning domain models. In practice, these ingredients constitute only a part of what is needed to construct and use operational AI planning systems (Georgievski and Breitenb¨ucher, 2021). Particularly, developing an AI planning system involves many complex activi- ties: choosing the correct underlying planning model, knowledge engineering, dealing with numerous plan- ning functionalities, architecting a design without an established interoperability mechanism for plan- ning software components, choosing suitable plan- ning tools, and collecting and analysing relevant data. As a result, building such AI planning systems is a complex process and demands immerse knowledge about the application domain of interest, expertise in AI planning, and proficiency in software engineering. While most of existing AI planning software arte- facts were developed as research projects, it is un- clear whether they were developed considering any traditional software development life cycle. Never- theless, AI planning faces many of the challenges in traditional software development, such as require- ments analysis, testing, code review, documentation, etc. AI planning systems, however, are different from traditional software in several ways, and present new challenges that are not accounted for in existing soft- ware development life cycles (see (Munassar and Go- Georgievski, I. One difference is that the objective in AI planning is to compute and execute plans often optimised with re- spect to some metric, such as energy cost, instead of only achieving functional requirements. This im- plies developers would need to continuously improve a planning system (e.g., test newest underlying plan- ning models, update user goals) to achieve the aim (e.g., minimum cost paid for consumed energy). Fur- thermore, AI planning systems seem to be more com- plex to manage because their performance depends on data representing the world, planning domain mod- els, tuning algorithms (e.g., selecting or devising suit- able heuristics), implicit feedback from the world and explicit user’s feedback, in-depth data analysis (e.g., to design a planning domain model, identify or con- sider biased/ethical implications of automated plan- ning decisions), distributed computation of a global plan, etc. Finally, AI planning systems are likely developed by people with different expertise, where transferring planning artefacts among them might be challenging. For example, a planning expert might create and transfer a planning domain model to a soft- ware engineer for use in the planning system being developed. Any issues that may arise in relation to this might lead to incorrect behaviour (e.g., the system computes plans but they are not valid), which would be hard for the software engineer without planning ex- pertise to identify and address. As none of the traditional software development life cycles covers the complexity and specificities of AI planning, and no other methodology exists that covers and treats all relevant phases AI planning sys- tems could and should go through, we propose a soft- ware development life cycle for engineering AI plan- ning systems. The life cycle is an agile and iterative process consisting of ten phases as preliminary con- ceptualised in (Georgievski, 2023). We describe each phase in detail, including its purpose, the approaches, and tools currently available to execute it. Our contributions are manifold. On the one hand, we present a complete software development life cy- cle aimed at addressing engineering challenges in AI planning. On the other hand, through this lifecycle, we (1) provide a common understanding of how AI planning software is designed, developed, deployed, and refined; this will enable not only cooperation between involved parties (e.g., individuals, groups, mixed AI-human teams) but also facilitate the deploy- ment of AI planning in real applications, 1 (2) render or highlight for the first time some essential aspects of AI planning one needs to consider when building AI planning systems, (3) support the incorporation of quality and effectiveness in the engineering process of AI planning systems, and (4) provide a basis for dis- cussion in AI planning and AI engineering fields and a stepping stone for future research in this direction. The rest of the paper is organised as follows. Sec- tion 2 introduces the proposed life cycle. Section 3 presents an analysis of the lifecycle scope and open challenges. Section 4 describes related works, and Section 5 concludes the paper. 2 PROPOSED LIFE CYCLE To address the question of what phases a typical AI planning system should go through, how these phases relate to one another, and how they can be conducted, we present the Software Development Life Cycle for Engineering AI Planning Systems , called PlanXflow. Figure 2 illustrates the proposed life cycle, which is based on more than ten years of research, develop- ment, and teaching experiences in the field.
