Requirements Analysis AI Planning Model Formulation Domain Model Design System Architecture and Design AI Planning Tools Selection Implementation Testing Deployment Monitoring Analysis Software Development Lifecycle for AI Planning 1 2 3 4 56 7 8 9 10 Figure 2: Overview of the Software Development Life Cycle for AI Planning Systems. 2.1 Requirements Analysis The first phase is Requirements Analysis, which in- dicates that the development of AI planning systems must begin with the identification of requirements by the relevant stakeholders (Grady, 2014). In the con- text of AI planning, one can distinguish functional, non-functional, domain-oriented and user-related re- quirements. Functional requirements define the ba- sic behaviour of the AI planning system, including not only the required functionality but also the kind of planning problems to be addressed and possible restrictions that should be considered in the overall planning and execution process. In particular, plan- ning systems for real-world applications go beyond plan generation only. Such applications often require a wider spectrum of functionalities that range from support for modelling planning domains and prob- lems, to solving planning problems, to executing, val- idating, and explaining plans and planning decisions, to managing and monitoring the overall planning sys- tem. In fact, one can select from and combine at least 19 types of different planning functionalities as reported in (Georgievski, 2022). While all types of planning functionalities can be used to create an ad- vanced AI planning system, not all of them may have the same role in a system. For example, in an on- line AI planning editor, the Modelling and Parsing production-ready AI systems (Gartner, Inc., 2020). functionalities would be core functionalities, while the Solving functionality would be a supporting one as it is not essential for modelling planning problems but it may make the online editor complete. Non-functional requirements define the quality properties that affect the experience of using AI planning systems, such as performance, scalability, reusability, or maintainability. With the exception of performance of planning systems in terms of time needed to solve planning problems, non-functional re- quirements are often not considered as important fac- tors in the AI planning literature even though their early detection and addressing into architecture de- signs can lead to reduction of cost and effort as known from developing software in other contexts. Domain-oriented requirements define the relevant entities an AI planning system can use and objectives it should achieve in the application domain of inter- est. These requirements cover the goal-oriented re- quirements defined in the context of AI planning (van Lamsweerde, 2009; Ambreen et al., 2018). Neverthe- less, domain-oriented requirements are used to cap- ture knowledge needed for the planning domain and specific planning problems. The acquisition of these requirements is expected to be done in an integrated form, which would enable the translation of these re- quirements into formal models needed by some plan- ning functionalities (Silva et al., 2020). User-related requirements define requirements relevant for the user. As Asimov’s laws express Software Development Life Cycle for Engineering AI Planning Systems 753

that robots must never harm humans in their op- eration (Asimov et al., 1984), user-related require- ments can specify that AI planning systems should not put at risk the safety of humans, disclose privacy- sensitive data, affect the effectiveness and comfort of users in their intentions or when performing their tasks. Finally, the decisions and actions taken by AI planning systems may need to be explained to users (Chakraborti et al., 2020). The requirements should be attributed with met- rics and documented so that the resulting AI planning system can be validated, verified, or evaluated in other lifecycle phases, such as the Analysis phase (see Sec- tion 2.10). For example, the quality of planning do- main models can be assessed concerning their accu- racy, consistency and completeness, the adequacy of the representational language, and the operationality of the software component with a Solving functional- ity concerning the planning domain model (see (Mc- Cluskey et al., 2017)). 2.2 AI Planning Model Formulation The AI Planning Model Formulation phase is per- formed to decide and formulate a suitable planning model as a blueprint for the AI planning system. We define a planning model as a specific form of plan- ning distinguished by a planning type, world context, and user features. A planning type encompasses a set of planning approaches or planning algorithms that share the same underlying structure, assumptions, or qualities. One can distinguish various types of plan- ning. Classical planning is the most basic and re- strictive type, where actions play a key role. This planning type is based on several restrictive assump- tions that simplify how the world looks like and oper- ates (e.g., the world is static, fully observable, deter- ministic, and instantaneous). There exist other plan- ning types that relax one or more of those assump- tions by adding expressiveness or some algorithmic features. These planning types include numeric plan- ning, temporal planning, probabilistic planning, con- tingent planning, conformant planning, conditional planning, distributed planning, continual planning, etc. A line of planning structurally different than the aforementioned planning types is represented by hier- archical planning (Georgievski and Aiello, 2015). In addition to actions, hierarchical planning uses tasks and other expressiveness constructs to organise the domain knowledge at different levels of abstraction. Furthermore, we define a world context as a char- acterisation of an aspect or a situation in the world. A planning model may disregard world contexts to simplify planning problems. A planning model may tolerate or exploit a world context by anticipating un- expected events in the environment and/or controlling and interacting with the world. So, including a world context in the planning model makes the planning process more complete or realistic. A user feature is a something of importance to the user. For example, a domain expert may want to model planning prob- lems or an end-user may need to be provided with an opportunity to explore found plans before their execu- tion. Note that a planning type might exist that covers some world context or user feature. Analysis of their mutual inclusiveness is out of the scope of this work. The kind of planning model dictates different needs and considerations when developing planning domains and when designing and realising the over- all AI planning system. Consequently, the formula- tion of an adequate planning model is a critical phase. The formulation should be based on all requirements from the previous phase, particularly the functional and domain-oriented requirements. Formulating an adequate planning model is a complex task and may require expertise and experience in AI planning. It can also be time-consuming. 2.3 Domain Model Design As AI planning is a knowledge-based AI approach, the design of systems requires engineering of applica- tion domain knowledge in a precise and correct form so that the systems can produce and execute valid plans. In AI planning, one sees knowledge engineer- ing as a modelling process (Studer et al., 1998), which involves constructing a domain model that abstractly and conceptually describes the knowledge of the ap- plication area. A planning domain model is a formal representation of such a domain model. The Domain Model Design phase is dedicated to the creation of a planning domain model. In gen- eral, the design process starts by deriving domain in- formation from the requirements collected in the first phase, specifically, from the domain-oriented require- ments. On the one hand, the domain information in- cludes object classes, properties, relations, actions, and tasks, and on the other hand, assumptions and features that are essential for the representation of the planning domain model (e.g., propositional logic at minimum). The domain information is then con- ceptualised and formalised using a selected planning language compatible with the planning model formu- lated in the previous phase. Examples of planning languages include Planning Domain Definition Lan- guage (PDDL), Hierarchical Domain Definition Lan- guage (HDDL) (H ¨oller et al., 2020), SHOP2 (Nau et al., 2003), etc. When encoded in such a language, ICSOFT 2023 - 18th International Conference on Software Technologies 754

the planning domain model can be fed in into a soft- ware component with a Parsing and Solving func- tionalities, assuming the component supports the cho- sen planning syntax and all expressiveness constructs used in the planning domain model. Domain modelling is a tedious and error-prone task without a clear and established methodology for approaching it and engineering the knowledge in the required form. However, some studies analyse do- main modelling issues and propose separate design processes one could follow, e.g., (Vaquero et al., 2011a; Silva et al., 2020). Some modelling tools can smooth down the difficulty of knowledge engineering and support the domain modelling, e.g., itSimple (Va- quero et al., 2013). 2.4 System Architecture and Design Addressing a real-world planning problem will likely require combining several planning functionalities into a single planning system that can solve the prob- lem and satisfy stakeholders’ requirements. That is, using the functional requirements, planning model and planning domain model defined in the previous phases, the System Architecture and Design phase is concerned with conceptualising an abstract architec- ture that consists of suitable planning components and relationships between them. Doing this enables not only analysing the planning system’s behaviour but also making early design decisions that can impact the development and deployment of the resulting plan- ning system. The planning model is essential here as it directs the conditions for interactions between the planning components to ensure their compatibil- ity and correctness of the entire process. That is, the interaction constraints represent the allowed con- nections among the constituting components. If nec- essary and possible, the system architecture can be refined considering the specificities of the involved planning tools, such as data structures or supported features (e.g., some planning tools may not support logical negation even though logical negation is part of PDDL). In any case, the resulting system architec- ture design should provide sufficient information for the selection and/or implementation of required com- ponents in the next phases. Consider that existing planning tools are mostly developed in isolation without considering communi- cation and interoperability issues, i.e., the tools are designed, developed, and tested per type of planning functionality. For example, domain modellers are de- signed and developed independently from planners, which the domain modellers would eventually depend upon. Placing needed planning functionalities (i.e., their components) into context is investigated on sev- eral occasions where only a limited number of coarse- grained planning components are organised into sys- tem architectures. For example, CPEF (Myers, 1999), PELEA (Alc et al., 2012), and SOA-PE (Vulgar- akis Feljan et al., 2015) provide planning architec- tures that consist of components for solving planning problems, executing plans, monitoring the execution, and replanning hardwired to operate in a predefined order. In CPEF, a central component manages the op- eration of the entire planning system. To design and develop new AI planning systems that are robust, flexible and scalable, the different planning functionalities could be designed and re- alised as services (Georgievski, 2022), and their co- ordination and data exchange can be accomplished using workflows (Georgievski and Breitenb ¨ucher, 2021), which represent a proven and effective ap- proach for orchestration in many applications (Ley- mann and Roller, 1997). 2.5 AI Planning Tools Selection When we have a planning problem we want to solve, we usually look for an off-the-shelf tool. In this con- text and in line with the reusability intention within the AI planning community in terms of providing domain-independent tools and the reusability goal of AI engineering (Georgievski and Breitenb ¨ucher, 2021; Bosch et al., 2021), we should explore and select if available existing planning tools before en- tering the phase to implement the required planning components. In the AI Planning Tools Selection phase, existing planning tools (e.g., code, tools, ser- vices) are searched to find and select appropriate im- plementations for the needed planning functionalities. Research in AI planning has traditionally concen- trated on developing techniques and algorithms that are continuously enhanced with delicate features. The result is a large corpus of planning tools, most of which offer a Solving functionality and are called planners. For example, one can count 235 planners as participants in International Planning Competition from 2006 to 2020. Other planning tools focus on modelling planning problems, learning planning do- mains, and validating plans. In addition, the plan- ning tools are diverse in terms of supported operating systems, dependencies, programming languages, and supported planning languages. Suppose one analy- ses the ten most cited planning tools. One can ob- serve that many of them are restricted to running on a Linux environment, they have at least three dependen- cies without support for their management, they are implemented in various programming languages with Software Development Life Cycle for Engineering AI Planning Systems 755

C, C++, Java, and Common Lisp being the most com- mon ones, and most of these planners support some version of PDDL. The presented discussion indicates it is challeng- ing to keep track of all the planning tools and know their characteristics and the features they support. Some initial work has been carried out in collect- ing and categorising planning tools. For example, Georgievski and Aiello characterise several hierarchi- cal planners (Georgievski and Aiello, 2015), while Planning.Wiki provides a list of planners accompa- nied by a short description and references (Green et al., 2019). In any case, those interested in integrat- ing a planning tool into a planning system have much work to do when looking for a suitable planning tool. 2.6 Implementation The Implementation phase is devoted to implement- ing the planning system based on the system archi- tecture design. The implementation includes the de- velopment of components for planning functionalities for which no existing tool can be found, and the de- velopment of communication mechanisms, depend- ing on the type of communication required between the planning components. This phase may also be concerned with the modification of planning domain models as a consequence of the capabilities of se- lected planning tools (e.g., a planning domain model may need to be updated to account for the inabil- ity of a planner to deal with negative propositions). For each planning component to be implemented, the classical software development lifecycle can be en- tered at this point. 2.7 Testing In the Testing phase, the AI planning system is tested to validate and verify its behaviour concerning the requirements, quality attributes, and corresponding metrics specified in the first phase. As for other software, two types of testing should be performed: isolated tests and integration tests (Wu et al., 2003). All planning artefacts, such as planning components, the planning domain model, problem instances, and workflow models, should be tested in isolation. To our knowledge, there is only an established strategy for testing planning domain models. In particular, a planning domain model is typically debugged and validated by testing a selected planner to solve a par- ticular problem instance using the planning domain model. The quality of a planning domain model is conventionally assessed concerning adequacy, while other metrics include accuracy and operationality. The AI planning research community has estab- lished a practice for testing planners in occasional competitions for the best planner in terms of planning time and plan quality on a set of benchmark planning domains. While some benchmark planning domains are inspired from real-world applications, most of them represent synthetic knowledge suitable for test- ing the speed of computation and possibly for debug- ging purposes. Georgievski and Aiello Georgievski and Aiello (2016) present a strategy for testing plan- ners with the purpose of understanding how well the planners meet the application requirements. The strat- egy consists of specifying a testing configuration, al- gorithmic configuration, knowledge base about rele- vant planning problems, computational factors, and scalability considerations. Integration tests are needed to verify that all plan- ning artefacts can work correctly together. To the best of our knowledge, a holistic testing approach for plan- ning systems has not been established yet. 2.8 Deployment The Deployment phase is used to make the AI plan- ning system ready and available for use. A cen- tralised AI planning system can be deployed to an environment with enough processing power. Here, the constituent planning components can be deployed manually. However, the manual process of installa- tion, configuration, and deployment of existing plan- ning tools not only requires technical proficiency given their heterogeneity but also is time consuming and error prone given the obscurity of setup instruc- tions (Georgievski and Breitenb ¨ucher, 2021). Au- tomated deployment represents a better fit for cen- tralised AI planning systems. Unfortunately, not much information on this topic can be found in the AI planning literature. Moving an AI planning system with distributed planning to production can be even more challenging, mainly for two of its processes, plan generation and plan execution. Distributed planning and execution require distributed planning components to have com- mon objectives and representations, exchange infor- mation about their current plans, and plans iteratively refined and revised until they fit together. There are many possible deployment environments (e.g., cloud, fog and edge), however, there is no standard way to deploy the planning elements (e.g., which parts of planning domain models should be deployed where) to these diverse environments and guarantee success- ful and correct operation of the AI planning system. The successful operation of AI planning systems depend on not only on how well their software com- ICSOFT 2023 - 18th International Conference on Software Technologies 756

ponents and planning domain models are engineered, but also on the reliability of the entire process start- ing from collecting data from the world environment, transforming it to correct planning problem instances, to computing and executing valid plans back in the world environment. All this requires care in repro- ducing the software environments, the entire process with relevant parameters, etc. used in development. 2.9 Monitoring In the Monitoring phase, the planning system and ex- ecution environment are monitored to understand the system’s behaviour and its constituent components, especially the cases of problems and unexpected be- haviour. Monitoring entails collecting data prove- nance. Generally, provenance is the documentation of the information that describes the origin and pro- duction process of an object or a piece of data (Her- schel et al., 2017). The information typically in- cludes metadata about entities, data, processes, activ- ities, and people involved in the production process. The collection and processing of provenance provide several benefits, such as improving the understand- ing of the process and the result, quality assessment and quality improvement, ensuring reproducibility, and technical requirements, such as runtime perfor- mance and scalability. Of interest in our treatment is data provenance, which is defined as the information about individual data items and operations involved with those data items (Herschel et al., 2017). In the context of AI planning, the literature has mostly focused on studying provenance of plans, par- ticularly plan rationales, which deal with “why a plan is the way it is” and “the reason as to why the plan- ning decisions were taken” (Polyak and Tate, 1998), and plan evaluation rationales, which deal with “why a certain plan element does or does not satisfy a cri- terion” or “why a plan was classified into a specific quality level” (Vaquero et al., 2011b). However, data provenance is crucial not only for understanding the life cycle of plans, but also the correctness, accuracy, and other quality attributes of other planning artefacts (e.g., planning domain model, problem instances), improving the planning process, establishing causal- ity and dependency, establishing responsibility (e.g., who is responsible for which data), and explainabil- ity. Also, data provenance can be used to support the selection of planning tools and to improve the perfor- mance of the overall planning systems. Based on this discussion and from our own ex- perience, we present a preliminary collection of data provenance types that can be collected and analysed in AI planning systems. We organise data provenance Planning Provenance Planning Process Domain Knowledge System Data Plan Goals Actions Constraints Preferences Input Output Planning state Heuristics Plan Structure Plan Quality Plan Execution Figure 3: Preliminary Types of Data Provenance in AI Plan- ning. in AI planning into four categories as shown in Fig- ure 3. The category of Domain Knowledge indicates that information about the planning domain should be collected, such as identification of new constraints or preferences that were initially not obvious, or identifi- cation of additional requirements for goals or actions. The collection and analysis of this category of data provenance would enable refining the planning do- main, including both the domain model and problem instances. The category of Planning Process focuses on data provenance about the state of world used in the planning process and heuristics used to guide the plan generation. The Plan category includes prove- nance about the structure and quality of plans, which relate to the plan rationales and plan evaluation ratio- nales, respectively, and provenance about plan execu- tion, which is especially important as sensors, soft- ware components, unexpected events, people, and ex- ecution of a previous plan can influence the execution of the current plan (Canal et al., 2020). Finally, the category of System Data refers to the input data and output data that are needed for the operation of the resulting planning system. 2.10 Analysis The Analysis phases is dedicated to analysing data provenance collected in the previous phase. The anal- ysis requires capabilities to identify problems, ask questions and generate relevant insights with the ob- jectives of improving all aspects of the planning sys- tem (e.g., domain knowledge, planning process), en- able traceability, reproducibility, and explainability. When this phase is concluded, the next iteration of PlanXflow can be started where actions are taken ac- cording to the generated insights in the analysis phase, e.g., refine the planning domain model or integrate an alternative component with a Solving functionality. 3 DISCUSSION PlanXflow represents a general process for design- ing, developing, and deploying AI planning systems. As such, adjusting some of the lifecycle phases to the specific requirements of some AI planning sys- tems might be necessary. For example, the Domain Model Design phase can be adjusted to include the verification and validation steps of the planning do- main model (Silva et al., 2020). Using our structured approach for engineering AI planning systems may conflict with a more loose approach adopted in the re- search. However, the proposed life cycle has a certain degree of flexibility. Developers can work with se- lected phases and adjust the order of those phases as needed. Some phases are part of the general life cycle because of the limited understanding of AI planning by non-experts. For example, the AI Planning Tools Selection phase might not be needed if a planning ex- pert is available to point out the right tools for ad- dressing the problem at hand. Furthermore, we sug- gest using workflows to orchestrate non-trivial plan- ning applications in the System Architecture and De- sign phase. However, the life cycle can still be used even if workflows might not be needed for a planning system. Some phases can drastically change due to new advancements of AI planning or other technology. For example, the Requirements Analysis phase could be adapted to include AI-driven requirements (Bosch et al., 2018), the AI Planning Model Formulation phase can be adapted or completely discarded if some method appears to be good at providing relevant rec- ommendations, or the System Architecture and De- sign phase may need to be adjusted if a toolbox of standardised planning services becomes available. The presented software development life cycle is intended to provide the basis for discussions among practitioners and researchers of AI planning, and to potentially enable future research in this direction. For example, there are several open challenges that can be addressed to support individual phases and im- prove the current life cycle. One such challenge is the formulation of suitable planning models, which could be addressed by developing a decision-support system. Another challenge is the accessibility and se- lection of suitable planning tools. One option to ad- dress this would be to have a database of available planning tools with details relevant to development, a toolbox, or even a recommender system that will as- sist users in finding which tool is suitable for address- ing which part of the planning problem, thus facil- itating the development of planning systems. In this context, portfolio-based approaches, especially online ones, could be useful as they learn to suggest the right planner for a given task (Ma et al., 2020). Further- more, the design of a holistic strategy for testing plan- ning systems and the development of isolated testing strategies for individual planning artefacts are open research challenges. For deploying AI planning sys- tems, we need to investigate appropriate deployment models for both centralised and distributed planning where all required planning components and deploy- ment information are described in a standard manner, providing for reusability and maintainability. One could upgrade the life cycle by defining sep- arate life cycles for selected planning artefacts and interweaving them in the corresponding phases. For example, a separate life cycle for designing domain models can be created and integrated in the Domain Model Design phase. Finally, a further analysis of data provenance in AI planning might be necessary to refine even more the hierarchy presented in Figure 3, and new approaches are needed to collect and analyse data provenance for all categories. 4 RELA TED WORK To the best of our knowledge, there is no work that studies the software development life cycle for con- structing AI planning systems. There are some stud- ies, guidelines and established practices that are re- lated to some aspect of some of our individual phases. For example, Silva et al. (2020) focus on the pro- cess of designing planning domain models for which they present several phases. This process is compati- ble with our phase of Domain Model Design and can even serve as a basis for creating a separate Domain Model Design life cycle. Pellier and Fiorino (2018) provide guidelines on how to setup and build PDDL4J on a host platform accompanied with a set of planning problems encoded in PDDL to test the planners avail- able in PDDL4J, and on how to integrate the avail- able planners in third-party applications. Muise et al. (2022) provide guidelines for using PLANUTILS, a library for setting up Linux environments for devel- oping, executing, and testing planners. The guidelines explain how to use the planners available in the library and how to add a new package to the library, for ex- ample, if one wished to add a new planner. Outside the AI planning field but within AI, one can observe the appearance of a couple of new soft- ware development life cycles created for specific types of systems. Zaharia et al. (2018) analyse chal- lenges in developing machine learning based systems and describe a platform that can be used to struc- ture and streamline the machine learning development ICSOFT 2023 - 18th International Conference on Software Technologies 758

lifecycle. Olszewska (2019) describes challenges in engineering intelligent vision systems and proposes an adapted software development life cycle with the aim to support developers create quality intelli- gent vision systems of the new generation. Outside AI, Weder et al. (2022) discuss the challenges quan- tum computing introduces when engineering quantum applications and proposes an adapted software devel- opment life cycle aim at developing and executing such applications. 5 CONCLUSION AI planning originated in the mid-1960s, and since then, many approaches have been proposed mainly around two concerns, namely knowledge representa- tion, and reasoning. Those approaches have demon- strated the excellence of AI planning by prototyping planning tools and evaluating them in experiments. The prominence of AI planning is growing by being integrated into real-world applications, highlighting the need to build AI planning systems for prototyp- ing and experiments, and industrial deployments. De- spite the fruitfulness of the discipline with algorithms and planning tools, especially planners, a complete and integrated overview of the phases needed to de- sign, develop, and deploy planning systems is miss- ing. Moreover, a common understanding of relevant phases is needed, which would not only serve inter- disciplinary development teams and non-experts but would also enable discussion within the AI planning community and the emerging AI engineering commu- nity and possibly foster new research. Therefore, we introduced PlanXflow, a software development life cycle for engineering AI planning systems, which consists of ten phases that may happen during the design, development, deployment, and use of plan- ning systems. For each phase, we described the ob- jective, the approaches, and the tools available for its execution. In addition, we explained and highlighted the need for formulating adequate planning models, selecting suitable planning tools, production deploy- ment, and activities typically taken for granted. We also motivated and highlighted the need for prove- nance in AI planning to collect and analyse data in relevant phases. We also pointed out several open challenges, which along with the application of our life cycle on a case study and comparison with other lifecycle models, are of interest for future work. Abstract Domain model generation is a foundational challenge in automated planning, requiring models that are both syntactically correct and semantically robust for effective plan synthesis and execution. Creating planning domain models in languages such as the Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) is time-consuming, error-prone, and requires substantial expertise. This limitation has become a principal bottleneck in scaling AI planning to complex, real-world domains. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have showcased their ability to generate structured, code-like representations from natural language descriptions, fueling optimism that these models might automate the transformation of human intent into formal planning models. However, fully automating the generation of domain models from natural language is still a challenge. Outputs from LLMs often have semantic errors, logical faults, and lack the reliability needed for dependable planning. Additionally, current processes frequently need manual adjustments or corrections from experts, which goes against the aim of total automation. To address these limitations, this thesis proposes a novel feedback-driven framework that enables LLMs to generate PDDL domain models through a fully automated pipeline with no human intervention. The first step is to have the LLM generate intermediate representations called Answer Set Programming (ASP) rules. These ASP rules are then used, again through the LLM, to generate corresponding PDDL domain models via structured prompts and iterative feedback. Semantic coherence and context relevance are ensured through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), offering PDDL samples to facilitate generation and correction. Once the domain models are generated, plans are created using the Fast Downward planner and then validated using VAL to ensure logical soundness and successful goal achievement. The frameworkisevaluatedusingfiveadvancedLLMs—Gemini1.5Flash,Gemini2.5Flash,DeepSeek V3, DeepSeek R1, NVIDIA: Llama 3.3 Nemotron Super 49B v1—in the benchmark domains of the International Planning Competition (IPC). Performance is assessed based on accuracy, generation time, makespan, and plan cost, revealing differences in how effectively each LLM adapts tostructuredfeedback. TheresultsdemonstratethatLLMscanreliablygenerateplanner-compatible models with few errors through targeted prompting and automated refinement. 3

1 Introduction Automated planning, also known as AI planning, is a key area of artificial intelligence that enables intelligent agents to autonomously determine sequences of actions to achieve specific goals in complex and dynamic environments [NGT04]. At the heart of these systems is the domain model. This model formally outlines the actions, preconditions, and effects that describe the possible interactions between an agent and its environment [Geo23; MGH+98]. The quality and usefulness of the plans that are produced are directly impacted by the domain model’s expressiveness and accuracy. The generation of high-quality domain models is seen as one of the biggest challenges in scaling automatedplanningsystemstoreal-worldsituations. WritingPlanningDomainDefinitionLanguage (PDDL) models requires not just defining the structure of actions and predicates but also capturing complex semantic dependencies, causal relationships, and constraints that represent the intended behavior of the domain accurately [Geo23; Pat24; TZM25]. This process is inherently iterative, requiringrepeatedvalidation,revision,andoftencollaborationbetweendomainexpertsandplanning specialists. Constantly updating and verifying domain models can be expensive in contexts which modify frequently. This creates a significant maintenance burden and slows down the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) planning technologies at scale. Asreal-worldapplicationsofplanninggrowtoincluderobotics,industrialautomation,logistics,and complexsoftwaresystems,thechallengeofscaling,maintaining,andadjustingthesemodelstomeet changing needs has become more pressing. Even small mistakes, such as missing preconditions, unreachable goals, or contradictory effects, can make models unusable. This can lead to plans that fail or are logically flawed [Pat24; SJCG24a]. The development and implementation of planning systems would be simpler for non-experts if the process for generating domain models from natural languagewereautomated. Itwouldalsospeedupprototyping,helpadapttonewfields,andimprove resistance to errors in specifications. More data-driven and AI-supported approaches have replaced traditional, expert-driven workflows in the planning community in recent years. This change has come from the growing complexity of tasks and the need for more flexible, user-friendly planning solutions. As planning areas become more varied and dynamic, often involving multiple agents, uncertain situations, or rapidly changing goals. The responsibility on human modelers to cover all possible scenarios has increased significantly. Meanwhile, improvements in natural language understanding and machine learning have pushed efforts to connect informal user needs and formal planning representations. With Large Language Models (LLMs) showing a growing ability to process, interpret, and create structured content from text,wehaveauniquechancetorethinkthemodelingprocess. ThischangecouldmakeAIplanning more accessible, easier to maintain, and more aligned with user intent. Achieving this level of automationcouldopenupnewareasforapplicationandspreadthebenefitsofsmartplanningacross different industries. 15

1 Introduction Beyond just being a technical convenience, automating the generation of domain models plays a crucial role in making AI planning more accessible to a broader audience while also lightening the cognitive load on users. Many sectors like personalized assistants, smart manufacturing, logistics optimization, and service robotics require regular updates to their planning models to keep up with new tasks, constraints, or user preferences. If there are delays or errors in updating these models, it can result in operational challenges, increased costs, or even safety concerns. By enabling users to express their planning tasks in natural language and converting those requests into accurate domain models, we can significantly speed up innovation cycles and encourage wider adoption of planning technology. LLMs like GPT-4 and DeepSeek have sparked considerable interest in using their strong natural language processing abilities to connect informal human intent with the formal symbolic represen- tations needed by planners [KVG+24; OSK+24a; VK23]. Moreover, their ability to learn from previous modeling experiences and feedback allows for ongoing enhancements as planning systems adjust to new challenges and requirements. With their extensive training on diverse datasets and emerging reasoning skills, LLMs provide a promising route to streamline domain modeling and encourage innovative human-AI collaboration in the planning field. The generation of semantically correct domain models from natural language in an completely automated, end-to-end manner is still an open problem. The challenge now lies in converting these capabilities into robust, transparent, and verifiable pipelines that planners can rely on in practice. ThisthesisbridgesthegapbycombiningLLM-generatedmodelswithsymbolicvalidation, improving both the automation and reliability of domain model generation in AI planning. 1.1 Overview of the State of the Art An increasing number of research focused on the automated generation of planning domain models using LLMs. The goal is to convert structured or semi-structured natural language input into PDDL or similar formats [KVG+24; OSK+24a; SJCG24b; VK23]. Early research demonstrated that, when provided with well-crafted prompts or templates, LLMs could produce legitimate PDDL fragments and even genuine action schemas for traditional planning tasks. Nevertheless, thorough analyses have repeatedly demonstrated that LLM-generated models frequently contain semantic flaws. Theseincludeunattainablegoals,lackinginvariants,andactiondefinitionsthatareinsufficient orinconsistent. ThereasonfortheseissuesisthatLLMsareessentiallystatisticalmodelsoflanguage rather than systems that comprehend logic unique to planning. Because of this, they frequently lack the resources to guarantee action consistency or adhere to domain restrictions [Pat24; SJCG24b; VK23]. To address these shortcomings, recent frameworks such as the Translate-Infer-Compile (TIC) pipeline have introduced intermediate logical representations—most notably Answer Set Programming (ASP)—and incorporated symbolic verifiers like Clingo to check and refine logical consistency prior to PDDL synthesis [ASS24; SJCG24b]. Other lines of work have focused on retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). This framework improves the context of LLM outputs by using validated domain examples. Another area is validation-guided refinement. In this method, external tools give feedback that is regularly included in repeated generation cycles [GVSK23; HLP+23]. Despite these advances, most systems still need manual intervention at various stages, either to correct remaining errors or to curate templates and examples. Ongoing challenges include the lack of integrated, automated correction tools, limited support for complex domain features, 16

The planning task is then cast as a search for a path through this state space from the initial state to one that satisfies the goals, using only allowed actions [AG24]. Classical planning operates under assumptions of a static, deterministic, and fully observable world. 2 Background 2.2 Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) The PDDL, which was first presented by [MGH+98], is the most widely used modeling language in classical planning. It standardizes the representation of actions, preconditions, effects, and domainconstraints. PDDLisadomain-specificlanguagedevelopedtostandardizethewayplanning problems are described [MGH+98]. It allows for defining two core files: • Domain File (domain.pddl): Describes types, predicates, and actions, each defined with their respective preconditions and effects. • Problem File (problem.pddl): Specifies objects, initial state, and the goal state to be achieved. With its Lisp-like syntax of nested parentheses, PDDL is predicated on first-order logic. Its formal structure is based on relations and objects: actions define possible transitions between states by defining preconditions and effects, while predicates explain facts about objects [AG24]. Logical connectives like not, and, or, forall (universal quantification), and existing (existential quantification) can be used in PDDL to characterize complex circumstances. The division of domain and problem descriptions facilitates benchmarking and modularity by enabling the reuse of a single domain definition across several problem instances. With each iteration, PDDL has grown to incorporate more complex features such as temporal actions, derived predicates, conditional effects, constraints, plan preferences, object typing, and numeric fluents. PDDL’sformalsyntaxenablesplannerstoreasonoveractionsandstatetransitionssystematically. It supportsawidearrayofplanningconstructsincludingconditionaleffects,numericfluents,temporal actions, and object typing. However, writing syntactically and semantically correct PDDL models remains a challenging task, especially for non-experts [OSK+24a; SATK22]. 2.3 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) RAG is a hybrid setup that improves the factual accuracy and performance of LLMs by combining generation with information retrieval. Traditional LLMs often have problems with outdated or inaccurate outputs because of limits in their training data. RAG solves this issue by allowing the model to search an external knowledge source, such as a database, corpus, or document store, during inference. It then integrates the retrieved information into its responses. The setup usually includes two main parts: a retriever that finds relevant documents based on the input query, and a generator that bases its output on both the query and the retrieved documents [HH24; LPP+20]. Thissetupclosesthegapbetweenstaticpretraininganddynamicknowledgeaccess. ItallowsLLMs to produce more accurate and current outputs. In planning contexts, RAG is key in grounding model outputs, such as PDDL domain models, using valid, reusable prior examples. This is especially helpful when models generate structured outputs that need to follow strict syntactic and semantic rules. By using a retrieval corpus, such as standard IPC planning domains, the generation process is informed by structurally correct samples. This improves both correctness and interpretability [HH24]. RAG is not just a way to improve knowledge; it is also a tool that helps match LLM outputs with expert-designed domain schemas. This is important for planning pipelines, like the one discussed in this thesis. 22

2.4 Answer Set Programming (ASP) 2.4 Answer Set Programming (ASP) A declarative programming approach called ASP is designed to solve challenging search and reasoning issues [GKKS14; Lif99]. Using logic rules, facts, and constraints, ASP enables users to model issues. It then depends on solvers to provide stable models (also known as answer sets) that meet the requirements. ASP is particularly powerful for nonmonotonic reasoning, where new information can invalidate previous conclusions [BET11]. ASP offers a concise and expressive method for encoding action preconditions, transition effects, and domain dynamics in the planning context. It makes it possible to model conditional effects, frame axioms, and inertia in a logical and natural way. Lifschitz demonstrated how ASP can be used to encode classical planning tasks by mapping states, actions, and goals into logic programs [Lif99]. The resulting answer sets correspond to valid plans. ASP’s structured logic makes it ideal for integration with symbolic verifiers like Clingo, which can identify structural and syntactic inconsistencies. For instance, consider a simple domain with locations A and B and an agent needing to move between them. In ASP, one might encode this as: • Facts: location(a). location(b). at(a, 0). • Actions: action(move(X,Y)) :- location(X), location(Y), X != Y. • Transition Effects: at(Y, T+1) :- occurs(move(X,Y), T), at(X, T). • Frame Axioms: at(L, T+1) :- at(L, T), not -at(L, T+1). • Goal: :- not at(b, maxTime). This formulation supports rigorous logical reasoning and is a natural fit for intermediate representa- tion in our pipeline. 2.5 Large Language Models (LLMs) and Prompting LLMs constitute a revolutionary innovation in artificial intelligence to the extent that machines can comprehend as well as produce human language with unprecedented expressiveness as well as flexibility. Composed largely using the Transformer architecture, LLMs are distinguished by their vast scale, with tens or even hundreds of billions of parameters in the case of typical LLMs. They are trained on huge corpora of text [WTB+22]. The history of language modeling has unfolded from statistical models, including the use of n-gram strategies, then neural language models using recurrent neural networks, to recent moves towards pre-trained language models (PLMs) using large-scale unsupervised or self-supervised learning [ZZL+25]. LLMs work through the generation of the probability distribution over word sequences, usually through the use of next-token predictability. Training the models is computationally demanding, with the use of distributed optimization techniques, as well as advanced engineering to deal with the size of the models as well as the data. With the growth in the size of the models, researchers 23

2 Background have observed the ’scaling law’ where enhanced model capability as well as better downstream task performance is bound to follow a definite trend with regard to model parameters, data size, as well as computational effort. A defining feature of LLMs is the emergence of novel abilities that are absent in smaller mod- els. These emergent abilities such as in-context learning, instruction following, and multi-step reasoning—manifest abruptly when the model surpasses a certain scale, rather than improving incrementally with size. This phenomenon is akin to a phase transition, where qualitative changes in model behavior arise from quantitative increases in scale. Take few-shot learning, for example: LLMs learn to tackle new tasks straight from the examples provided in the input prompt, without any new parameters being fitted. Similarly, with some smart prompting (for instance, with a CoT prompt), the resources of larger models can be organized to answer complex questions that are quite beyond smaller ones. A particularly effective prompting technique is CoT prompting, which encourages the LLM to decomposereasoningtasksintostep-by-steplogicalfragments[WWS+22]. Thisisespeciallyuseful when generating structured outputs like ASP or PDDL, as it forces the model to internalize the logical dependencies involved. However, despite their fluency, LLMs lack the formal reasoning abilitiestoensurelogicalsoundness. Thismakesthemidealcandidatesforintegrationwithexternal symbolic verifiers and refinement loops. LLMS have transformed from how Natural Language Processing (NLP) is approached, shifting from custom models, to general, adaptable systems that can be to a wide range of natural tasks and problems. Their impact can be seen in the wide array of problem to which they can be applied. 24

Early attempts mainly focused on using fully or partially observed plan traces, demonstrations, or state transitions to deduce preconditions, effects, and action structures. Several surveys have classified these approaches according to their data sources, levels of supervision, and the types of models they target. A significant contribution in this field is the work by [AJO19], which presents the learning of STRIPS action models as a classical planning problem. However, it relies heavily on human involvement, especially for creating and reviewing intermediate rules and correcting outputs that cannot be fully automated. TIC does not include step-by-step validation or correction with outside validators after PDDL generation. As a result, logical or semantic errors can remain after the initial compilation. TIC is important to our work because it clearly shows the value of using intermediate logic layers and modular design in text-to-plan systems. Our thesis builds on this by adding validator-driven checkpoints and automated feedback loops. This approach seeks to achieve ongoing, validator-guided improvement while reducing human involvement in generating the domain model [al24a]. The article “VAL: Automatic Plan Validation, Continuous Effects and Mixed Initiative Planning Using PDDL” introduces the VAL tool as a standard for validating PDDL plans. VAL offers strong support for PDDL features like continuous effects and allows for mixed-initiative planning cycles. In these cycles, humans and automated systems work together to generate and refine plans. While VAL plays a key role in making sure plans are semantically correct and executable, its design supports workflows in which humans construct or revise plans with guidance from VAL. The main innovation of VAL is its semantic depth and ability to manage complex planning features in the real world. However, it mainly serves as a post-hoc validator instead of an automated part of the domain model generation process. Our thesis builds on VAL’s strong feedback mechanisms by integrating its semantic validation directly into the model-building pipeline. We adapt and expands the use of VAL from a post-hoc plan checker to an active participant in model development, using its semantic feedback not only to ensure plan soundness but to identify and resolve domain modeling errors throughout the construction process [HLF04]. 4.2 Intermediate Representation via ASP Generation 4.2.1 Why Intermediate Result End-to-end direct translation of natural language into executable PDDL domain models with LLMs has proven to be unreliable because of inherent limitations in symbolic reasoning and structural fidelity. [OSK+24a; SATK22] show that the frequent output of such models is syntactically acceptable but semantically incomplete domain specifications, with high rates of ill-formed predicates, inconsistent effects of actions, and absent typing constraints. [SJCG24a] add that while such models are structurally possible, they tend to fail under formal verification, which reflects an enduring disparity between linguistic fluency and logical correctness. This shortfall derives from the token-level, distributional character of LLMs, which have no explicit representations of causal relations and domain-specific constraints essential in symbolic planning. As explained in [KVG+24], LLMs are not independent planners but need to be embedded in mixed neuro-symbolic architectures that unite generative power with symbolic verification. To solve this, the suggested pipeline places an explicit intermediate representation, in-between the input natural language and the output PDDL model. This decoupling at the architecture supports staged reasoning and verification, where incremental imposition of syntactic and semantic constraints is performed. The use of IR in the design not only obviates the semantic inconsistencies seen in direct LLM-to-PDDL pipelines but also offers formal support for feedback refinement procedures. 4.2.2 Selection of Intermediate result Numerous intermediate formats have been proposed in the earlier research to organize planning knowledge prior to PDDL translation. These include domain-specific logic templates [AF18], XML/JSON abstractions like itSIMPLE [VTS13], hierarchical task networks (HTN) [GA15]. However, each of these formalisms has limitations in terms of expressiveness, tool integration, or formal verifiability. By contrast, ASP presents an excellent tradeoff among logical expressiveness, solver support, and translatability. [HDN12] effectively utilized ASP in robotic navigation with semantic constraints, confirmingthepotentialofASPinreasoning-intensiveapplications. Itwasalsonotedby[JYW+18] that representations based on ASP performed well in logistic applications that included complex precondition modelings and default reasoning. Additionally, ASP allows for dynamic validation and refinement because it is semantically meaningful and compatible with external verifiers like Clingo, unlike XML/JSON formats. ASP is, therefore, utilized in this work as the preferred intermediate representation because of its representational power, certifiability, and multi-stage neuro-symbolic pipeline compatibility. Its use supports layered verification, error identification at an early stage, and traceability from intent to executable planning logic—enabling improved robustness and correctness in domain models produced by LLM. ASP, which is a declarative logic formalism with established semantics [Lif99], can support rule-based representation of preconditions, fluents, and effects and is easily verifiable via ASP solvers like Clingo [GKKS19]. In addition, the use of ASP is consistent with more recent developments in neuro-symbolic planning, particularly the efforts of [HDN12] and [JYW+18], 33

4 LLM-Modulo Framework where representations at an intermediate logic stage improve interpretability, error localization, and future translatability. The use of IR in the design not only obviates the semantic inconsistencies seen in direct LLM-to-PDDL pipelines but also offers formal support for feedback refinement procedures. Incorporating ASP as an IR, then, plays both functional and methodological roles: it decreases the cognitive load upon LLMs, imposes symbolic coherence before PDDL generation, and facilitates iterative refinement through programmatic verification—as all are necessary to produce runnable, planner-compliant domain models. 4.3 ASP Verification with External Verifier and Feedback Loop Once the intermediate ASP representation has been generated, the pipeline proceeds to a crucial validation phase that ensures its syntactic correctness before moving on to downstream translation stages. This validation is performed using an external verifier, a dedicated tool designed specifically to parse ASP programs and analyze their structural integrity. Acting as a standalone checkpoint within the broader system, this verifier is responsible for identifying a variety of common syntactic issues. These include, but are not limited to, improperly grounded rules, the presence of unsafe variables, references to undefined atoms, and other malformed or ill-formed rule structures that could compromise the logic program’s validity. This stage showcases widely accepted best practices in developing neuro-symbolic systems, where early formal verification is crucial for ensuring the integrity of the entire process. By identifying structural issues early on, the system can prevent the risk of cascading errors that might carry over into later stages, making them tougher to spot and fix. When the verifier detects a syntactic issue, it creates detailed and structured diagnostics that clearly explain both the type of violation and its location in the program. These diagnostics aren’t just noted down—they’re actively turned into feedback prompts that are sent back to the LLM, providing it with specific guidance for making necessary revisions. This feedback mechanism is not just open-ended; it operates inside a preset repeating cycle. The LLM is given a set number of opportunities to refine and correct the ASP code in response to the verifier’s errors. The method focuses on improving the code in every cycle by resolving the specific issues that the verifier found. The code is sent back for validation after revision, and this cycle is repeated until the code either satisfies the maximum number of permitted iterations or passes all syntactic checks. The most recent iteration of the ASP representation, however maybe prone to errors, is saved and proceeded to the subsequent step in the pipeline. By combining automated syntaxcheckswithastep-by-steprefinementprocess,thisframeworkguaranteesthatwell-structured logic programs make it through the pipeline. This method enhances the structural integrity and overall reliability of the system, reducing the likelihood of failures later on and enhancing the robustness of the domain modeling process as a whole. 34

This generationg process leverages multiple sources of information: • Original Natural Language Input: Retaining the original user scenario ensures that high-level goals and domain intent are preserved, reducing the risk of semantic drift in pddl generation. • Verified ASP:The syntactically valid ASP serves as an intermediate logic-based represen- tation, offering a modular and error-localizable foundation for PDDL generation [ASS24; GVSK23]. • RAG: Contextual examples are dynamically retrieved from a curated database of planning models—such as the IPC PDDL corpora—using RAG methods. RAG was used in this pipeline to tackle the known limitations of LLMS in generating logically consistent and domain-specific structured outputs. While LLMs excel at generating fluent text, they often invent functions, types, or predicates in formal languages like PDDL, especially when trained on general data without specific domain knowledge [KVG+24; OSK+24a]. RAG mitigates this problem by using dependable PDDL corpora, like IPC planning domains, to guide the generation process. During generation, this retrieval step guarantees that the model can access authentic syntactic structures and significant planning notions. Consequently, it raises the likelihood of generating outputs that complement planners. Empirical studies in the neuro-symbolic planning literature (e.g., [ASS24; SFHK25]) show that adding RAG to code or domain model synthesis pipelines boosts structural fidelity and success rates in plan generation. RAG provides LLM2 with concrete, high-quality domain model templates, addressing the common LLM issues of hallucination and lack of generalization [KVG+24; OSK+24b; SFHK25]. 4 LLM-Modulo Framework 4.5 Syntactic Validation of PDDL and Iterative Correction After generating the domain and problem files in PDDL format, we introduce a crucial validation step to make sure the models stick to the formal syntax of the planning language. This syntactic check acts as a protective measure, catching issues like undeclared predicates, undefined types, and poorly formed expressions. To support this, the framework incorporates an external validation mechanism capable of parsing the generated models and producing structured diagnostic outputs. If the external verifier identifies any syntax or format errors, these diagnostics (including explicit error messages and faulty PDDL sections) are automatically formatted as prompts and sent back to LLM2 for correction using feedback loops. The LLM refines its output accordingly, and the loop continues until both domain.pddl and problem.pddl are validated as shown in Figure 4.3. This iterative refinement ensures that errors are eliminated early, preventing failures in planning or until we hit a set limit on the number of refinement attempts. By adding this layer of validation and correction early on, we reduce the chances of failures later in the process and boost the structural reliability of the models before they go into planning execution[ASS24; KVG+24]. 4.6 Plan Generation and Semantic Feedback Loop Following syntactic validation, the PDDL files are passed to a classical AI planner, which attempts to generate a valid plan for the given problem [Hel06]. • Rationale: Planning execution is the only way to guarantee that the generated PDDL models are not just syntactically correct but also operationally complete and goal-attainable—a limi- tation often observed in models generated by LLMs without plan-level feedback [OSK+24a; SJCG24a]. • Semantic Feedback Loop:As shown in Figure 4.3, if the planner fails to find a valid plan indicating possible semantic or modeling errors—its error messages, along with the PDDL files, are used to construct a targeted feedback prompt for LLM2. This feedback loop enables LLM2 to iteratively repair and refine the PDDL models until the planner successfully generates a plan. 4.7 Semantic Validation of the Generated Plans While syntactic correctness of the domain and problem models is essential, it does not guarantee that the generated plan will be logically sound or executable. In order to determine whether the generated plan satisfies all preconditions, attains the desired goal states, and appropriately applies effects across state transitions, the last stage of the suggested pipeline incorporates an external plan validationstep. Thisadditionallayerofverificationensuresthatevenwhenthedomainandproblem files are syntactically valid, any latent semantic inconsistencies such as incorrect operator effects or missing causal links can be identified and addressed before model acceptance. Prior work such as [GVVK24] and [SFHK25] have highlighted the common failure of LLM-generated models in handling execution-level correctness, necessitating such semantic validation layers. 5 Implementation The framework proposed for generating PDDL domain models from natural language descriptions is based on the cohesive coordination of several components during both the generation and verification phases. The implementation is described in detail in this chapter, including the prompts, choice and setup of the Large Language Models (LLM1 and LLM2), and the incorporation of external verification tools. The implementation is organized into sequential phases ranging from input processing, candidate construction, validation, refinement, to final synthesis to provide an overall reliable pipeline to facilitate syntactic correctness as well as semantic soundness of the produced models. The methodologies adopted at each phase are meant to reduce human interaction, facilitate reusability, and achieve the scalability of automated planning systems, finally enabling the production of reliable and planner-compliant domain models. 5.1 Prompt Design Our approach begins with the use of domain-specific natural language prompts derived from AutoPlanBench1, a publicly available benchmarking framework specifically designed to evaluate the planning capabilities of LLMs in classical planning domains. AutoPlanBench automatically generates domain encodings by extracting symbolic components such as actions, preconditions, and effects from PDDL domain files. These components are then mapped to templated natural language descriptions and refined using GPT-4, resulting in logically structured and fluent domain narratives. A key strength of these prompts lies in their clarity and structure: they describe object types, available actions, preconditions for those actions, and their effects in a precise, step-by-step format. As shown by [SFHK25], these automatically generated prompts perform on par with the human- authored ones in terms of accuracy and consistency across planning tasks. Their stepwise nature facilitates model interpretability and supports structured reasoning, making them well-suited for use in neuro-symbolic planning pipelines. AutoPlanBench contains a large collection of classical planning domains, many of which include multiple variants with different constraints or action formulations. For the purpose of this thesis, a representative but limited subset of base domains was selected at random. No domain variations were included in the evaluation to maintain consistency and avoid introducing confounding factors across experiments. 1https://github.com/minecraft-saar/autoplanbench 39

5 Implementation In our framework, these prompts serve as a foundational input to LLM1, which uses them to generate ASP logic. The same prompt is reused in the second stage (LLM2) to support the generation of PDDL domain and problem files. This dual use maintains semantic consistency across intermediate representations, ensuring that the core meaning of the original task description is preserved throughout the pipeline. 5.2 CoT Strategy To enable reliable logic generation from natural language, we integrate the domain prompts into a structured CoT prompting framework. This framework explicitly decomposes the reasoning task intosequentialsubtasks,guidingtheLLMtoprocessthedomaindescriptioninalogicallygrounded manner. The CoT prompt used for LLM1 instructs the model to: (1) identify the initial and goal states, (2) extract all relevant object types and predicates, and (3) apply predefined transformation rules to convert natural language descriptions into ASP-compatible facts and rules. These transformation rules are embedded directly into the prompt and are based on a set of hardcoded patterns implemented in our pipeline. They account for various linguistic and structural representations, such as atomic and relational predicates, grid-based spatial mappings, and time- indexed logic. In addition, the prompt enforces formatting constraints to ensure compatibility with Clingo, for instance, by specifying correct use of negation with ‘not‘, grounding all variables, and ensuring consistent rule structure. For LLM2, a similar CoT prompting strategy is employed to support PDDL domain and problem file generation. The prompt combines the validated ASP output, the original domain encoding from AutoPlanBench, and specific syntactic requirements for STRIPS-compliant PDDL. In cases where errors are detected by VAL or the AI planner, the pipeline reuses this prompt structure, augmented with the error message, to automatically refine the output. This feedback-driven refinement loop ensures that each generated model adheres not only to formal syntax but also to the intended semantics of the planning problem in order to generate valid plans. By integrating structured CoT prompts at both stages, our approach achieves a high degree of reliability, enabling transparent reasoning, consistent transformation, and automated repair of logic representations. As shown in Figure 5.1, the domain descriptions are given from the AutoPlanBench repository as the initial user input to the LLM. 40

For example, DeepSeek explicitly characterizes DeepSeek R1 as a logic-focused model that was trained with a robust focus on reasoning abilities, coding challenges, and sequential reasoning [DGY+25]. Traditionally, these models brought together rule-based reasoning (RBR), which uses clear logic rules, and case-based reasoning (CBR), which draws on past experiences or known cases to tackle new, similar problems. This combination helped expert systems work well even in areas with both clear and uncertain information. In modern neural language models (LLMs), hybrid reasoning means using designs or control methods that balance general language understanding with structured, logic-based reasoning like multi-step reasoning, code generation, or planning. Initially developed by [HLF04] for the IPC , VAL has since become a standard for verifying both domain/problem files and the correctness of plans with respect to them. Its first role in this pipeline is to act as an external verifier immediately after LLM2 generates domain.pddl and problem.pddl files. VAL is used to perform strict syntactic validation, catching errors such as unmatched parentheses, missing colons, undefined predicates, or ill-formed parameters. The VAL error messages are parsed, formatted, and structured as targeted feedback prompts for LLM2 refinement if any such problems are found. This iterative correction loop continues until VAL confirms that both domain and problem models conform to expected PDDL syntax standards or has reached maximum iterations. The second and equally important role of VAL occurs after the planning stage, where the AI planner has produced a plan based on the validated PDDL files. Here, VAL serves as a semantic validator,ensuringthateveryactionintheplanrespectsprecondition-effectconstraints,achievesthe stated goals, and adheres to causal links defined in the domain logic. This includes computing key plan metrics such as makespan and step-wise consistency, as demonstrated by works like [Pat24; SJCG24a], who used VAL not just for plan validation but also for computing execution feasibility, 44

5.5 AI Planner- Fast Downward cost, and timeline accuracy . Unlike the earlier syntactic verification stage, semantic plan validation does not initiate another LLM correction loop; instead, it serves as a final checkpoint. If a plan fails, it is not accepted as a valid outcome. This two-tiered integration mirrors best practices from recent literature, where symbolic tools like VAL serve as essential backstops for LLM-generated artifacts, bridging the gap between linguistic generation and logical execution. Overall, VAL provides a robust mechanism for elevating both the formal soundness and practical executability of the plans in this neuro-symbolic architecture. 5.5 AI Planner- Fast Downward Fast Downward [Hel06] is a domain-independent planning system employed widely in automated planning research, particularly in benchmark environments like the IPC. It is a multi-stage planning architecture to enable search scalability in large planning spaces. Internally, it first transforms the PDDL problem to a finite-domain representation, then preprocesses it via causal graphs, domain transition graphs, and invariant synthesis, finally executing heuristic-guided search by means of selection methods such as Fast-Forward (FF) search or landmark heuristics. Fast Downward has been widely used in recent studies that combine symbolic planning and LLMs. In the TIC pipeline by [al24a], Fast Downward is employed to validate PDDL domain models after logical compilation from intermediate ASP representations, ensuring that generated models are not only syntactically correct but also operationally sound. Similarly, [LHZ+23] show how useful Fast Downward is for connecting natural language inputs with executable plans by integrating it into their LLM+P methodology, which blends LLM-based translation with external planning validation. In neuro-symbolic pipelines with LLMs, Fast Downward performs a vital operational function in both plan generation and implicit validation. Recently, in works like those by [OSK+24a], [SJCG24a],aswellas[VK23],FastDownwardwasincorporatedtocheckifLLM-generateddomain and problem files can produce executable plans. When a planner fails to generate a plan even for syntactically correct PDDL, it’s often a sign of semantic inconsistencies, i.e., unreachable goals, unmet preconditions, or conflicting effects, which syntax checkers like VAL might fail to identify. In this thesis, Fast Downward was used at the backend stages of the pipeline. Once PDDL files have been checked by VAL for syntax, they are passed to Fast Downward. If no valid plan can be found, resulting error trace along with PDDL files as well as a fixing prompt are backprompted to LLM2 to suggest a revision to a domain model. The feedback loop allows for semantic refinement in an iterative manner, making the domain model not only valid in terms of its structure but also executable. 45

Every loop could be started by: • Syntacticerrors,identifiedbyeitherVAL(whenvalidatingonlythedomainandproblemfiles) or by Fast Downward during its parsing stage. These include missing brackets, undeclared predicates, malformed :goal or :init blocks, and structural mismatches. • Failures in plan generation occur when Fast Downward can parse the input but is unable to produce a valid plan. This includes scenarios like ’no solution found’, ’goal not reachable’, and ’initial state is a dead end’. Monitoring this indicator gives us information on the quality of the LLM’s original output as well as the efficacy of the refining logic. The LLM produced a nearly accurate model the first or second time since there were fewer feedback loops. 49

6 Experimental Evaluation 6.3.6 Accuracy To determine how accurate the LLM-generated domain.pddl files are, we compare them to the groundtruth reference domains available in the AutoPlanBench benchmark repository. Previous research has introduced a variety of automated metrics for this evaluation. For example, the Action Reconstruction Error and Heuristic Domain Equivalence Metric developed by [OSK+24a] assess the exact symbolic and structural similarities between action schemas in both the ground truth and the generated domains. Similarly, [SJCG24a] and others check domain accuracy by ensuring that the entire planning and execution process works correctly with the generated model. However, these methods assume a strict symbolic alignment, meaning that predicate names, type names, and object constants must match exactly between the domain and problem files. Even small lexical differences—like has_image versus have_image or pointing_at versus pointing—can cause planner failures,makingtheseevaluationsoverlysensitiveandoftenunfairtoLLMoutputsthatarelogically correct but lexically different. Additionally, [GPQ+25] demonstrate that LLM-generated domains frequently struggle to generate valid plans, not because of flawed logic, but due to inconsistent naming between the domain.pddl and problem.pddl files, which standard planners see as undefined references. To overcome this limitation, we’ve turned to a method that incorporates logic-aware predicate normalization along with fuzzy matching to evaluate accuracy. Our method is based on fuzzy lexical alignment, which uses the difflib library to calculate predicate name similarity ratios. This allowsustomatchtokensthatdifferintheirphrasingbutareconceptuallycomparable(has_imageis basically equivalent to have_image, for example). In order to explicitly normalize known predicate variations as needed, we also keep an optional synonym map (for example, connecting has_image and have_image to a single term, have_image). In our evaluation, we extract all actions from both the groundtruth and generated domain files, calculating a weighted similarity score based on the similarity of action names and the Jaccard index for normalized preconditions and effects. This method allows for semantic alignment, even when there are variations in naming, resulting in a more lenient and realistic estimate of domain accuracy. Although this unique combination of fuzzy predicate matching and structural action comparison is new to our research, similar elements have been examined separately: [SJCG24a] suggest name normalization to enhance consistency in domaingeneration,andtheTICframework[al24a]alignslogicthroughintermediaterepresentations tominimizesymbolicmismatches. However,tothebestofourknowledge,therehasn’tbeenametric that directly compares generated and ground-truth domain.pddl files using both fuzzy matching and synonym normalization for evaluating structural similarity. Our method addresses this gap by delivering a scalable, interpretable, and semantically grounded accuracy score for LLM-generated PDDL domain models. In Figure 6.1, you can see a practical example of how we compute and present this logic-aware accuracy evaluation. It details the results for the Satellite domain generated using the DeepSeek V3 model. The figure illustrates how the tool identifies and matches five actions between the LLM-generated domain.pddl and the corresponding ground-truth file. The average logic match score, which is derived from predicate-level fuzzy similarity across preconditions and effects, is an impressive 0.984, showing a nearly perfect alignment. We also provide individual similarity scores for each matched action, and because the average score exceeds the 0.85 threshold we established, we confidently return a final verdict of MATCH. This logic-aware evaluation gives us a more nuanced and semantically accurate measure of domain model accuracy than simply relying on strict symbolic comparisons. 50
