2 Background 2.1 AI Planning 2.1.1 Definition and evolution AI planning is a process of solving a planning problem. It produces a plan consisting of a set of steps to be carried out to reach the goal state. The planning problem has an initial state, a goal state to be reached. The planner is provided with a domain model along with a planning problem that consists of a set of actions that can be performed which should be used to reach from initial to goal state [Geo22]. AI planning has been researched since AI itself existed. However, there were certain major leaps in the research and development of AI planning that helped it advance. The evolutionary steps in the area are formulated here. • STRIPS: Stanford Research Institute Problem Solver (STRIPS) was a problem solver developed that created a world model using a collection of arbitrary first-order predicates. It attempted to reach the goal formula state from this initial world model using a sequence of operators [FN71]. STRIPS which was introduced by Richard Fikes and Nils Nilsson in 1971, became the foundation for many future planning models. • Graphplan: A new planner was introduced by Avrium Blum and Merrick Furst in the 1990s that solved STRIPS-like domains using planning graphs. It was called graphplan which always returned the shortest possible partial order plan if a solution existed. The planning graph could be created in polynomial time and space and was more compact than the state space generated by STRIPS [BF97]. • HSP: Heuristic Search Planning (HSP) developed soon after graphplan using heuristic search which is estimating the distance to the goal state from the initial state. The benefit of HSP was deriving a heuristic function from the high-level representation of goals and actions for domain-independent planning [98]. • HTN Planning: Hierarchical Task Network (HTN) is a network that decomposes high-level tasks into simpler formats. HTN planning that used a task network as an objective was proposed in the early 1970s, but remained controversial until a Simple Hierarchical Ordered Planner (SHOP) was developed in 1999 which led to its popularity [GA15]. HTN planner reaches from the initial state to the objective task network. It uses domain knowledge of networks consisting of tasks that are in the simplest form or need to be decomposed further. The controversy for this planner arose because of well-defined task network requirements [GA15]. 19

2 Background • ICAPS and IPC: International Conference on Automated Planning and Scheduling (ICAPS)(previously known as Artificial Intelligence Planning and Scheduling (AIPS)) conferencewasfirstorganizedin1992fortheadvancementofthefieldofAIplanning. ICAPS became a hub where many benchmark problems were developed. International Planning Competition (IPC) which encourages researchers and developers to build more effective and efficient AI planning systems was also introduced by ICAPS. They serve to understand the current state of the art with advancements and challenges. 2.1.2 Components • Planningdomainmodel : AsmentionedinthedefinitionofAIplanning,theplanningsystem providesaknowledgemodel. Thismodelistermedadomainmodelwhichformallyrepresents the application domain in a conceptual and abstract manner [AG23]. More information about domain models is explained in Section 2.2 of this chapter. • Planning problem: A planning problem is an instantiation of a scenario in the application domain and needs to be solved by the AI planner with the help of a domain model [AG23]. • Plan: A set of operations or tasks generated by the AI planner to solve the given planning problemiscalledaplan. Incertaincases, asingleplanningprobleminagivendomainmodel can be solved in more than one way. Most AI planners either provide multiple plans or give one plan from a set of possible plans. In some cases problems are unsolvable and no plan is generated. In common terms, the planning domain model and planning problem are inputs to the AI planner while the plan is the generated output. 2.1.3 Types of planning AI planning can be divided into many types and although more types exist, the four mentioned have been popular and researched in depth. • Classical planning: Classical planning is a simplistic but widely used form of planning. It uses a domain model that assumes that the application domain is static, deterministic, fully controllable, and observable in implicit time (non-temporal) [AG23]. Classical planning formally defines set theoretical representation (“a finite set of propositional symbols intended to represent various propositions about the world.”) in a domain model using first-order predicates and action operations [Chr10]. The assumptions in classical planning reduce the use case of domain models in real-world applications but form good benchmark models. • Temporal planning: The actions defined by the domain model are not instantaneous but require some time unit. Temporal planning is when the non-temporal assumption of classical planning is negated to provide temporal values to actions and interactions between them [AG23][CKMW07]. 20

2.2 Domain Models • Probabilistic planning: Real-world scenarios are often non-deterministic. The same action may not yield the same result. An example can be leaving the house at 6:15 to reach the destinationat6:30onaroutethattakes15minutesgenerallycanchangeonthedaywithtraffic or an accident. Probabilistic planning removes the determinism and assumes a probabilistic distribution over the domain state [KHW95]. • Hierarchical planning: In contrast to traditional classical planning, which generates a plan with a sequence of actions, hierarchical planning creates a Hierarchical Task Network. HTN planning is explained in detail in section 2.1.1 2.2 Domain Models 2.2.1 General components of domain models Every domain model is made of various components and the domain model language used has its own semantics for components. Every domain modeling language has its own set of components but some components remain common across these modeling languages. These components are compiled below. • Types: Types define the category of objects that are used in the planning domain model. Example [GPAA24]: (:types satellite direction instrument mode) • Predicates: Predicates are variables that are used to define relationships between different objects. Predicates are generally used as preconditions to actions and effects. Example [GPAA24]: (on_board ?i - instrument ?s - satellite) • Actions: Action is a component that can be executed to change the state of the world in the domain model. For an action to be performed, certain pre-conditions need to be met. Once an action is performed the effects of the action reflect the change. Example [GPAA24]: (:action put-down :parameters (?x - block) :precondition (holding ?x) :effect (and (not (holding ?x)) (clear ?x) (handempty) (ontable ?x)) ) • Effects: Effects are the changes that update the state of the world as an action is processed. It is generally a sub-component of action. Example [GPAA24]: effect (and (not (holding ?x)) (clear ?x) (handempty) (ontable ?x)) 21

2 Background 2.2.2 Domain languages Domain independent planners, take any compatible domain and problem statement and try to solve it. Due to this reason, the domains need to be standardized to fit the planner. This has given rise to domain languages based on the type of planning. Popular ones are described below. • PDDL: PDDL was introduced in AIPS’98 with the intention of standardizing the domain model and planning problem specification. It expresses domain area using types, predicated, actions (both simple and compound), and effects of performing those actions. Similar to STRIPS formalism explained in Section 2.1.1 of this chapter, many other formalisms are developed. Through the requirements component in PDDL, they can be mentioned and used by AI planning systems that support multiple of them [AHK+98]. PDDL is mainly used for classical planning and its derivatives. • HDDL: HDDL is an extension of PDDL that is developed as a common language for HTN planning domain modeling. The types and predicate definitions remain the same as PDDL, but abstract tasks and decomposition of tasks are introduced in order to create an HTN. Methods to decompose the task based on predicates and parameters also need to be specified [HBB+20]. • HPDL: HPDL similar to HDDL is a PDDL-based language. It was developed earlier than HDDL and boasted to be the first common language for HTN planning domains. In fact, HDDL is a modification of HPDL [GG21]. • RDDL: Relational Dynamic Influence Diagram Language (RDDL) was developed to capture the non-deterministic nature of application domains. The popularity of RDDL stems from its abilitytointegratebothdiscreteandcontinuousscenarios. Otherthanthegeneralcomponent, it additionally has a cost-reward component to reward or penalize an action and static state variable for the application domain that remains constant [ARSJ24]. • NDDL: New Domain Description Language (NDDL) designed by NASA is focused on temporal relationships. The constraints and tasks are not treated as an instantaneous entity but as an interval period. An example of a temporal relationship can be that task A can only be performed after completion of task B. Task B takes X units of time and Y units of energy [McG05][SFC08]. • ANML: Action Notation Modeling Language (ANML) was developed as an alternative to existing domain languages like PDDL. The purpose was to improve user convenience by makingitmorehigh-levelandexpressive. Itsupportstemporalconstraintsanduseskey-value pairs. Both generative and HTN plans can be computed by ANML [SFC08]. 2.3 Value cards A value card is a document that is associated with an entity (an example can be a machine learning model) that provides detailed information about that entity [MWZ+19]. It can be described as a compilation of meta information for a given entity. It records details such as the description of the entity, sources used to derive the entity, parameters of the entity, applications and use cases of the 22

2.3 Value cards entity and ethical and social impact of the entity. The purpose of value cards is mutlifaceted: • Understand the intended use case of the entity and how to use it [MWZ+19]. • Understand the impact of the entity and the effect of its outcomes [MWZ+19]. This helps to improve transparency and accountability. • Compare the performance metric and trade-off between different entities at the same time [SDC+21]. An example of a value card structure can be found in a research paper by Mitchell et al., where the paper outlines potential model card entries for machine learning models to encourage transparent model reporting and specify intended use cases [MWZ+19] described in Figure 2.1. Figure 2.1:ML model card details [MWZ+19] 23

2 Background 2.4 Fairness and Transparency in the field of AI Fairness in AI can be defined as the presence of only non-discriminatory and just algorithms. Technical fairness can be explained using three concepts, “parity, equalized opportunity, and equalized odds” [MD23]. Principles for promoting fairness in AI can be objectified as follows [AOOU24] : • Analysis of the algorithm to identify bias and unfair implications. • Using diverse data during training to avoid targeting certain individuals or groups. • Continuous enhancement of the algorithm or model based on frequent monitoring results. Transparency in AI can be divided into two parts. One can be related to business policies, business intentions, and outcomes. The other part is related to the transparency of AI algorithms implemented. In technical terms, transparency should convert black-box processes to white-box [MD23]. TransparencyforAIcanbeimprovedusingthefollowingprinciples[Men23][BKHK22]: • Improving the explainability of AI algorithms used in a system. • Promote open-source models. • A standardized framework can help users understand AI systems better. 24

Another study evaluates the temporal domain models specifically. The paper investigates and concludes that IPC temporal domains are inherently sequential and their lack of concurrency creates a gap between these domains and domains required for the real world [CWK+07]. Another study with focus on HTN planning, analyses few domains and suggests ways to bring those domain models closer to reality. This can then be extended to other domain models in HTN planning [AGA22]. Eventhough these studies provide frameworks to improve the realistic aspects of planning models, there is no standardized structure to evaluate the domain models for their real-world aspects. 25

4 Value Cards 4.1 Introduction ValueCardforplanningdomainmodelisinformationtoexplainmoreaboutthedomainmodel. The value card design is compact to only include meaningful information for the user. The card also divides information into sections to enhance readability. The objective of this value card is to help the stakeholders of the AI planning system understand the domain model and domain modeling better. 4.2 Sections in value card We propose to have a value card consisting of five sections, namely general overview, basic information, descriptions, model parameters, and real-world score information. Since the amount of details provided by value cards was huge, we divided the entire value card into smaller sections. Each section satisfies a purpose that a user might be interested in. The general overview provides high-level information about the domain. The applicability of the domain is consolidated in the description section and model parameters provide the implementational details. Basic information gives logistics details of the domain while real-world score information explains how the realism of the domain was calculated. In this manner, the group ensures that data points within themselves are tightly coupled and serve a single objective. 4.2.1 General Overview The general overview section holds the information to identify the domain model and some other information that briefly defines the model. The purpose of this section is to hint the reader about the domain model. It consists of six data points. • Model name: The model name is an identifier for the planning domain model. It helps to give a vague idea about the model and its possible use case. Being an identifier, it is a good parameter to search the domain model. • Model language: We define domain model language in Section 2.2.2. Domain model language helps to identify the type of planning the domain model was developed for. It also implies whether the planning domain model was built using standardized language. 31

4 Value Cards • Is the domain model evaluated against a planner?This data points assert whether the developed domain model has undergone at least some preliminary testing. A tested domain model is generally ready to use. If a domain model has been evaluated, then developers of a new AI planning system can use this model to test the correctness and performance of their system. • Ethical consideration: The field of AI planning generates plans that can be followed to achieve the results. This generation of plans needs to be explained in order to understand the ethical impact on society. This field mentions if there are any ethical considerations a user should know when understanding or using the model. If a plan is generated that impacts a particular group of society, it needs to be justified. Example: can certain medical conditions happen only in females and the plan generated therefore is only valid for females. • Parser check: The parser check is a yes/no field that informs whether the domain model has gone through a parser check and passed. A ‘no’ indicates that either the domain model did not undergo a parser check which can be due to non-standardization of the domain model or lack of availability of a parsing tool or it failed the parsing check. • Real-world score: This field outputs a score between 2 to 40. This score is an indication of realistic aspects of the domain model. A score of 2 means the model has very little realism and is close to being a benchmark. As the score approaches 40, the model contains more and more realistic aspects and might be ready for real-world application. The real-world score is calculated using various factors such as physical constraints. Details on those factors are specified in the real-world score information subsection of this section. 4.2.2 Basic information The logistic details of the model are defined here. It provides information about the development of the model and its licensing. The purpose of this section is to get information on where to reach out to for more information about the model and how to use it. It consists of eight fields which are explained below : • Model developer: The individual or team who developed this planning domain model. • Creator date: The date on which this model was first developed. • Last updated: If there were any updates to the model, when was it last modified? It gives the latest state of the model. • Modelversion: Ifthedomainmodelhasbeenupdatedaftercreation,theversionnumberwill determine the amount of updates. This helps to understand what changes were made to the domain model and how it affects it. Versioning of the model might also come in handy to roll back to a previous version in case of a flaw or test all versions of a particular domain model. • License: License is an important aspect of basic information that allows users to understand under which license the planning domain model is published and whether it can be used freely or not. Many domain models are built upon source under GNU license or MIT license which allow them to be used freely. 32

4.2 Sections in value card • Contact details: Where to contact in case of further queries. This can be any text such as email, website, or link to a contact form. The purpose of this field is to strengthen the domain model understanding by bridging the gap between model developer and model user. • Reference document: Many planning domain models developed are also published in research. The reference document holds the citation or link to this article. Apart from the metainformationprovidedbythevaluecard,referencedocumentscanprovideadditionaldata such as motivation, methodology followed by model development, and scope for future work. • Model source: The model source contains the link to the original source file of the domain model if available. It can be a GitHub repo or a remote server. The main purpose of this field is to verify the consistency of the domain model present on the registry and on the source location. It can help to modify/ identify if the source has been updated or modified. 4.2.3 Description • Purpose: The purpose section specifies for what reason the planning domain model was developed. It helps the reader understand the specific problem area the domain model is trying to address. An example can be the ‘navigation of a rover to collect images and soil samples.’ • Use case: A use case describes the scenarios in which planning domain models can be applied. It can be one or more scenario descriptions that briefly explain how the problem on this domain model can be addressed and certain constraints it will not violate. It tries to eliminate the use of domain models for inaccurate solutions. • Category: Category section informs about the real-world category to which the domain model is applicable. The types of categories include logistics, space exploration, robotics, healthcare, game theory, manufacturing, smart building, autonomous vehicles, and others. Some categories in which domain models are developed are mentioned in Chapter 2. Associatingacategorywithadomainmodelalertstheuseroftheideawithwhichthedomain model was developed. The user can thus proceed with caution if the domain model would be used in some other category or used to develop another domain model. 4.2.4 Model parameters • Sub - language: Sub-language specifies the formalism followed by the domain modeling language. In PDDL, this can be specified in the required field. Some commonly used formalisms are STRIPS and Action Description Language (ADL). ADL is an extension of STRIPS to allow more expressive descriptions of actions. • Is the model typed?A typed model has types defined in the planning model. This boolean entry specifies if the model is typed or not. • Number of types: This field specifies the number of types present in the planning domain model if the model is typed. 33

4 Value Cards • Types: If the model is typed and there are ‘n’ number of types then this field mentions all the types that are present in the planning domain model. The purpose of this field is to help readers of the domain model to get more transparency while reading the model contents. • Number of actions: All planning models have executable actions. This field specifies how many actions are present in the planning domain model. • Actions list: This field lists all the actions that can be performed using the domain model along with descriptions of each other. Actions help understand whether the model can be used to solve a particular scenario. An example of an element of an action list is “move: to move the airplane” 4.2.5 Real-world score information The parameters using which the real-world score is calculated are mentioned in the section. The parameters are based on how the planning system can be moved from a simple static state to a more complicated system that resembles closely to real-world applications. With every parameter there is a score associated . Final real-world score is sum of all individual parameter scores. • Temporal: Temporal field specifies whether time constraints are present in the planning domain model. As discussed in the background section, temporal planning extends classical planning by adding time constraints, making it more real-world. Score: +2 if domain model has temporal contraints. • Spatial: Similar to temporal, spatial field checks if the domain model considers space constraints. Alnazer Ebaa and Ilche Georgievski [GPAA24] explain in the framework that the spatial and temporal are physical constraints and can help to understand realistic aspects. Score: +2 if domain model has spatial contraints. • Deterministic: Very few things in the real world are deterministic. If the planning domain model incorporates non-deterministic abilities that reflect the real world, then it brings the model closer to real-world application. Deterministic field specifies whether the model is deterministic or not. Score: +2 if domain model is non-deterministic. • Complicated actions: Actions that can be performed by planning a domain model can be intertwined. Such actions are called complicated actions. These increase the complexity of domain models and get them closer to the real-world state. The field mentions if any complicated actions are present in the domain model. Score: +2 if domain model has complicated actions. • Standard language: For a planning domain model to be used in real-world application, it should be easily integrable which makes it important for the model to be standardized and written in standard language. The field checks for language standards. Score: +2 if domain model is in standard language. • Contradicting predicates: In a few cases, two predicates can contradict each other if certain conditions occur. This makes the domain more vulnerable and less fit for the real world. The value of this field defines the existence or absence of this vulnerability. Score: +2 if domain model does not have contradicting predicates. 34

4.3 Benefits of value cards for planning domain models • Parseable: Parseable field states if the planning domain model can be parsed by available parsing tools or not. A usable domain model should be parsable easily without requiring any modification and thus this value impacts the real-world score. Score: +2 if domain model is parsable. • Scalable: Planning domain models that can be used in real-world applications need to adapt to changing scalability. That means it needs to scale up when required and scale down when necessary. This should happen without any updates to the domain model itself. The field is true if the model is scalable. Score: +2 if domain model is scalable. • Number of simplified actions: Every required action that is manipulated to become simpler, distances the planning domain model from the real-world domain and pushes it to the benchmark domain. This field gives a numeric value for how many actions have been simplified. A value of 0 means the domain model is close to the real-world aspect and with every increasing value it moves towards the benchmark aspect. An example of simplified action is ‘Dropping continuous wait criteria for an entity.’ Score: if n is the number of simplied actions then if n>= 5: +0 else: +(5-n)*4. 4.3 Benefits of value cards for planning domain models • Provides documentation to readers and users to better understand the domain model. It also divides the content to make it easily readable. • Provides the readiness of the domain model using parsing and testing checks. • Provides a real-world score to rate the domain model on a model scale from the benchmark domain to the real-world application domain. 4.4 Sample value card Value card created for the satellite domain model [GPAA24] is defined in Table 4.1 and Table 4.2. 5 System Design Registry for domain model should primarily allow users to publish and view published domain models. System design elaborates on the system components and functionality. It consists of five parts: requirement analysis, architecture diagram, sequence diagrams, database diagrams, and sketches for User Interface (UI). 5.1 Requirement analysis The requirement analysis document specifies the requirements of software system design for the registryofplanningdomainmodels. Thesystemcanbeusedtoperformstorage,retrieval,searching, and managing of domain models. Creation, testing, and complexity evaluation of domain models is out of scope. The requirements gathered are result of literature review on registry platforms mentioned in Section 3.3, discussion with supervisor and professional experience as software developer. System overview The system will serve as a centralized repository for planning domain models, allowing users to store, retrieve, and search these models efficiently. Description and other meta-information about themodelwillalsobemadeavailable. Thesystemwillbecreatedwithservice-orientedarchitecture and Application Programming Interface (API)s will be created to facilitate integration and for inter-process communication. 5.1.1 Functional requirements User requirements: • Users should be able to upload and store planning domain models and value cards for the models. • Users should be able to search for and retrieve value cards for models and then download the models if desired. • Users should be able to apply filters during the search operation. • Users should have certain domain model statistics available to them. System requirements: • Search functionality: The system must offer filter-based and text-based search options based on certain model attributes. 37

5 System Design • Publish functionality: Functionality to publish the domain model in the registry. Within the publish functionality parser check and real-world scoring should be computed. • Parser check: The domain model should be parsed using the appropriate domain definition language to check for the correctness of syntax. • Real-world scoring: The domain model should be scored for realistic aspects and graded between 2 to 40 where 2 means close to a pure benchmark and 40 is almost complete real-world application. • Analytics functionality: Certain analytics need to be compiled for domain models present in the registry. All these analytics should be generated by a service. • Database access service: A service specifically to manage interactions with the database instance. The service needs to form and maintain the connection with the database system, executeStructuredQueryLanguage(SQL)queries,andreturntheresultstothecorresponding caller. 5.1.2 Non-functional requirements • Performance: The system should be able to handle multiple concurrent users. Also caching of data needs to be present for frequently requested data to improve performance. • Scalability: The system should be scalable to accommodate growing data. • Usability: The system should have an intuitive UI that is easy to navigate. All functionalities should be readily available without in-depth findings. • Availability: The system should always be available to users for all functionalities. 5.1.3 Other requirements and assumptions Data requirements: The system will use a relational database to store model data and model meta-data. Valuecardswhicharethemodelmeta-dataareahugeset. Logicalandphysicaldivisions need to be formed for storing and organizing the data. The relational database should also store domain model files. Interface requirements • User interface: The user interface should be web-based, responsive, and user-friendly. • API: The system should provide Representational State Transfer (REST) APIs for integration with other systems. Assumptions • Users have basic knowledge of AI planning systems and planning domain models. • Most of the published domain models should have almost complete value cards. 38

5.2 Architecture 5.2 Architecture The architecture diagram depicted in Figure 5.1 gives the overview of the entire system and the components the system comprises. 6.4 Implementation of business logic Figure 6.7:Web UI: How it works? 6.4 Implementation of business logic Business logic is implemented in the backend server. It consists of 6 components. Each component is provided as a service. Each service has its own controller that accepts API requests and forwards them to appropriate service methods. 6.4.1 Services (server components) Search service: The search service accepts requests related to domain model search and answers them. The search controller processes all requests arriving at the REST API served by the service. The following functions are executed by the search service: • Load domains: Function that loads a small set of parameters for all domain models. The parameters include model name, model language, model category, real-world score, is model typed, is model parsable, and if the model has a citation. These parameters are included as they form the base for search criteria. A Java bean is populated with all these parameters. All domains are stored as a list of these beans. • Search domains: The method takes search criteria as an argument and runs against the loaded domains to form a set of search results domains. • Get domain data: Function that returns the data of the selected domain model. Data for the requested domain model is collected from the database access service. • Get domain model: This function gets triggered when the user wants to download the domain model. The method gets the domain model from the database via a database access service and forwards it to the web UI. Publish service: Service tasked with publishing the domain model submitted through UI. Publish service controller performs the following steps to publish the domain model: 51

6 Implementation • The service selects the correct parser and forwards the model for parsing check. Updates the parser check value. If the parser check fails and the user has selected to not publish the model on check fail, then returns the result object to UI with the appropriate failure message. Else goes to the next step. • Calls the score service to compute the real-world score for the domain model. Updates the score. • Calls the publish service to publish the domain model. If successful, populates success data in the result object else failure data. Returns the result object. Result object: The result object contains the following elements: • Int result: 0 signifies success, anything else means failure. • String message: “Success” if the result is 0, else reason of failure. • String parserCheck: results of parser check. • Int score: computed real-world score (subjective for failed publish). Scoreservice: Aservicetocalculatethereal-worldscoreofadomainmodel. Thescoringservice gets the request from the publish service to compute the score. The request consists of parameters required by the score service to calculate. All parameters are required as explained in the score information section of the value cards chapter. The following calculation algorithm is used: • Base score is set to 2. Say s = 2 • If n is the number of simplified actions then if n < 5: s = s + (5 - n)*4. • If the domain model is non-deterministic: s = s + 2. • If the domain model does not have contradicting predictions: s = s + 2. • For all other parameters that are boolean, a true value per parameter leads to s = s + 2. The highest score achieved by the domain model is 40 indicating high real-world aspects. Similarly, the lowest score achieved is 2 indicating low or no real-world aspects. Parse service: A parser check is performed by the parse service. Parse service consists of an abstract parent class that is inherited by child class implementation that integrates actual parsers for different model languages. Currently, parsers for model language PDDL, HPDL, and HDDL are implemented. The inheritance nature of the parent class makes it easy to extend the parser check functionality. This is implemented using the strategy pattern. PDDL and HDDL parser is implemented using the PDDL4J library [PF18]. This library is implemented in JAVA making it easy to integrate in our application. For the HPDL parser, source code from a research study by Georgievski et al. [GPAA24] developed in Scala is integrated. Scala is compatible with Java as they both run on JVM, which made the process creation of Java ARchive (JAR) file required for integration simple. Analytics service: Analytics generated by this service are managed by a controller. This service implements 2 functions for providing two types of statistics but can be extended to provide more. The 2 statistics provided are in line with the tables displayed on the home page of the web UI. The 2 52

These challenges are related to user-friendly UI, the creation of value cards, and the integration of parsing tools. 1. User-friendly UI Challenge 1: Certain default values in publish form were not intuitive. For example, if a check box is not checked the default value selected would be false. Solution: Replace the checkbox with a yes/no radio button. Challenge 2: Display of value card is a set of continuous key-value pairs making it long and easy to lose track. Solution: Create multiple cards where each card contains related key-value pairs to allow users to focus on the section they are interested in. 2. Creation of value card Challenge: Values for certain entities of value cards are not present in the domain model file. Solution: Find the related literature/research and go through the documentation to find the missing values. 3. Integrating parsing tool Challenge: ParsingtoolsarepresentasJavaandScalacoderepositoriesandarenoteasilyintegrated. Solution: Since both Java and Scala are Java Virtual Machine (JVM)-based, create compatible jars for the parsing tools add them as libraries to the backend codebase, and use their functionality. 54

8 Fairness, Transparency, and Standardization in Domain Models The relevance of fairness, transparency, and standardization in AI planning domain models and the fundamentals to promote them are highlighted in the chapter. The chapter first mentions the interpretation of fairness, transparency, and standardization in planning domain models. The benefits of having these concepts are specified and finally the principles to promote them. These sections altogether argue for these topics with implementation guidelines. 8.1 Definition The definitions for fairness, transparency, and standardization mentioned in relevant work are extended to fit the realm of AI planning domain models. Fairness As defined in Section 2.4, equalized opportunity and equalized odds can be used to explain fairness. In domain models, fairness can be defined asequal opportunity to components that implement the same objectives. For example, instantiating an action A with an object of a particular type T should be equal for all objects relevant to that type and action. In mathematical terms, if P(Oi) is the opportunity probability of object Oi having type T then: 𝑃(𝑂𝑖) = 1𝑛 ∀𝑖 ∈ { 1, . . . , 𝑛} ∧ 𝑂𝑖 is an object of type𝑇 This definition is not restricted to types and actions and can be extended to all components of domain models. Transparency Transparency in AI algorithms means a way for algorithms to explain themselves and make the outcomes apparent [MD23]. Transparency in the domain model can be defined in two parts. The abilitytoexplainallthecomponentsandrelationshipsbetweenthem. Anotherpartistheavailability of resources used to create the domain model for the users of the domain model. Technically, it means to present the domain model as a white-box knowledge entity. Standardization Standardization can be explained in domain models as the availability of common definitions, frameworks, principles, or protocols to develop, maintain, and document AI planning domain models. This is inline with discussion in Section 3.4. 63

8 Fairness, Transparency, and Standardization in Domain Models 8.2 Benefits of fairness, transparency, and standardization In AI planning domain models, the benefits of fairness, transparency, and standardization can be described as follows: • User trust: A fair and transparent domain model helps to improve trust in the users of the domain model. It also promotes the applications that utilize the domain model. • Addressing ethical and legal concerns: Fairness principles analyze and eliminate biased data and targeted attacks [AOOU24]. Due to this reason, it makes it easy to address any concerns in ethics. Transparency gives clarity on domain models and tackles any legal issues. • Avoidmiscommunication: Standardizationandtransparencyinformthereaderofthedomain model and all necessary aspects to avoid any miscommunication. • Building AI planning domain model community: Standardized protocols, development cycles, and frameworks help in forming communities that use and build this standardization. A strong community in turn strengthens the credibility of domain models. Standardized domain modeling languages such as PDDL, HDDL, HPDL, and few others are efforts in this direction. • Research and education: Standard, fair, and transparent practices make analysis of the domain model easier which can be beneficial to identify concerns and shortcomings of the model. Research can then be performed to address them. These principles can be used to provide knowledge training. 8.3 Principles to promote fairness, transparency, and standardization The following principles can be analyzed and implemented to improve fairness, transparency, and standardization in domain models. • Explainability of domain models[AOOU24]: It means to improve the understanding of domain models by adding descriptions to domain models or providing supplementary material. This will improve the transparency of the domain models. One way to implement explainability is through value cards. Detailed information can be found in Chapter 4. • Open sharing of domain models[Men23]: Open sharing implies making domain models open-source and freely available. Open sharing will lead to scrutiny of domain models that identify caveats and ultimately improve the fairness and transparency of those models. It also helps build necessary documentation and makes it available. Implementation involves open-source license and publishing models on popular platforms or domain model registry. • Frameworksfordomainmodeling : Frameworkscanincludegenericdevelopmentprocesses orreusabledevelopmentmaterialfordomainmodeling. KnowledgeEngineeringforPlanning and Scheduling (KEPS) is a branch of AI planning that is trying to determine design process for domain modeling [SSV20]. These frameworks can be used by communities to promote the standardization of the domain modeling process. Standard description languages and value cards can be instances of frameworks. 64

8.3 Principles to promote fairness, transparency, and standardization • Evaluationofdomainmodels [BKHK22]: Domainmodelscanbeevaluatedonmanyfactors such as usability, correctness, performance, etc. Evaluation can improve understanding and therefore affect transparency. A research paper creates a framework that maps the aspects that affect the quality of developed domain model. The parameters that affect the quality of domain model outlined in the paper are modeling language, the domain requirements, interpretation of those requirements, representation of requirements in language, the planner, and the generated plan [VM21]. Tests such as measuring realistic aspects of the model and parsing readiness are a few evaluation methods. • Continuous monitoring[AOOU24]: As the use of domain models increases and it is used in a wide range of applications, continuous monitoring of domain models becomes necessary. This can reveal if certain bias results are generated for particular cases. Fixing these biases improves the fairness of models. • Use of standard terminology: Standard terminology means that a concept definition in the AI planning domain model field has a single term that is used throughout the field. Currently few concepts have multiple terminologies. Example can be domain model and knowledge model mean the same thing in AI planning. This will improve standardization within the field. Usingconferencesandcommunitymeetstosetstandardtechnologiescanensureproper logical outcomes. 65

9 Conclusion and Future Work 9.1 Summary Domain model, an important component of AI planning is addressed in the thesis. The lack of documentation and communication standardization formed the base motivation of this thesis. The thesis developed a framework to improve the explainability of the domain models, developed a central registry for domain models, and suggested principles to promote fairness, transparency, and standardization of AI planning domain models. • Value cards: Value cards are designed as a standardized framework to document the domain model. Itprovidesdetailsaboutreadinessandrealisticaspectsofthedomainmodel. Themain purpose of value cards is to allow the domain model user to understand the characteristics and use case scenarios. A value card is a supporting document that needs to be developed by domain model creators. • Registry for domain model: The registry for domain models acts as a central repository for the storage of domain models. This will bridge the gap between domain model creators not having a standardized publishing guideline and the unavailability of a common platform for domain model readers. The creator also has to enter value card details while publishing, making documentation availability easier. • Principlesto promote fairness, transparency, andstandardization: All threeconcepts are heavily researched in the field of AI and are extended to domain models in this thesis. Along with other measures, the value card is a framework designed to promote standardization and transparency through documentation. Limitations: • ValuecardsaregeneratedforPDDL,HPDL,andHDDLonlyandareassumedtobeextendable to other modeling languages. • Only common components across domain models are specified in the value card section of model parameters. • In the registry application, the parsing service only supports PDDL, HPDL, and HDDL parsers. • Value card is generated based on the information provided by the publisher on the publish page of UI and there is no mechanism to verify it. User evaluation found that completing all fields on publish page is tedious and time consuming. 67

9 Conclusion and Future Work Implications: The outcomes of this research have significant implications for the AI planning field. The standardized value card design and principles provide a solid foundation for documentation and communication of planning domain models. The registry application demonstrates the practical feasibilityofhavingacentralizedrepositoryalongwithmetadata(valuecards)fordomainmodels. 9.2 Future Work While this thesis has made substantial contributions, there are several areas where future research and development could enhance the applicability of domain models and the AI planning field: • Studies on value cards: Future research can validate the usefulness of value cards through user studies. The study can also identify areas of enhancement. • Refinementofreal-worldscorecalculation : Thecurrentscorecalculationalgorithmdefined in Section 6.4.1 considers many physical constraints and a few subjective aspects of the domain model to find the realistic belonging of the model. Refinement can be made in this area to include more aspects to improve the evaluation. The starting point for more aspects cancombinetheachievementsofthisthesisandresearchbyAlnazerandGeorgievski[AG23]. • Additional features to registry application: Software development is a continuous process and even though existing features are well supported, additional features can be implemented. Some features can be derived from the feedback collected during user study. Other features can be related to extending the parsing tool supported, additional search parameters, etc. In conclusion, this thesis has laid a strong starting base for standardization in AI planning domain models. The thesis targets two gaps in research for domain models. One related to the lack of standardized documentation format and proposed value card framework to bridge the gap. Another one related to the unavailability of a common platform for the exchange of domain models and solved by developing a central registry for domain models. 68

tools_for_Debugging.pdf.text: Fixing PDDL Domains Using Delta Debugging Thomas Eckstein, Marco De Bortoli and Gerald Steinbauer-Wagner Institute for Software Technology Graz University of Technology, Graz, Austria e-mail: steinbauer@ist.tugaz.at Abstract Developing planning domains can be a chal- lenging task, because existing planners pro- vide little feedback regarding the correct- ness of the domain and the reasons for fail- ures in planning. In this paper we present an automated approach that can identify faulty preconditions in actions and show a work- ing prototype implementation. Our debug- ger takes a faulty planning domain along with one or more problem instances as in- put. We use the delta debugging algorithm as the basis for our implementation, because it works by creating variations of the code in question and then testing it while essentially treating the interpreter, in our case the plan- ner, as a black box. In our evaluation we in- troduce various errors into a set of selected domains taken from the International Plan- ning Competition. We show that our debug- ger correctly identifies the mistakes in most cases and consistently outperforms a base- line based on brute force search. 1 Introduction The field of AI planning [1] aims to solve plan- ning problems that occur for instance in logistics and robotics by modeling the problem in a declarative lan- guage such as the Planning Domain Definition Lan- guage (PDDL) [2] and developing powerful planners that act as solvers for such problems. Based on an ini- tial situation, the planner has to find a sequence of ac- tions that lead to a specified goal when executed. The planning domain describes how the world may evolve, containing a set of fluents and a set of actions com- prising preconditions and effects modeled using those fluents. The planning problem defines what objects are present, how the world looks like in the beginning and the goal that should be reached. In practice how- ever, developing planning domains can be quite cum- bersome, because there are many mistakes one can make while at the same time receiving little feedback from the planner regarding syntactical or semantical issues. There is a wide variety of planners that use dif- ferent algorithms and may or may not support certain features. 1 To the domain developer, these planners might appear like a black box that often gives nothing more than “no plan found" if there is an issue or runs into a timeout in the worst case. Research in Explain- able AI [3] aims to develop methods to tell the user in an easy to understand way why a complex intelligent system has made a certain decision or has failed. For example, a doctor should know why an expert system suggests a diagnosis based on the given symptoms. In a similar fashion, the user of a planner should re- ceive an explanation why a plan couldn’t be found[4]. There are three main questions that arise when using a planner: 1. No plan can be found given a planning domain and a problem instance. It is certain that the prob- lem instance is modeled correctly or is there an error in the planning domain? 2. Why can’t a plan be found for a problem instance given that the planning domain is modeled cor- rectly? 3. Why did the plan execution fail? In this paper, our goal is to find a way to answer the first of these questions. Using different algorithms, we aim on developing a simple debugger that is able to identify possible errors in a planning domain given that one or more problem instances for that domain are given where it is known that a plan exists. Subse- quently we evaluate our debugger by systematically modifying domains from the International Planning Competition (IPC) and checking how many errors are found by our debugger. Finally, we discuss the ob- tained test results and analyze the performance of the different algorithms tested. 2 Related Work PDDL is a declarative specification language first in- troduced by [2] with a LISP-like syntax that allows de- velopers to model planning domains and problem in- stances. A domain consists of a set of fluents that rep- resents the current state of the world as well as a set of 1https://planning.wiki/ 0

actions that have effects on those fluents. Each action has a precondition that determines in what state that action can be executed. The problem instance con- tains information about which fluents hold in the ini- tial situation and what condition must hold so that the planning goal is met. PDDL is widely accepted in the field of AI planning, as evidenced by the wide range of planners understanding that language. A planner is a program that parses domain and problem files and then tries to find a plan that meets the goal. If successful, the planner outputs the plan as a sequence of actions. Otherwise, the planner returns an error or runs out of time or computational resources. Different planners support various features and versions of PDDL and use different algorithms internally. An existing tool used to debug planning domains is the Plan Validator, developed by [5]. At first the program reads a domain file along with a plan. Then, the validator checks if the plan is executable in respect to the domain. It applies the actions given in the plan to an internal model while keeping track of the state of the fluents along with the actions that are responsible for altering each fluent. Fi- nally, it checks if each action precondition holds and provides a detailed report containing all precondition violations as well as possible explanations for these vi- olations. The Plan Validator can be useful when it is known in advance what the resulting plan should look like. In our scenario however, only the initial situa- tion and the goal are known. With the goal of debug- ging systems too complex to understand in mind, the Delta Debugging algorithm has been proposed by [6]. It isolates failures by simplifying a test case to the bare minimum so that the failure still occurs. For example, the Delta Debugging algorithm has been used to re- duce a large web page that crashes a browser down to a file containing a few HTML tags that still pro- duce the failure. Aside from the Plan Validator, there exist other tools designed to help users in developing PDDL domains. PDDL Studio [7] is a simple IDE that helps the user to write and test PDDL domains. It pro- vides graphical support such as syntax highlighting as well as marking syntactical and semantical errors. An- other small collection of tools for the purpose of aiding PDDL developers is myPDDL, which has been devel- oped by [8]. It contains a syntax highlighting scheme, a script to generate type diagrams from a domain as well as a tool to generate fluent assignments. There is also a PDDL plugin for the widely used editor Vi- sual Studio Code, developed by [9]. It offers syntax highlighting, auto completion, and integration of sev- eral planners. In addition to that, it provides tools from planutils, a collection of other smaller tools for plan- ning maintained by[10]. It could be useful to integrate our debugger into such a tool in the future. 3 Methodology 3.1 Delta Debugging We decide to use the Delta Debugging algorithm first proposed by [11] as the basis of our implementation, because it doesn’t require detailed knowledge of the system that it should debug. The input of the algo- rithm is a program C and a test case test(h) that de- cides whether a hypothesis h ⊆ C passes or fails. The algorithm can be applied to any input program that can be split into multiple fragments, such as lines of code. A diagnosis is obtained by repeatedly generating and testing hypotheses that are generated by systematically omitting or re-adding fragments. The algorithm runs until a set of fragments can be identified that causes the failing of the test case. An empty set of fragments is an empty program, meaning that it passes the test case, such that test() =PASS. The set containing all fragments is the original program that doesn’t pass the test case, such that test(C) =F AIL. Algorithm 1 Iterative version of the min delta debug- ging algorithm. The set of all fragments C is given as input. The algorithm returns the smallest subset of C that still produces the failure. 1: c ← C 2: n ← 2 3: while |c| ≥n do 4: subsets ← getSubsets(c, n) 5: if ∃c′ ∈ subsets : test(c′) = F AILthen 6: c ← c′ 7: n ← 2 8: else if ∃c′ ∈ subsets : test(c \ c′) = F AILthen 9: c ← c \ c′ 10: n ← max (n − 1, 2) 11: else if |c| > nthen 12: n ← min(|c|, 2n) 13: else 14: break 15: end if 16: end while 17: return c There are two variants of the Delta Debugging algo- rithm that were originally described in their recursive forms. The min algorithm finds the smallest set of fragments that need to be present in order to cause a failure, as shown in Algorithm 1. It works by using the set of all fragments C as initial working set c, where test(c) = F AIL. The variable n holds the current level of granularity, which is 2 in the beginning. This means that at first getSubsets(c, n) splits the working set into two disjoint subsets. If it is found that one of those subsets c′ is sufficient to produce the failure, the hypothesis is accepted and the subset shall become the working set, with the granularity being reset to2. Oth- erwise the algorithm checks whether the complement of a subset c′ in respect to the current working setc\c′ produces the failure. In that case, c \ c′ becomes the next working set and the granularity is decremented. If no subset or the complement of a subset is sufficient to produce the failure, the level of granularity is in- creased. The iteration stops if the cardinality of the working set becomes smaller than the granularity. In contrast to the min algorithm, the diff algorithm keeps two working sets where test(cs) = PASS and test(cf ) = F AIL, as shown in Algorithm 2. It aims to minimize the difference cf \ cs. In the original pa- 1

Algorithm 2 Iterative version of the diff delta debug- ging algorithm. The set of all fragments C is given as input. The algorithm minimizes the difference be- tween the failing set cf and the passing set cs. The difference between those sets are the faulty fragments. 1: cs ← ∅ 2: cf ← C 3: n ← 2 4: while |cf \ cs| ≥n do 5: diff ← cf \ cs 6: subsets ← getSubsets(diff , n) 7: if ∃c′ ∈ subsets : test(cs ∪ c′) = F AILthen 8: cf ← cs ∪ c′ 9: n ← 2 10: else if ∃c′ ∈ subsets : test(cf \ c′) = PASS then 11: cs ← cf \ c′ 12: n ← 2 13: else if ∃c′ ∈ subsets : test(cs ∪ c′) = PASS then 14: cs ← cs ∪ c′ 15: n ← max (n − 1, 2) 16: else if ∃c′ ∈ subsets : test(cf \ c′) = F AILthen 17: cf ← cf \ c′ 18: n ← max (n − 1, 2) 19: else if |diff | > nthen 20: n ← min(|diff |, 2n) 21: else 22: break 23: end if 24: end while 25: return cf \ cs per, it is referred to as the general Delta Debugging algorithm. It is able to handle cases where test(h) is neither PASS nor F AIL, which can occur when the hypothesis can’t be tested due to compile errors for example. Such a scenario won’t occur in our setup however, but for the sake of completeness we will test the diff algorithm nonetheless. Additionally, we introduce a third variant of the Delta Debugging algorithm which we call the max algorithm that finds the largest set of fragments where no failure occurs. The code for the max algorithm is shown in Algorithm 3 and resembles the min algorithm in most parts. Unlike the min algorithm it accepts a hypothesis h if test(C \ h) =PASS. The function getSubsets(c, n) is used by all three algorithms and splits the set c into n disjoint subsets of roughly equal size. For example, getSubsets({0, 1, 2, 3, 4}, 3) ={{0, 1}, {2, 3}, {4}}. 3.2 Why planning fails There exist multiple causes why a planner can’t ob- tain a plan for a domain and problem instance. The most common issue is that the domain is correct, but the problem is either not solvable or too complex, re- sulting in a timeout. Using a different planner can also have a significant impact on the result, because they use different search algorithms with specific heuris- tics. Within a domain there may be multiple sources of errors, such as missing action effects, incorrect pre- conditions or the domain being abstracted wrongly. For example, the following excerpt from a PDDL do- Algorithm 3 Iterative version of the max delta debug- ging algorithm. The set of all fragments C is given as input. The algorithm returns the largest subset of C that doesn’t fail. Parts that differ from the min algo- rithm are marked red. 1: c ← C 2: n ← 2 3: while |c| ≥n do 4: subsets ← getSubsets(c, n) 5: if ∃c′ ∈ subsets : test(C \ c′) = PASS then 6: c ← c′ 7: n ← 2 8: else if ∃c′ ∈ subsets : test(C \ (c \ c′)) = PASS then 9: c ← c \ c′ 10: n ← max (n − 1, 2) 11: else if |c| > nthen 12: n ← min(|c|, 2n) 13: else 14: break 15: end if 16: end while 17: return c main contains an error in an action precondition, so that no plan can be found even if the problem instances is solvable. In the domain, a robot can transport items between several places. The robot can carry at most one item at once. Upon closer inspection, it becomes obvious that the line (holding ?i) ; p3 must be deleted to fix the domain, because the robot can’t be empty and hold an item at the same time. stances. We want to obtain a diagnosis without any additional hints or assistance by the user. As of now, we have decided to limit our work to finding faults in preconditions, because removing preconditions leads to a relaxation of the planning domain, increasing the chance that a plan can be found. Finding errors in effects is harder because the debugger would need a good understanding of the domain to identify which effects are needed to reach the planning goal. As shown in the PDDL code above, an action precon- dition P a can be broken down into the conjunction P a0 ∧ P a1 ∧ . . .∧ P an . If the precondition takes another form, such as a disjunction or a single predicate, then P a = P a0 . From now on, we will refer to a single P an as a precondition. In the code above, the preconditions are P take = p0 ∧ p1 ∧ p2 ∧ p3 and P put = p4 ∧ p5, meaning that the two actions have 6 preconditions in total. The Delta Debugging algorithm comes in handy when debugging action preconditions, because we can set C = {p0, p1, p2, p3, p4, p5}. Removing elements from the set results in preconditions being deleted from the domain. To the algorithm, it doesn’t matter how the preconditions are distributed among actions, because it uses the full set of all preconditions as in- put. For example, the hypothesis {p0, p1, p4} gives the following modified domain: ( : a c t i o n t a k e : p a r a m e t e r s ( ? p − P l a c e ? i − Item ) : p r e c o n d i t i o n ( and ( r o b o t − a t ? p ) ; p0 ( r o b o t −empty ) ; p1 ) : e f f e c t ( and ( h o l d i n g ? i ) ( n o t ( r o b o t −empty ) ) ( n o t ( item − a t ? p ? i ) ) ) ) ( : a c t i o n p u t : p a r a m e t e r s ( ? p − P l a c e ? i − Item ) : p r e c o n d i t i o n ( and ( r o b o t − a t ? p ) ; p4 ) : e f f e c t ( and ( n o t ( h o l d i n g ? i ) ) ( r o b o t −empty ) ( item − a t ? p ? i ) ) ) This way the debugger identifies one or more precon- ditions that may contain an error. In our example, the final diagnosis should be {p3}. 3.4 Implementation We develop a prototype that takes an erroneous PDDL domain file and a set of correct problem files as input. The type of Delta Debugging algorithm to be used, the planner to be called along with the timeout can also be configured. As shown in Figure 1, the debugger starts by parsing the domain and then extracting the preconditions. The structure of the domain is stored in a simple syntax tree that holds actions and other def- initions such as fluents or constants. Each precondi- tion gets assigned a unique ID for further processing. The recompiler takes the parsed domain file and a set of preconditions to include as input and generates a new, temporary domain file. Before calling the Delta Debugging algorithm, the debugger tests each prob- lem file against the original domain. All problem files where a plan is found are ignored. If all problem files pass, we assume there is no error and the debugger exits. Additionally, the debugger generates a tempo- rary domain file with no preconditions at all so that h = ∅ and then calls the planner on each problem file. If there is a problem file where no plan is found, it is highly likely that action effects are incorrect and the debugger exits. Otherwise the specified version of the Delta Debugging algorithm is called. The procedure test(h) is passed to the Delta Debugging algorithm and executes the following steps: 1. Obtain a new hypothesis h = {p0, p1, . . . , pn} from the Delta Debugging algorithm. 2. Call the recompiler to generate a temporary do- main file containing only the preconditions ac- cording to the hypothesis. 3. Call the planner. If a plan can be found, the test passes. If no plan can be found or the planner runtime exceeds the given timeout, the test fails. In case there are multiple problem files, the Delta De- bugging algorithm is called once for each problem file, resulting in multiple diagnoses, with each diagnosis consisting of one or more errors. Since each diagno- sis might contain some false positives, returning the union of all diagnoses would even further increase the amount of false positives. Our line of reasoning is that errors that are contained in multiple diagnoses are more likely to be true positives. Hence, our debug- ger counts how often each error is reported. Only the 3 most reported errors are then presented to the user. Algorithm 4 gives a broad overview of the control flow within our implementation. The debugger is written in Java. When called, different arguments can be set, like (1) the algorithm to be used (min, max or diff), (2) the timeout for the planner, and the paths (2) to the domain file and (3) to the problem folder. 4 Evaluation 4.1 Setup In order to evaluate how well our implementation per- forms, we use a set of selected working planning do- mains, introduce errors in those domains, and then check whether our implementation correctly identifies those errors. Instead of coming up with new domains, we decide to use existing domains from the Interna- tional Planning Competition (IPC) [12], as they re- flect typical planning scenarios. The IPC is a recurring event where developers can benchmark their planners and compete with each other. A large repository is 3

Algorithm 4 Proposed Implementation. 1: procedure MAIN (domainFile, problemFiles, algorithm) 2: syntaxTree ← parseDomain(domainFile) 3: allPreconds ← syntaxTree.preconds 4: for problemFile ∈ problemFiles do 5: if test(problemFile, allPreconds) = PASS then 6: remove(problemFiles, problemFile) 7: end if 8: if test(problemFile, {}) = F AILthen 9: return OTHER_ERROR 10: end if 11: end for 12: if is_empty(problemFile) then 13: return NO_ERROR 14: end if 15: diagnosedCount ← {} 16: for precond ∈ allPreconds do 17: append(diagnosedCount, ⟨precond, 0 ⟩) 18: end for 19: for problemFile ∈ problemFiles do 20: currentProblemFile ← problemFile 21: diag ← runDelta(allPreconds, algorithm) 22: for precond ∈ diag do 23: incrementBy1(diagnosedCount, precond) 24: end for 25: end for 26: sortDescending(diagnosedCount) 27: return getF irst3P reconds(diagnosedCount ) 28: end procedure 29: procedure TEST (problemFile, h) 30: compiledDomain ← recompile(syntaxT ree, h) 31: writeFile(temp, compiledDomain) 32: result ← callP lanner(temp, problemF ile) 33: if result = TIMEOUT then 34: return F AIL 35: end if 36: return result 37: end procedure maintained where hundreds of domains from previous competitions are archived. Each domain is accompa- nied by up to a few dozen problem instances. Further- more, we decide to use the Optic planner as the main planner in our evaluation, because it performs well and supports a wide range of features [13]. In order to narrow down the number of domains, we developed a script that calls the Optic planner on each domain and discards all domains that contain unsupported fea- tures or where obtaining a solution takes more than 10 seconds on our machine equipped with an AMD Ryzen 9 5950X and 32GB RAM. In addition to the domains from the IPC, we also include a crafting do- main in our evaluation, since it contains some interest- ing mechanics such as durative actions and functional fluents. It was designed by us for teaching purposes and simulates a simple manufacturing process. This gives a total of 10 domains to be evaluated, described in Table 1. The covered scenarios comprise navigation in grids, controlling rovers and satellites, logistics, or board games. In our evaluation, we consider 5 differ- ent types of errors that can occur in preconditions of planning domains, as listed in Table 2. These errors break the domain so that the planner is unable to ob- tain a plan for some of the problem instances. It is still possible that the fault does not affect the solving of a simpler problem that does not utilize all actions. Each testcase is then solved with the three variants of the Delta De- bugging algorithm (min, max and diff) with a timeout of 1 second or 10 seconds, resulting in a total of 900 test runs. The execution of the tests is fully automated using a script. We decide to use a timeout of 10 sec- onds, because for the domains we have selected for this evaluation, the planner usually finds a plan within that time. Additionally we want to run our tests with a timeout of 1 second, because we expect that it will increase the rate of timeouts and will thus negatively affect the quality of the results. The test script logs the total number of planner runs r and how often the plan- ner fails. The planner can fail because either a timeout occurs (counted as cto) or it reports that the problem is unsolvable (counted as cu). Among the reported erro- neous preconditions, the script documents the number of true positives, false positives and false negatives. 4.2 Results Since the full dataset of test results contains 900 rows, we decide to summarize the results within a few ta- bles and compare the performance of the different al- gorithms, timeouts and error types. Each domain has a set of preconditions P and the subset Pe of faulty preconditions with n = |Pe|. Our debugger returns a diagnosis, which is the set Pd. As evident from the results in Table 3, the max al- gorithm has the highest chance to correctly identify faulty preconditions, correctly diagnosing at least one error in 82% of testcases. The min algorithm in con- trast does the worst at 57%, with the diff algorithm doing slightly better at 64%. Both the min and max al- gorithm need about the same number of planner calls, while the diff algorithm does less than half and re- quires the least runtime as a consequence. However, there is a strong difference in runtime between the min and max algorithm. This is because the min algorithm attempts to construct a domain as simple as possi- ble that produces the failure, while the max algorithm builds a domain as complex as possible that does not fail. It is reasonable that more complex domains typ- ically require more computational power, effectively increasing the runtime as well as the number of time- outs. tσ[s] in relation to tµ[s] is fairly high, meaning that the runtime of the debugger depends mostly on the complexity of each individual testcase. Lowering the timeout from 10s to 1s has a relatively low impact on the quality of the results, while drastically improving the runtime of the debugger. As expected, the number of timeouts is higher when the timeout is lower. In our case, a timeout of 1s still gives good results because the domains and problems chosen for this evaluation can mostly be solved in less than a second. The max algorithm has the lowest number of timeouts among failures. As we aim to use the debugger online while developing domains, response time of the debugger matters. The chance of finding at least one error is higher when two errors are present, as shown in Table 4. In the min and diff algorithms, the runtime and number of plan- ner calls do not show much variation depending on the error type. The max algorithm however makes less than half of calls when there is one error instead of two. When considering just the max algorithm, test- cases with additional preconditions take longer pro- cessing time than ones with modified preconditions. This is because each additional precondition increases the number of total preconditions, thus increasing the number of combinations the Delta Debugging algo- rithm has to test. The error types AA, MM and AM require a higher number of planner runs than A and M, because unlike the min or diff algorithms, the max algorithm attempts to find all errors present instead of stopping when one error is found. Furthermore, it seems easier to identify additional preconditions than modified ones. When comparing the different domains in Table 5, we find that the max algorithm gives the best results in all of them. Other than that, the diff algorithm performs better than the min algorithm in most domains. There is plenty of variation regarding the runtime among do- mains, which can be explained by the varying com- plexity of the domains. The simplest domain is ar- guably 1998-griper-round1-adl with only 6 precondi- tions, resulting in an average runtime of 23 seconds and a very low timeout rate. dn is highest among all domains and f pµ is the lowest. A more challenging domain is 1998-mystery-prime-round-1-strips, taking an average of 117 seconds and having a high timeout rate. Consequently, d1 and dn are lower while f pµ is high. The number of planner calls is well below the number of tries it would take to find an error by brute force in all domains. 5 Conclusion Our goal was to debug planning domains with min- imum user interaction. In our use case, the domain developer provides a broken planning domain along with one or more problem instances to the debugger. We started by discussing the problems surrounding this task and limited the scope of our research to find- ing errors in the action preconditions. Then we ex- plained how planning domains can be debugged using the Delta Debugging algorithm. In addition to the two already existing variants of this algorithm, min and diff, we proposed a third variant called max. Sub- sequently we developed a prototype that implements all three variants of the Delta Debugging algorithm and can interact with a planner. It systematically al- ters the planning domain until one or more faulty pre- conditions can be identified. After that, we performed a large number of tests where we introduced differ- ent kinds of errors to publicly available domains and checked how well our debugger can find those errors.
